chapters.title: Chapter 651
paragraphs: There are plenty of things in this world that suspicion alone can’t settle.
That’s true of the twenty-first century I’d lived in all my life, and just as true of Murim, which might as well be lawless by comparison.
Especially when the person in question stands second only to one man and above ten thousand others in the vast land of Nanman.
But...
—Great Chieftain Baeksang has colluded with Dark Heaven.
Well, that changed things.
I set down the chopsticks I’d snapped without realizing it. The old stall owner grumbled at the sight, but all my attention was on Heugung.
—Are you certain?
—I am. No... at least, I believe I am.
What?
I barely stopped myself from frowning.
—That sounds like you have no concrete evidence. “I believe I am” isn’t enough for this. You have to be certain.
—B-but...
Heugung swallowed hard before continuing his Sound Transmission.
—This is the best I can tell you. Great Chieftain Baeksang keeps that many secrets. I lead one of Nanman’s four great tribes myself, but... he never discusses anything important with me in depth.
It lasted only an instant, but I caught the emotion that crossed his face at those last words. It was unmistakably humiliation.
Perhaps it had been piling up inside him for a very long time.
I studied him, then moved my lips.
—Is that why?
—Why? What do you mean?
—Is that why you betrayed the man you followed, sent me a secret missive, and told me all this? Because of how you feel about Baeksang?
—B-betrayed him? That’s...
—If this isn’t betrayal, then I’m not Han Chinese—I’m from Nanman. Don’t bother denying it.
As if I had hit the mark, Heugung bit his lip hard and gave a small nod.

—Fine. I won’t deny it. Ever since my father died in the Great Faction War, I’ve lived under Great Chieftain Baeksang’s shadow. I was a runny-nosed child then, and I’m still under it now. No—I should say he’s dragged me around on an invisible leash. But that isn’t the only reason I decided to meet you.
—Then what is?
—I want to protect Nanman. My people.

—The Great Chieftain Baeksang I’ve known has always been coolheaded and capable. That’s why he’ll never back down. He’ll believe the choice he made was right. But if this goes on... Nanman is finished.
I silently stared at Heugung.
How much of this secret conversation at a little stall on a crowded street was I supposed to believe?
Can I trust him?
My doubts weren’t limited to what he’d told me. They extended to Heugung himself, who had suddenly arranged this secret meeting.
In some ways, trusting him mattered more than anything else. If I couldn’t do that, how could I trust the details he hadn’t told me yet?
He’s seemed sincere so far. But what if it’s all an act?

Murim was a fierce, unpredictable place. Heroes, Third Rate thugs, fiends, hypocrites—every kind of person was mixed together, deceiving and being deceived, drawing hidden blades to stab one another in the back.
Nothing would surprise me here.
As I weighed the situation, the old stall owner broke the silence.
Clack.
Setting down the bowl seemed to take all his strength. His hand trembled, and broth spilled over the rim.
The cheap somyeon, worth only a few iron coins, lay tangled in the bowl. Rather like the thoughts in my head.
“Finally. Try the broth first. That’s the best part.”
Heugung tried to sound cheerful, but his eyes darted around the street.
—Be careful. Great Chieftain Baeksang has eyes and ears you won’t see. I need to return within half an hour if I’m to avoid suspicion.
—Did you slip away while you were with him?
—No. But there’s always someone nearby watching me. A plant put in place long ago to track my movements. Today should be safe, though.
He didn’t name the person who’d planted that watcher. He didn’t have to.
Baeksang.
Sitting there staring at steaming somyeon would only attract attention. I started eating and sent another Sound Transmission.
—How long have you been watched?

—I don’t know. I first noticed it around the time I came of age. I’ve been wary of Great Chieftain Baeksang for more than twenty years since. That’s why I secretly learned the Bone-Shrinking Technique. It’s difficult to master, but unlike other martial arts, the training leaves almost no trace.
I had to revise my opinion of him.
Not bad.
It was ridiculous for me to judge a man well past forty like that, but he was nothing like the fool who’d been grinning at everyone a few hours ago.
So he found his own way to survive.
His sudden approach still gave me reason to be suspicious. But the more I heard, the more I believed him. The somyeon tasting far better than I’d expected probably helped, too.
Slurp.
I finished the rich broth, took a few iron coins from my robes, and set them beside the empty bowl. Then I stood and patted Heugung’s shoulder. He looked startled.
“You were right. The broth here is good.”
“I-I’m glad you liked it. But where are you going...?”
“Why? I’ve eaten, so it’s time to get moving. You look like you’ve got somewhere to be, too. Don’t you?”
His eyes widened slightly. He must have heard the Sound Transmission I’d sent along with the words.
—Follow me. Slowly. Keep your distance.
The somyeon had taken care of the appetizer. Now for the main course.
—Tell me everything you’ve seen and heard at Baeksang’s side.
The street was so crowded there was barely room to walk.

Heugung and I slipped into the throng and moved slowly, keeping about ten feet between us. Now and then we watched fireworks burst overhead or turned our heads to look along the street. Our Sound Transmissions, though, stayed fixed on one subject.
—Let me get straight to it. Have you seen anything that points to Baeksang colluding with Dark Heaven?
—I have no concrete evidence. But from what I’ve observed, I’m certain of it.
—Without evidence, that isn’t enough.
—I couldn’t help it. Until now, I’ve lived like livestock inside a fence Great Chieftain Baeksang built around me.
—Then when did you begin to suspect him, and why?

—Being raised inside a fence didn’t mean I could never look outside it. I may lead the Yi people in name only, but I’m still their great chieftain. I was occasionally present when Baeksang met with others. Or perhaps he simply thought I wasn’t worth worrying about. He wouldn’t have been wrong.
His Sound Transmission took on a self-mocking edge.
—Do you know what sort of man Great Chieftain Baeksang is? Or what you know of the Bai people?
—I don’t know much about Nanman, but I’ve heard various things from a reliable source. I’ve also formed a certain judgment of Baeksang myself.
—An opinion. Interesting.
—What’s interesting about it?
—Simple. I’ve known him since I was very young, yet I’ve had to revise my opinion of him again and again. The older I got and the more I understood, the more often it happened.
—That’s the kind of man he is. Dense forests, deep swamps, every sort of treacherous ground—this land doesn’t let secrets escape. For instance...
He trailed off.
The next moment, I felt someone’s gaze and turned my head. Heugung’s eyes met mine, shining brightly.
—The finest Bai warriors, waiting for the right moment in a secret refuge somewhere in Nanman even now.
My feet stopped before I could help it. I turned toward a nearby stall as naturally as I could and moved my lips.
—Go on.

—Have I told you about my father? He was a respected great chieftain and an outstanding warrior. The loyal men who followed him helped me at the cost of their lives. Their sacrifice is how I learned of that refuge.
—Do you know exactly where it is?
—I did. Twenty years ago.
—...Twenty years ago?

—The only thing that came back that day was a messenger pigeon carrying a missive written in blood. None of my father’s men returned. A few days later, I went to the location in the message, using a hunt for ferocious beasts as my excuse. I saw the mountain engulfed in flames before I even reached its foot.
—The fire burned for a month and seven days. When it finally died, nothing remained but ashes. Strange, isn’t it?
His Sound Transmission turned bitter.

—Every time one of my loyal retainers died, I learned something new. Great Chieftain Baeksang exchanges missives to unknown destinations on the first day of every month, between Insi and the hour of the Rabbit. He also disappears somewhere alone once every three months... Ah, since last year, that changed to once a month. The person who followed him then was the last subordinate I could trust. I never saw him again after that.
A heavy silence settled between us.
All around us, people chatted and cheered. Heugung and I didn’t join them.
Baeksang and Dark Heaven. Dark Heaven and Baeksang. And...
Heugung.
Which parts were true? Which were lies?
My thoughts were hazy, as though I had been swallowed by Poison Mist.
Yet beyond that haze, I could still make out the figure I’d followed with my eyes and thoughts from the beginning.
Baeksang.
And then there was someone else who had yet to appear.
A name came to mind. I sent Heugung another Sound Transmission.
—What about the other person?
—Other person? Who?
—The other great chieftain. Yohi.
—I’ve been wondering why you haven’t said a word about her.
Through the passing crowd, I saw his gaunt frame jerk. His gaze met mine, trembling faintly.
—She hasn’t done anything wrong.
—What?
—She only made the wrong choice. All she wanted was to restore the Yao people...
His voice gradually faded.
I blinked blankly at Heugung, and the back of my head began to tingle.
Fuck. Don’t tell me...
—Wait. That wasn’t an act? You really like Yohi?
—I don’t like her. I love her.
—Sorry, but are you out of your fucking mind?
This was driving me crazy.
I had suspected as much, but all those foolish grins whenever Yohi appeared had really been genuine.
He had even put up a soul shield strong enough to make Magic Johnson cry.
I barely managed to restrain myself from pushing through the crowd and marching over to him. Instead, I sent a Sound Transmission that was almost a shout.
—Would you say that in front of Sir Yayul, too? That Yohi did nothing wrong?
—That’s why I came to you. First, I didn’t think the Palace Lord would trust me over Great Chieftain Baeksang. Second, I thought he wouldn’t forgive our Yohi.
—Wow. Listen to this “our Yohi” bullshit.
—Ah, sorry. But you really are an idiot. Anyway, I understand now. Your Yohi defected to that side.
Heugung’s face stiffened at my choice of words. He opened his mouth as if to object, then sighed.
—I made up my mind before coming here. If you and the Palace Lord want me to, I’ll testify at tomorrow’s Tribal Grand Council. But you must promise to protect both Yohi and me.
The first offer was good. The second sat badly with me.

Neither was mine to accept on the spot. Protecting Heugung was one thing; protecting Yohi would practically mean pardoning a defector. I wasn’t Syngman Rhee taking in pro-Japanese collaborators. How could I decide that alone? At best, I was the U.N. forces.
But if the Beast Miao King agrees...
If Heugung’s words were true, we could not only root out Dark Heaven’s threat from Nanman, but might even drag the Nanman Beast Palace into the Murim Alliance as one enormous headache.
If he was telling the truth.
—This had better be true. Every word.
Fsssh!
I sent a wave of qi bearing down on Heugung alone. His face went pale under the force of it, and his lips moved.
—My life. I stake my life on it.
I held his gaze a moment longer, then withdrew my aura.
He stood panting, glanced around, gave a small nod, and disappeared into the crowd. The half hour he’d warned me about had passed.
“...Phew.”
Only then did I take a full breath and start walking. Before I told the Beast Miao King, I wanted to stop at our quarters and talk it over with the Fire Dragon Pavilion members.
Those damn men. I’ll consider it a success if they haven’t caused any trouble.
Sama Pyo had come out to the clearing in front of the quarters to train when a thought occurred to him.
Was he simply born unlucky, or had the karma from that damn Pavilion Master’s misdeeds flowed all the way here like a stream?
“So let me ask you.”
Shing.
The Black Dragon Saber slid free with a cold ring. Sama Pyo stepped forward, his favored weapon in hand.
“What do you lot think?”
Rustle.
The grass around the clearing shook.

chapters.title: Chapter 652
paragraphs: Rustle.
Sama Pyo knew it wasn’t a passing breeze stirring the thick grass.
The killing intent of dozens of enemies pointed at him like invisible blades.
“You show up uninvited, and when I ask a question, you don’t answer...”
Unwelcome guests didn’t get much worse than this.
He clicked his tongue and let his Black Dragon Saber hang at his side.
“Come out. We can at least talk face-to-face.”
A dozen or so throwing blades came in reply.
Whoosh! Clang!
Sama Pyo knocked them aside with a lightning-fast swing of his saber and turned smoothly on his heel. Saber energy wrapped around the dark blade, then swept through the grass like a gale.
Sh-sh-sh-shk! Slash!
Hundreds of leaves flew apart in pieces. A faint line appeared across the trunk of a massive tree.
Sss, crash!
The giant tree slid to the ground. Sama Pyo vaulted over it and stared at the figures approaching the clearing.
East, west, north, south. Roughly thirty enemies moved slowly into position around the pavilion. Every one of them wore a black mask.
“Hard to get a look at your faces. When you come uninvited, the polite thing would be to take off your masks and apologize... but I doubt you’re going to do that.”
Sama Pyo took stock of the situation calmly.
Masked intruders at this hour of the night, greeting him with throwing blades. Their purpose could hardly have been clearer.
Worse...
Of all times, this had to happen while he was away.
He thought of that Pavilion Master bastard, with a mouth as foul as a Third Rate thug’s and a habit of punching someone whenever the chance arose.
Jin Taekyung.

The man was impossible to predict and forever causing trouble. But in a situation like this, there was no one Sama Pyo would trust more. At only twenty-two, he had already left his mark on Murim—a monster of a man.

But whether by coincidence or fate, Jin Taekyung was currently away. Song Ilseom and Ju Hwaran, who would have been a great help if they had remained, were absent as well. Hyuk Mujin was gone, too—although he might not have been able to match them, he was at least worth one person.
That left Sama Pyo, Taishan—who had gone to bed early—and Namho, an ordinary old man against whom Sama Pyo couldn’t use his full strength.
Against nearly thirty enemies.
No. Their numbers aren’t the problem.

Sama Pyo muttered inwardly and quickly swept his gaze across the surroundings. The killing intent radiating from the enemies slowly tightening around him like a net was not that of some clumsy martial artists.
By Central Plains standards, each of them is somewhere between Supreme First Rate and Peak. Where in Nanman did they come from?
The Central Plains Murim was truly vast, but even among the countless martial artists scattered across it like grains of sand on a beach, Peak masters were not common.
Yet in Nanman, which could not compare to the Central Plains, someone had mobilized thirty warriors of this caliber to launch an attack.

Fortunately, none seemed to be at a particularly high level. Still, their presence was startling—especially because this remote stretch of land belonged to the Inner Palace of the Nanman Beast Palace.
“Who are you?”
Whoosh! Crack!
Instead of an answer, a short spear skimmed past his neck and smashed through the pavilion door.
That was the signal to begin.
Papapat!
Hidden weapons and arrows flew in, blotting out the faint moonlight. Shadows rushed forward like streaks of light.
Sama Pyo’s Black Dragon Saber cut through the wind.
Whiiiiing! Slash!
Powerful saber energy swept the projectiles aside. The instant he broke through the barrage, blades lunged for him from left and right.
Whoosh!
Neither attacker hesitated to strike at his vitals. Their movements were timed perfectly together. An ordinary Peak master would have been badly wounded, if not killed.
But Sama Pyo was no ordinary Peak master.
He was not a young prodigy lacking real combat experience, nor was he as rigid as a Peak master from an orthodox faction.
Above all else, demonic, heterodox arts valued survival.
Click, crunch!
The two Peak masters attacking from either side crumpled like rotten trees.
Their eyes stared wide above their masks. A small arrow, a span long, was buried deep between each man’s brows.
It worked.
There was a simple reason Sama Pyo wore a thin robe instead of a lighter martial uniform in this heat: its full sleeves gave him room to hide weapons.
Twist his wrist to the right angle, and the mechanism fired a loaded arrow. It was simple, but against an enemy who didn’t expect it, few things were deadlier.
“Idiots.”
He pulled the falling bodies toward him and held one in front of himself, the other behind.
Thud-thud-thud!

A fresh volley of hidden weapons struck the men who had been the attackers’ allies moments before, riddling their corpses. From behind his makeshift shields, Sama Pyo aimed his sleeve past the side of one body.
Click, thud!
This time, the enemy knew what to watch for. The arrow struck a forearm instead of the space between the brows he had aimed for.
He had shown them the trick twice. It wouldn’t work again.
Then...
Snap.
Sama Pyo made his decision at once. He released the mechanism hidden in his sleeve and charged, shouting as he went.
“Taishan!”
Sh-sh-sh-shk!
The remaining twenty-seven masked men closed around him like wolves.
Bang!
Namho had finally fallen asleep after a long stretch of tossing and turning. The instant he opened his eyes, one thought came to him.
What fucking bastard is this?
Growing old came with no end of indignities. One of the cruelest was how little sleep he got at night.
And now someone had dared to disturb what sleep this eighty-year-old could manage. His joints creaked as he sat up.
If that gluttonous bastard Taishan woke me up because he was eating a midnight snack... this time, I absolutely will not let it slide.

He had spent fifty years in the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, whatever anyone might think to look at him. After everything he had sacrificed during the Great Faction War, the Thousand-Faced Fox might overlook it just this once if Namho wrote to Henan and had Taishan declared an enemy of Murim.
Would he believe me if I said the bastard worked for Dark Heaven?
The thought vanished when he heard the commotion outside.
“Taishan!”
Sh-sh-sh-shk! Clang!
Cha-cha-cha-chang!
Namho stared down at the clearing through the window. He rubbed his eyes, wondering if he was seeing things.
He wasn’t. An enemy’s Sword Energy, dodged by Sama Pyo, swept past Namho’s window.
Slash! Crash!
At last, he understood.
An ambush!
A planned one, too. They had struck while that madman—no, while Jin Taekyung—was away.
What the hell is going on? Who would...?
Being woken up no longer bothered him. In a moment, he might lose his head instead of his sleep.
Sama Pyo was fighting better than Namho had expected, but he couldn’t hold out against so many enemies forever.
And then—
Papapat!
When Namho spotted several masked men approaching the pavilion while leaving Sama Pyo behind, he no longer had even a moment to hesitate.
“Gah!”
Namho bolted from his room with a speed that belied his eighty years. He raced down the corridor and flung open the door at its end.
Bang!
“Ambush! We’re under attack! Your lord is outside—!”
Taishan, the room’s occupant, answered with a mighty roar.
“Grrrrrrrk. Hooooooonk!”
“You damn bastard!”
“Guh-hoooooonk!”
Namho couldn’t believe it.
He can sleep through this? Is he even human?
Parts of the pavilion were breaking apart. The clash of weapons was loud enough to be heard in Henan. Yet here Taishan lay inside it, snoring.
“You! Wake up this instant!”
Thud! Thud-thud!
With a soul-rending cry, Namho’s fist—its strength diminished by the passing years—slammed into Taishan’s jaw.
As though heaven had been moved by his efforts, Taishan finally stirred.
“Mmm. Taishan...”
“Yes! Get up! Hurry!”
“Mmmm. Don’t like mosquitoes. Go away...”
“You son of a bitch!”
It came out almost as a wail.
Tears were gathering in Namho’s eyes when a dark shadow fell across the floor in the moonlight streaming through the open window.
He froze.
Slowly, he turned his head. Three masked men had slipped into the pavilion.
Those... those bastards.
They moved like ghosts. Their weapons flashed white in the moonlight, and Namho’s eighty-odd years rushed before his eyes.
Then he realized there was one way to wake Taishan.
“Taishan! You bastard!”
Sss.
The masked men raised their weapons as Namho shouted. Thinking of death, Namho squeezed his eyes shut and continued yelling.
“They’re going to eat all your meat!”
In the next instant—
“No! Taishan’s meat!”
Taishan’s eyes flew open as if by magic. He thrust a fist toward the masked men.
Wham! Krrrra-boom!
Hoo. Hah.
Sama Pyo fought to steady his breathing.
Blood soaked his upper body. The masked men watching him now had a trace of fear in their eyes.
He had fought more fiercely and brutally than they had imagined, with hidden weapons and poisons concealed all over his body and martial arts honed for one purpose: killing.
More frightening still, he showed no fear of death.
“Come on, any of you. I swear I’ll give everything I have to kill you.”
He charged them, panting, covered in blood. One by one, masked men fell beneath his hands.
Twenty bodies lay scattered across the ground. Seven of them belonged to Peak masters who would have been recognized anywhere in the Central Plains.
What a monster.
The same thought struck the masked men at once.
“No! Taishan’s meat!”
Crack! Krrrra-boom!
A real monster burst out of the collapsing pavilion.
Eight cheok tall, with an enormous frame. And...
“Taishan’s meat! Where’s the meat?”
A madness that seemed to belong to another world.
Gulp.
What the hell is that?
As the masked men swallowed hard, a small old man poked his head out from behind the giant and pointed at them.
“See those men?”
“Taishan sees them!”
“I saw everything earlier, and those bastards ate all your meat.”
“Taishaaaaaan! Cannot forgive them!”
What meat? What were they supposed to have stolen and eaten?
The bewildered masked men faltered. Sama Pyo bared his bloodstained teeth in a grin.
But he wasn’t looking at Taishan. He was looking at the hill above the clearing—or, rather, at someone ambling down it.
“I had a feeling this might happen even while I was away for a little while.”
Step. Step.
Jin Taekyung approached at an easy pace and asked Sama Pyo, “Are those your friends?”
Sama Pyo burst out laughing and shook his head.

The killing intent of dozens of enemies pointed at him like invisible blades.

chapters.title: Chapter 653
paragraphs: “Are those your friends?”
Sama Pyo laughed aloud before answering in a weary voice.
“As if.”
“Yeah, you do seem to be on pretty bad terms for friends.”
I scratched my chin and slowly looked around.
The already ancient pavilion had collapsed. Blood stained the weeds that grew thick across the clearing.
All right. Situation assessed.
What a complete fucking mess.

I’d only been away from our quarters a little while, and now there were some twenty corpses to clean up. We could have used a snail bride to handle that. Instead, we’d gotten snail assassins in the middle of the night.
I glanced at the assassins who had faltered when I appeared, then shrugged at Sama Pyo.
“Oh, you’re better than I thought.”
Blood drenched his upper body. He answered between ragged breaths.
“Yeah, I’m not bad. For an unorthodox goon.”
Honestly, I was starting to feel bad calling him that. He’d been badly outnumbered by skilled enemies, and fighting this hard against them meant he’d truly put his life on the line.
Impressed, I nodded.
“You’ve done enough that I can’t keep calling you an unorthodox goon... From now on, you’re an unorthodox hardcase.”
“An unorthodox hardcase. How kind of you.”
“Oh, you’re grateful? That’s a surprise. I thought you’d start cursing me as soon as you heard it.”
“Cursing takes energy. I’m about to collapse, so stop talking to me.”
His honesty drew a quiet laugh from me.
“Then collapse.”
“What?”
“I said collapse. Don’t worry about the rest.”
“Damn it. You could’ve said that sooner...”
His words trailed off as his eyes began to close. At the same time, Sama Pyo’s body slowly tilted to the side, and I stepped toward him.
Whoosh. Thud.
The three-zhang gap vanished in an instant.
Just as I caught him before he could pitch face-first into the ground, a sharp whistle split the air and wind whipped up behind me.
Whoosh!
It happened behind me, but I could see it. No—I could sense and read everything through my sharpened instincts.
Now that I’d stepped into this space, it was practically my domain.
Crack!
Without turning, I threw a punch. Something shattered beneath my fist, and a masked man with his head crushed like tofu fell into a pool of blood.
Splash.
Sticky blood sprayed across my back. Ignoring it, I laid Sama Pyo on a relatively clean patch of ground and raised my head.
The masked men stood frozen like stone statues.
“Why are you just standing there? That was pretty much your last chance.”
“What’s so surprising? Were you planning to ding-dong ditch me, you fucking bastards?”
In the suffocating silence, the more than ten pairs of eyes visible above the masks shook violently.
Papap!
Whiiiiing!
A gale far fiercer than the first swept out in every direction.

Every masked man still standing was a Peak Master capable of injuring others with Sword Energy. Swords, sabers, spears, sickles... Destructive qi surged from their weapons, tearing through the air toward the vital points across my body.
I watched it all without the slightest fear.
The flow of qi. The direction of each weapon.
Even the faint fear in their wide eyes.
That settled it. They had already lost. They knew they were no more than wolves, yet they refused to accept it and charged at a tiger anyway.
Then I’d better teach them. Teach them that they should have run somehow.
Dozens of forms flashed through my mind. I chose the cruelest, most destructive one and moved.
Whoosh! Crunch!
I twisted smoothly aside. Four weapons missed me by a hair and tangled together as their paths crossed. I brought my straightened hand down through their center.
Slash!
Force cut the weapons apart. I struck one of the masked men in the abdomen as he stood frozen, still gripping what remained of his prized weapon.
Flame Divine Palm.
Boom!
Terrible heat burned away the life force inside his body. I lowered my head as he crumpled behind me, smoke pouring from his seven apertures.
Shaaak! Whoosh!
A strike had come from behind without warning. The long sickle meant to reap my neck swept through empty air, while my backward-thrust elbow struck its wielder square in the chest.
Crack!
More than a dozen ribs broke. He gave a dying gasp.
But my blow wasn’t what killed him. His comrade’s spear did.
Thrust!
Look at these bastards. Not a shred of comradeship.
Clicking my tongue, I seized the spearhead jutting from his chest and squeezed.
Crack!
He was a Peak Master who had reached the level of injuring others with Sword Energy. I was a Supreme Peak master who had entered the realm of Sword Energy Becoming Force.
I snapped the spearhead off as easily as a wooden chopstick and returned it to its owner.
Whoosh! Thunk!

The result was instant death. The spearhead lodged between the masked man’s brows, and he collapsed without a scream. His comrades swallowed their gasps. Three of them had died in less time than it took to call it a moment.
Seven left.
I counted them calmly and took a step.
Whoosh!
Space vanished with the wind, and another enemy appeared right in front of me. No—I was the one who had reached him.
His wide eyes seemed to be trying to say something. Too late. I tightened my grip around his neck.
Crack!
Six.
I felt the life leave him as his body went limp. I took the sword from his hand and hurled it at the nearest enemy.
“Hng!”
With a panicked gasp, the man raised his curved moon saber diagonally. My sword flew straight into the saber, which was charged with saber qi.
Boom!
The ground heaved with a deafening roar. A staggering figure emerged from the billowing dust.
The moon saber had shattered against the qi in my sword. Dozens of fragments were embedded across its wielder’s body.
“Grrk. Grrr...”
Thud.
The largest fragment was lodged in his throat. Perhaps that was why he fell without even managing a last word, blood bubbling in his throat.
I pushed aside the corpse with the broken neck and spoke quietly.
“Five left.”
I could feel the fear filling the suffocating silence. Five Peak Masters had fallen in mere moments, and I didn’t have a scratch on me as I looked for my next target.
“Who’s next?”
No one answered.
Then the masked men, frozen in place and staring at me with eyes wide as if they had seen a ghost, chose to target someone else instead of me.
Papap!
Of the five, three went for me. The other two went for Namho and Taishan.
I had to admit, it was probably the best choice they could make. That didn’t mean it would end well for them.
“I saw it with my own eyes! Those bastards ate both chicken legs!”
“Legs? Not wings—legs? Both of them?”
Taishan blinked at Namho in disbelief, then drew the two-section staff from his side.
“Both chicken legs! Too far! You’re not human!”
We’d have needed a vote to settle who wasn’t human, but Taishan made voting irrelevant with his enormous two-section staff.
Wham! Crack!

His innate divine strength was enough to make a defense useless. One masked man instinctively raised his sword to block the staff. Both his wrists broke, and before he could scream, Taishan smashed his head along with the other man’s.
Crack!
The two bodies hit the ground without so much as a dying cry.
From behind Taishan, Namho clenched a fist and shouted, “That’s it! You commendable bastard, I could kill you!”
“Uaaaaaah! Taishan is commendable!”
“Well done, you goddamn bastard! All you ever do is eat, but you’ve finally earned your keep!”
I gave a quiet laugh at Namho’s praise—or abuse; it was hard to tell—then turned to the remaining enemies.
“All right. Three left.”
Their eyes twitched. They understood.
Even as their comrades died, they had been backing away, unable to bring themselves to attack me.

“I’m telling you this just in case, but if you run, you’ll die. Of course, unlike your friends who went sightseeing at Mount Beimang first, you’ll die much more painfully after lingering a long time before your breath finally stops.”
At my quiet warning, someone’s throat bobbed as he swallowed.
They’d all watched their comrades die. If they ran, they would end up wishing they’d died the same way.
“But surrender here and tell me what I want to know, and I’ll keep you alive no matter what it takes. If you don’t believe me, I’ll stake my life on it.”
I didn’t want to spare men who had come here to do this. But I had to find out who was behind the ambush.
I named the people who came to mind, one by one.
“Baeksang. Heugung. Yohi. If one of them is your master, tell me now. If someone else sent you, tell me everything you know about them.”
Who was it?

I had my suspicions, but I couldn’t be certain. Only a handful of people were bold enough to stage an attack inside the Inner Palace, powerful enough to send warriors of this caliber, and well-informed enough to know I was gone.
It has to be one of the three Great Chieftains.
I’d moved so discreetly. How had anyone noticed? I didn’t know who had found out, or how. The timing of the ambush was too perfect, too.
I couldn’t even rule out Heugung. We’d parted barely fifteen minutes ago, after he promised to cooperate.
Did he ask to meet me just so he could stab me in the back? Fool me first, then seize the Fire Dragon Pavilion members and use them to threaten me?
Or it could have been Baeksang, who had been watching Heugung, or Yohi.
One thing was certain: whatever name came from these masked attackers’ mouths would belong to a Dark Heaven hound.
“Who is it? Tell me.”
Ssssss.
I pressed down on them with an overwhelming wave of qi. The foreheads visible above their masks creased in pain.
Then, in the next moment, I saw the corners of the masked men’s mouths twitch.
Crunch.
A chill swept over me. I hurriedly fired Finger Qi and struck their pressure points, but dark-red blood burst from the mouths of the men who had severed their own heart meridians.
“Grrrk. Cough.”
Fuck.

That was pretty much your last chance.”
“What’s so surprising?
Were you planning to ding-dong ditch me, you fucking bastards?”
In the suffocating silence, the more than ten pairs of eyes visible above the masks shook violently.
Papap!
Whiiiiing!
A gale far fiercer than the first swept out in every direction.
Every masked man still standing was a Peak Master capable of injuring others with Sword Energy.
Swords, sabers, spears, sickles...
Destructive qi surged from their weapons, tearing through the air toward the vital points across my body.
I watched it all without the slightest fear.
The flow of qi.
The direction of each weapon.
Even the faint fear in their wide eyes.
That settled it.
They had already lost.
They knew they were no more than wolves, yet they refused to accept it and charged at a tiger anyway.
Then I’d better teach them.
Teach them that they should have run somehow.
Dozens of forms flashed through my mind.
I chose the cruelest, most destructive one and moved.
Whoosh!
Crunch!
I twisted smoothly aside.
Four weapons missed me by a hair and tangled together as their paths crossed.
I brought my straightened hand down through their center.
Slash!
Force cut the weapons apart.
I struck one of the masked men in the abdomen as he stood frozen, still gripping what remained of his prized weapon.
Flame Divine Palm.
Boom!
Terrible heat burned away the life force inside his body.
I lowered my head as he crumpled behind me, smoke pouring from his seven apertures.
Shaaak!
Whoosh!
A strike had come from behind without warning.
The long sickle meant to reap my neck swept through empty air, while my backward-thrust elbow struck its wielder square in the chest.
Crack!
More than a dozen ribs broke.
He gave a dying gasp.
But my blow wasn’t what killed him.
His comrade’s spear did.
Thrust!
Look at these bastards.
Not a shred of comradeship.
Clicking my tongue, I seized the spearhead jutting from his chest and squeezed.
Crack!
He was a Peak Master who had reached the level of injuring others with Sword Energy.
I was a Supreme Peak master who had entered the realm of Sword Energy Becoming Force.
I snapped the spearhead off as easily as a wooden chopstick and returned it to its owner.
Whoosh!
Thunk!
The result was instant death.
The spearhead lodged between the masked man’s brows, and he collapsed without a scream.
His comrades swallowed their gasps.
Three of them had died in less time than it took to call it a moment.
Seven left.
I counted them calmly and took a step.
Whoosh!
Space vanished with the wind, and another enemy appeared right in front of me.
No—I was the one who had reached him.
His wide eyes seemed to be trying to say something.
Too late.
I tightened my grip around his neck.
Crack!
Six.
I felt the life leave him as his body went limp.
I took the sword from his hand and hurled it at the nearest enemy.
“Hng!”
With a panicked gasp, the man raised his curved moon saber diagonally.
My sword flew straight into the saber, which was charged with saber qi.
Boom!
The ground heaved with a deafening roar.
A staggering figure emerged from the billowing dust.
The moon saber had shattered against the qi in my sword.
Dozens of fragments were embedded across its wielder’s body.
“Grrk.
Grrr...”
Thud.
The largest fragment was lodged in his throat.
Perhaps that was why he fell without even managing a last word, blood bubbling in his throat.
I pushed aside the corpse with the broken neck and spoke quietly.
“Five left.”
I could feel the fear filling the suffocating silence.
Five Peak Masters had fallen in mere moments, and I didn’t have a scratch on me as I looked for my next target.
“Who’s next?”
No one answered.
Then the masked men, frozen in place and staring at me with eyes wide as if they had seen a ghost, chose to target someone else instead of me.
Papap!
Of the five, three went for me.
The other two went for Namho and Taishan.
I had to admit, it was probably the best choice they could make.
That didn’t mean it would end well for them.
“I saw it with my own eyes!
Those bastards ate both chicken legs!”
“Legs?
Not wings—legs?
Both of them?”
Taishan blinked at Namho in disbelief, then drew the two-section staff from his side.
“Both chicken legs!
Too far!
You’re not human!”
We’d have needed a vote to settle who wasn’t human, but Taishan made voting irrelevant with his enormous two-section staff.
Wham!
Crack!
His innate divine strength was enough to make a defense useless.
One masked man instinctively raised his sword to block the staff.
Both his wrists broke, and before he could scream, Taishan smashed his head along with the other man’s.
Crack!
The two bodies hit the ground without so much as a dying cry.
From behind Taishan, Namho clenched a fist and shouted, “That’s it!
You commendable bastard, I could kill you!”
“Uaaaaaah!
Taishan is commendable!”
“Well done, you goddamn bastard!
All you ever do is eat, but you’ve finally earned your keep!”
I gave a quiet laugh at Namho’s praise—or abuse; it was hard to tell—then turned to the remaining enemies.
“All right.
Three left.”
Their eyes twitched.
They understood.
Even as their comrades died, they had been backing away, unable to bring themselves to attack me.
“I’m telling you this just in case, but if you run, you’ll die.
Of course, unlike your friends who went sightseeing at Mount Beimang first, you’ll die much more painfully after lingering a long time before your breath finally stops.”
At my quiet warning, someone’s throat bobbed as he swallowed.
They’d all watched their comrades die.
If they ran, they would end up wishing they’d died the same way.
“But surrender here and tell me what I want to know, and I’ll keep you alive no matter what it takes.
If you don’t believe me, I’ll stake my life on it.”
I didn’t want to spare men who had come here to do this.
But I had to find out who was behind the ambush.
I named the people who came to mind, one by one.
“Baeksang.
Heugung.
Yohi.
If one of them is your master, tell me now.
If someone else sent you, tell me everything you know about them.”
Who was it?
I had my suspicions, but I couldn’t be certain.
Only a handful of people were bold enough to stage an attack inside the Inner Palace, powerful enough to send warriors of this caliber, and well-informed enough to know I was gone.
It has to be one of the three Great Chieftains.
I’d moved so discreetly.
How had anyone noticed?
I didn’t know who had found out, or how.
The timing of the ambush was too perfect, too.
I couldn’t even rule out Heugung.
We’d parted barely fifteen minutes ago, after he promised to cooperate.
Did he ask to meet me just so he could stab me in the back?
Fool me first, then seize the Fire Dragon Pavilion members and use them to threaten me?
Or it could have been Baeksang, who had been watching Heugung, or Yohi.
One thing was certain: whatever name came from these masked attackers’ mouths would belong to a Dark Heaven hound.
“Who is it?
Tell me.”
Ssssss.
I pressed down on them with an overwhelming wave of qi.
The foreheads visible above their masks creased in pain.
Then, in the next moment, I saw the corners of the masked men’s mouths twitch.
Crunch.
A chill swept over me.
I hurriedly fired Finger Qi and struck their pressure points, but dark-red blood burst from the mouths of the men who had severed their own heart meridians.
“Grrrk.
Cough.”
Fuck.

chapters.title: Chapter 654
paragraphs: If someone asked whether I could kill three Peak masters with a single move, I would nod without much hesitation.
But subduing three Peak masters in a single move was another matter, especially if they had the mindset of assassins.

In that case, persuasion was a better way to bring them under control than force. To stop them from killing themselves, I had to convince them they would survive—not that they would be tortured and die in agony.
But...
Crunch.
Apparently, my promise hadn’t convinced them. Or perhaps they feared their master even more.
Ssshhh! Thud!
The Finger Qi I fired a half-beat too late struck their acupoints, but the damage was already done.
Their bodies went rigid as their Paralysis Acupoints were struck. Blood sprayed from their seven apertures, and all three began to collapse.
Papap! Grab.
I crossed several zhang in an instant, caught them, and laid them on the ground.
Sticky blood welled from their mouths beneath their masks.
“Grrrk, cough...!”
Damn it. This was bad. No, it was the worst possible outcome.
Severing your own heart meridian was like setting off an explosion inside your body.
If the Eight Extraordinary Meridians—the most important meridians in the human body—as well as the hundreds of acupoints throughout the body were severed and blocked, there was no way to survive.
Especially for a Murim practitioner.
High risk, high return, as they say.

Through qi accumulation, a Murim practitioner gained abilities that surpassed those of ordinary people. But if their heart meridian was severed, they also got a bonus one-plus-one event called qi deviation.
Just like now.
“Cough. Kueeegh!”
Splaash!
Eyes, nose, mouth, ears. Dark-red blood and pale lumps that looked like internal organs poured endlessly from every opening I could see.
Namho and Taishan hurried over, only to stop short at the sight.
“Ugh. Taishan doesn’t want to look. Losing my appetite.”
“W-What is this?”
Namho swallowed hard and asked in a subdued voice, “Can they be saved?”
It was a pointless question. Things had already gone too far.
Before I could answer, the heads of two of the men, whose entire bodies had been twitching and convulsing, fell limply to the side.
Thud.
They were dead. No need to check.
But it was still too early to give up. I grabbed the last masked man's wrist and poured my internal energy into him with all my strength.
Sssaaaaah.
As the heat of my Scorching Yang Qi flowed through him, I could feel the ruin inside his body.
Not one of his organs was undamaged. Even the qi pathways that should have been broad and sturdy in a Peak master had crumbled like the walls of an abandoned house.
And qi deviation on top of it...
Even Mungyeong, the greatest Divine Physician under Heaven, couldn’t have guaranteed this man would live. I knew he was beyond saving, and I clenched my teeth.
I have to find out. No matter what.
I needed just one name: the person who had ordered today’s attack.
I poured in more internal energy, not to bring the chaos inside him under control—that was impossible now—but to make his last ember flare.
Rumble!
His entire body struggled violently as an even greater flow of internal energy entered him.
Then, like water settling after a violent storm, the masked man at death’s door regained a brief moment of calm and clarity.
A final rally.
This was my last chance. I stared into his newly focused eyes.
“Who was it? Tell me.”
I pulled the mask away from his mouth to hear his answer—and realized that everything I’d just done was pointless.
“Cough. Hhh. Haaah.”
“Grrk. Uhh...”
His jaw moved as though he were trying to speak, but no words came out.
No. He couldn’t speak.
I froze. Above me, Namho muttered something that sounded like a groan.
“Vicious bastards. Their tongues...”
He couldn’t finish, and the masked man had almost no time left.
“Grrk.”
A death rattle took the place of his last words. His pupils went vacant, and the shortened tongue that had been moving inside his open mouth fell still.
I stared silently at the man who had finally met his death, then spat out the curse I had been holding back.
“...Fuck.”
I’d known these men were no ordinary attackers. I hadn’t imagined their tongues had been cut.
That was why they hadn’t spoken a word from beginning to end, apart from their screams. Even if they’d wanted to, they couldn’t.
“Hmm. The others are the same. Judging by how the severed ends of their tongues have healed, it looks like this was done a long time ago.”
Namho quickly examined the corpses like the Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent he was, then let out a low groan.
“These men... They’re all Nanman.”
“No Han Chinese?”
“Not one. They’re dressed alike, so I can’t tell which tribes they came from, either.”

The most reliable way to distinguish the Nanman was by their clothing and eating habits. But since every one of them wore black clothes and a mask, it was only natural that they were difficult to identify.
Besides, there was only a subtle difference between the appearances of Han Chinese and Nanman. Trying to identify their tribe at a glance was practically absurd.
“...Damn it.”
As I muttered a curse mixed with a sigh, Namho fixed me with a deeply serious gaze.
“When you tried to persuade them, you named three Great Chieftains as possible culprits. Was it Heugung who sent the missive?”
I stared at him in surprise. That was answer enough.
“I see. So that’s what happened.”
“How did you know, Elder Namho?”

“Baeksang and Yohi were both people who could reasonably be named as culprits. But Heugung was different. Thinking about it, there could only be one reason you would have thought of him in this situation.”
His tone was calm and sharp. “Was it him?”
“Yes.” I nodded. “He was waiting for me at the place in the missive.”
“He chose to hide in the forest instead of behind a rock. But even in a crowd, a man of Heugung’s size would stand out. Did he come in person?”
“He had learned the Bone-Shrinking Technique. At first, I didn’t even suspect that he was Heugung.”
“Hah. The Bone-Shrinking Technique. He had more secrets than he let on. Fooled us all. Then again, if he were the man everyone thought he was, he’d never have sent you that missive.”
Namho seemed to be speaking to himself. Then his expression grew heavy.
“Go on.”
My account of Heugung was brief, but Namho listened to every word without interrupting. By the time I finished, the furrows between his brows had deepened.
“What a goddamn mess.”
I agreed. An attack had taken place, and we were no closer to identifying who had ordered it.
Baeksang, Yohi, Heugung. I couldn’t rule out any of them. And behind today’s attack lay another name: Dark Heaven.
I can tell just from the fact that they severed their heart meridians instead of taking a poison pill.
A deadly poison would have been easy to find in Nanman. You could go on a picnic in the grass outside the Outer Palace and find venomous beasts crawling everywhere.
But the masked men had chosen to sever their own heart meridians. Compared with a quick death by poison pill, it meant suffering several times more pain.
I had no choice but to assume that they already knew about it.
The Myriad-Poison Ring. Dark Heaven must already know that I have it.
Dark Heaven had sent the Blood Lord to cause the Shaolin Bloodshed. In Sichuan, it had sent the Western Heaven Demon Lord to seize the divine artifacts of the Emei Sect and the Sichuan Tang Clan.
For those artifacts, it had committed Supreme Peak masters who could match the Ten Kings—perhaps even the Three Saints—along with elite troops.
But even immediately after the Sichuan Blood Tragedy ended, nothing happened to the Sichuan Tang Clan.

The Sichuan Tang Clan had staggered after suffering more severe damage than any other sect in Sichuan during its battle with the Western Heaven Demon Lord. But the follow-up attack from Dark Heaven that everyone had feared never came.
I suspected the Myriad-Poison Ring was the reason.
So they made sure these men severed their heart meridians instead of taking poison. They didn’t want to leave even the slightest chance.
A drop of cold sweat ran down my spine.
My enemies were watching my every move, while I could not even identify the person hiding in the darkness.
The mere fact that an attack like this had taken place in the Inner Palace of the Nanman Beast Palace—the heart of Nanman—was threatening enough.
“When did the attack start?”

“I don’t know exactly. I woke up in the middle of it, but... It seems to have started less than half a shichen after you left. I went to check because I wondered what was happening, and everything outside was in chaos. That bastard Sama Pyo was fighting while covered in blood.”
He pointed to Sama Pyo, lying on the ground, and looked at me with concern.
“But is he all right? He seems to have lost a lot of blood fighting them.”
“I’ve stopped the bleeding. He should be fine. I didn’t find any wounds that looked immediately dangerous, and most of the blood on him seems to be theirs.”
Taishan returned from dragging the corpses into a pile and blinked his enormous eyes.
“Pavilion Master, true? Taishan’s Lord okay?”
“Yeah. He collapsed because he used too much strength.”
Tears filmed Taishan’s eyes.
“Sniff. Taishan was worried. If Lord died, Taishan wouldn’t eat meat for three years. Sniff.”
I’d heard of mourning for three years. Giving up meat for three years was new to me. Wouldn’t that make him the strongest vegan in Murim?
I swallowed the words and patted his Ural-Mountains-sized shoulder.
“Yeah. You worked hard too.”
“Sniff. Taishan used lots of strength. Taishan hungry.”
“...Yeah. Okay.”
Should I just punch him?
But as I was deep in thought, countless footsteps began approaching from far away, accompanied by torchlight.
And with them came the familiar roar of a beast.
—Rooar!
Ssshhh! Pap!
A silver figure, unmistakable against the darkness, reached the clearing first.
Yayul Mok sat astride the White Tiger, his face as stiff as a wooden doll.
“...I’m late.”
I answered evenly. “Yeah. Late enough that it’s hard to believe this happened inside the Inner Palace.”
A collapsed pavilion. Pools of blood scattered across the ground. A heap of corpses.
Yayul Mok bit his lip.
“The warriors on patrol were dead. We didn’t find out until half a gak ago. And...”
What he said next made me wonder if I’d heard him right.
“Heugung and Yohi. Both Great Chieftains have disappeared.”
...What?

chapters.title: Chapter 655
paragraphs: Nanman was like a small country cut off from the Central Plains, with the Nanman Beast Palace as its royal palace.

Naturally, the Inner Palace was enormous. Nearly a thousand people lived there—warriors, cooks, servants, keepers who tended the beasts, and more. Whenever the Tribal Grand Council convened, that number swelled several times over.
Yet among all those people, four mattered more than the rest: the Great Chieftains.

They led the strongest four of Nanman’s thirty-two tribes and had the power to become the next Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace. Their influence was immense, and for generations, the three Great Chieftains other than the Palace Lord had enjoyed special privileges.
Whoosh!
Yayul Mok, running beside me, was explaining one of them now.

“Every chieftain other than Father lives at their tribe’s main base and must give advance notice before entering the Inner Palace. The Great Chieftains are exceptions. They’re free to come and go, and each has a residence inside.”
East, west, south, and north.
The north had traditionally belonged to the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace. The other Great Chieftains each had a residence in one of the remaining directions.
They were official residences granted to high-ranking figures. In Central Plains terms, it was as though the Son of Heaven had permitted his vassal princes to establish their own princely residences.
But after running there at full speed, what I found waiting for me was blood pooled across the ground, corpses, and the wreckage of a building someone had destroyed.
“What the...”
Namho’s groan reached my ears. Feeling as though all the blood in my body had turned cold, I looked up.
A wooden plaque hung crookedly over the shattered gate. Three characters were written on it.
Western Yao Estate.
They told me whose estate this was. The image of a woman smiling with captivating eyes flashed through my mind.
Yohi. Great Chieftain of the Yao people.
“Bewitching” suited her better than “beautiful.”
I didn’t know whether she was behind tonight’s attack, but two things were certain. This splendid estate, so thoroughly shaped by Yohi’s tastes, was no longer as beautiful as it had been.
And Yohi herself had vanished without a trace.
Step.

I crossed through the half-destroyed gate. Bodies lay scattered everywhere, among them the carcasses of beasts. Flower beds that must once have bloomed in all different colors were soaked red with blood.
“...Fuck.”
I couldn’t keep the curse in. Just then, a warrior spotted Yayul Mok walking beside me and approached.
“Young Palace Lord. You’ve arrived.”
Yayul Mok nodded, his face grim.
“You’ve worked hard. Have you found anything else?”
“No. Only more bodies.”
Behind the warrior, corpses lay side by side. A few steps away, three or four warriors were hauling a tiger out of a well, its drenched body hanging limp.
“So far, we’ve confirmed at least a hundred dead, counting both Yao warriors and the beasts they commanded.”
“Any survivors?”
The warrior was silent for a moment before answering.
“...None so far.”
So far?
I doubted they’d find any. Keeping that thought to myself, I approached the bodies.

A warrior instinctively moved to block my way, but when our eyes met, he flinched and stepped aside. I examined the wounds, looking for how these people had fought the unknown attacker—and how they had died.
Then, just as I realized something, I heard Yayul Mok’s voice.
“Found anything?”
Dozens of pairs of eyes turned toward me. I gave a brief answer.
“Force.”
A ripple of unease passed through the crowd. My voice came out stiff.
“The attacker was undoubtedly a Supreme Peak master. Most of them probably didn’t notice the attack until the last moment. The gap in martial arts was that great.”
The Supreme Peak realm was open to only a chosen few. After enduring countless hardships and breaking through the barrier, its masters rose to a realm that made them, quite literally, superhuman.
With a single swing of a sword, they could kill dozens of First Rate masters. Even barehanded, they could beat a dozen Peak masters to a bloody pulp.
Whoever had attacked this place tonight was one of them.
Fast, economical, and utterly lethal.
I’d known as soon as I saw the wounds. The attacker was a seasoned killer.

They had slaughtered every living thing in the estate using no more force than necessary, and no less. Everyone in Murim knew that one chi of depth was enough to take a life. Only a Supreme Peak master could kill a hundred warriors and beasts that way.
The implication was clear.
—Are you saying Baeksang did all this?
Yayul Mok’s quiet Sound Transmission reached my ear. I looked at his rigid face amid the shocked crowd.
—Who knows?
—What do you mean, who knows?
—Only two masters in Nanman have reached this level. One is Baeksang, as you know. The other... is someone everyone in Nanman knows well.
Yayul Mok went deathly pale. His mouth opened as though he were about to shout, but he bit down hard on his lip instead.
—Are you saying Father did this?
—Of course not.
—Then why...
—I’m saying that would be too obvious. What’s certain is that Dark Heaven was directly involved.
Supreme Peak masters were exceedingly rare even in the Central Plains, and rarer still in Nanman. I might have my suspicions about Baeksang, but I wasn’t that much of a blockhead.
Dark Heaven had probably sent one of its own Supreme Peak masters.
They seemed content to watch from a step away. Have they finally decided to act themselves?
But what were they after?
I kept the question to myself and spoke aloud rather than using Sound Transmission.
“There’s something I want to check for myself. Shall we step away for a moment?”
Yayul Mok understood and gave the onlookers a glance. Their eyes turned away.

The three of us—Yayul Mok, Namho, and I—entered the pavilion at the center of the estate. As we’d expected, the place that must once have been filled with rare furnishings looked as though a storm had torn through it.
“Looks like they put up a real fight,” Namho muttered.
Yayul Mok answered, his face still grim. “But it was over in moments. With a Supreme Peak master against them, I suppose that was inevitable.”
“How do you know how long it lasted?”
“Because I heard a short but unmistakable boom. By the time I heard the report and arrived, everything was already over. All that remained in the Western Yao Estate was blood, corpses, and...”
Rattle.
Yayul Mok slid open a large door. His voice sank.
“Those.”
He meant two things lying in the wrecked room: a scent pouch, and something far more valuable in its use, though it gave off a terrible smell.
“Hmm.”
Namho let out a low groan. I walked over without hesitation and touched the second object. It was cold, and sticky blood coated my fingers.
This is...
Anyone with eyes would recognize it.
A wrist. Someone’s wrist, cleanly severed.
“Can you tell whose it is?”
How could I not?
I stared at the plump wrist for a moment before answering quietly.
“Probably Heugung’s.”
“That’s right. He came to see Great Chieftain Yohi with four guards. The Eastern Yi Estate confirmed it.”
If the Yao people had built the Western Yao Estate in the west, it seemed the Yi people under Heugung had established the Eastern Yi Estate in the east. I set Heugung’s wrist down.
“When was that?”
“Less than half a shichen ago, but at least half an hour.”
I worked out the timing. It was just after Heugung and I had parted. He must have gone straight to the Eastern Yi Estate, then come here to see Yohi.
...That lovesick bastard. He couldn’t wait even that long.
I struggled to keep the curse from coming out. I needed to stay calm.
I still didn’t know why Heugung had come to see Yohi. And until his death was confirmed, I had to suspect everyone.
“What happened to the guards he brought?”
“Dead. Along with the Yao warriors.”
Of course. Fuck.
I’d asked just in case. I’d gotten exactly the answer I expected.
“Whew.”

I let out a deep breath and slowly surveyed the room. Signs of resistance were everywhere. Beyond a wall that had probably collapsed under a powerful palm strike, I could see a rear garden that had kept its splendor.
There were faint footprints there, too.
They subdued the two of them quickly, then escaped through the rear garden.
The prints were too faint to tell me who had left them. But they did establish one thing: this wasn’t an attack staged by Heugung or Yohi. A third party had been here.
Less than half an hour ago, at least three people had occupied this room.
And one of them was a Supreme Peak master.
So who had left those footprints? The Southern Heaven Demon Empress? Or one of the Dark Heaven masters under her command?
I thought it over, then shook my head.

I wasn’t some old veteran of Murim. These clues could tell me only so much. Namho had encountered a wealth of information as an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, but his knowledge concerned fiends’ faces and other outward features.
In the end, I need someone with both a high level of martial arts and a high level of insight.
Only two names came to mind immediately, and one of them was someone I could never bring myself to trust.
I turned to Yayul Mok.
“When will Great Hero Yayul arrive?”
“I’ve already sent someone to notify him. By now, he should be on his way with the other chieftains.”

That was good news. I made sure Heugung’s wrist was where I’d found it, to preserve the scene, then sniffed the pouch Yohi had left behind. The silk had split along one side, and only the faintest trace of scent remained—almost nothing.
I’ll find out what happened. No matter what.
Just then, a commotion broke out beyond the pavilion.
“Father must have arrived at last,” Yayul Mok said. “He may be able to identify the attacker.”
But before I even stepped outside, I knew he was wrong.
The Beast Miao King wasn’t the first to arrive. And the person being named as the culprit was someone I hadn’t expected.
“The guilty party is coming out on his own.”
The moment I heard Baeksang’s flat voice, I understood.
Baeksang and the Beast Miao King weren’t the only Supreme Peak masters in Nanman capable of doing this.

chapters.title: Chapter 656
paragraphs: Silence fell over the Western Yao Estate.
The warriors gathering the corpses stopped. So did the tribal chieftains who had clearly just arrived. Everyone stood motionless, looking this way.
No. They were looking at one person.
Me.
Then a cold voice broke the silence.
“The culprit walks out on his own two feet.”
The instant I met Baeksang’s deeply sunken eyes, a hollow laugh escaped me before I knew it.
“Ha.”
Realization struck in a flash. I didn’t need to think any further about where this was going. Baeksang’s greeting had told me everything.
The culprit.
For a moment, I’d forgotten that I fit every condition myself.
Instead of holding up a lantern to search the distance, I should have looked at the ground beneath my feet.
“Uncle Baek, what do you—”
Yayul Mok had been staring at Baeksang in confusion. Now he seemed to understand and fell silent. Namho, who might have caught on even faster than I had, sighed softly.
“Hah. I must be getting old. To fall for a trick this shallow.”
Namho was only half right.
The trap was shallow, but the pit beneath it would be deep enough that, once I stepped in, I wouldn’t easily climb out.
Damn it.
I felt as though I were sinking into a swamp. My chest tightened, and my mouth felt gritty, as if I’d been chewing sand.
I closed my eyes for a moment. When I opened them, the estate had become a courtroom, and everyone’s place in it was clear.
“Did you hear what Great Chieftain Baeksang said?”
“The culprit? Then could that Han Chinese man really be...?”
The warriors whispered among themselves. They were the spectators.
“I knew this would happen! Didn’t I say over and over that we should drive the Han Chinese out from the start?”
“Hmm. It’s still too early to jump to conclusions.”
“Too early? Even now you’re saying that? Jin Taekyung is the only one capable of doing something like this!”
Unlike the whispering warriors, the chieftains were raising their voices to condemn me. They were the jury.
And then there was Baeksang.
“You stand there so boldly. As if you’ve done nothing wrong.”
He had spoken before them all. He was the judge of this damn trial.
I looked at his impassive face. “Of course I can stand here boldly. I haven’t done anything wrong.”
There was no point worrying about courtesy anymore.
One of the chieftains bristled at my answer. “You bastard! How dare—”
“How dare I what?”
Ssshh!
The wave of qi I released shot toward him. The chieftain who had stepped forward went white as a sheet.
“Ghk.”
I was already at the top of a hundred-foot pole. One wrong step and I’d fall. If I let the momentum of this turn against me, it would be over.
I kept the powerful wave of qi flowing and spoke quietly.
“This isn’t a place where any dog or cow can butt in. Stay out of it.”
Someone swallowed hard.
Then a deep voice carried on the wind.
“What a racket.”
Heads turned. A man everyone knew was walking through the gate of the Western Yao Estate.
The Beast Miao King.
His tiger-like eyes were wide, his frame as massive as a mountain ridge. He radiated a pressure like Mount Tai itself, and everyone hurried to one knee.
“We pay our respects to the Palace Lord!”
Their voices rang out as one.
The Beast Miao King advanced slowly, more chieftains following behind him. Then he spoke.
“Am I among the dogs and cattle you mentioned?”
There was no doubt who he meant. I shook my head.
“No.”
“Then I have a question for you.”
His low voice reached my ears.
“Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan. What connection do you have to the tragedy here today?”
He wasn’t asking because he suspected me. He was trying to help. I knew that better than anyone, and I answered without hesitation.
“None whatsoever.”
Whispers rose around us.
Baeksang, who had remained kneeling in silent respect, stood.

“Last year, a fire broke out in the western forest. It happened because of the carelessness of drunken Bai warriors, and as a result, more than two hundred livestock and more than thirty houses burned down.”
His voice remained dry.
“A crime demands punishment. I had to execute seven warriors of my own people with this hand. Yet when I asked for their last words, every one of them told me the same thing.”
His unreadable eyes stayed on me, but his words were for the Beast Miao King.
“I am innocent. I did not drink, and I did not start the fire.”
“Two Great Chieftains have disappeared from the Inner Palace, and some hundred warriors have been slaughtered. A few flimsy words will not excuse anyone from this.”
The Beast Miao King closed his eyes. I stared at Baeksang.
“Listening to you, I get the strange feeling I’ve already been declared the culprit without knowing it.”
“If you’re truly innocent, prove it.”
“Prove it?”
“Yes. That’s the simplest way. Produce evidence that you aren’t the culprit, and the matter is settled.”
I didn’t get a chance to answer. No sooner had Baeksang finished speaking than he turned to the murmuring crowd and called out:

“I, Baeksang, Great Chieftain of the Bai people, will establish my own innocence before questioning the culprit. Heaven and earth shall bear witness, as will the fifteen chieftains and hundred warriors who were with me!”
Damn it. Was this what he’d been after from the start?
I had fully expected Baeksang to have established a sufficient alibi, but the timing and flow with which he revealed it were too perfect.
As though they had been waiting for this very moment, the chieftains following Baeksang raised their voices more loudly than anyone.
“Palace Lord, Great Chieftain Baeksang speaks the truth. He was with us at the Southern Bai Estate from the moment the banquet ended.”
“The Jingpo Chieftain is correct! I, along with the Lahu people, swear it before Heaven!”
“The Wa people vouch for Great Chieftain Baeksang as well! When the tragedy occurred, we were meeting to prepare for tomorrow’s Tribal Grand Council!”
As their voices rose from all sides, Namho groaned behind me. The Beast Miao King’s expression grew grave.
Nearly half the chieftains had openly declared themselves part of a faction. But right now, not even the Beast Miao King could call them on it.

Two Great Chieftains had vanished from the Nanman Beast Palace, and close to a hundred lives had been brutally taken in the Inner Palace itself. Against a disaster like that, a factional struggle—even one that had become an open secret—was a mere ripple.
And then the moment came.
“Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan. Now tell me: where were you at the time?”
A question I couldn’t avoid. An answer I couldn’t refuse to give.
Baeksang’s words and the eyes fixed on me felt like an invisible noose tightening around my whole body.
At the same time, someone touched my waist.
Tap.
I didn’t turn around. Namho had been standing behind me all along; I knew it was his hand.
Why?
He had a reason. I sharpened my senses and followed the movement of his finger.
It lasted only a moment, barely brushing my clothes, but I understood what he was trying to tell me.
He was writing two characters.
Silence.
Namho was telling me not to speak. Or perhaps to think again before I said what I was about to say.
The situation was taking an ominous turn.
What if I tell them I met Heugung?
Would they believe me? More likely, Baeksang and his chieftains would turn it against me.
Heugung had said he slipped out of his residence without anyone noticing, and he had even changed his appearance with the Bone-Shrinking Technique.
I can’t prove it.
If Heugung were here, perhaps I could. But unless the wrist he’d left behind could testify, my alibi was worthless.
On the other hand, saying I’d left my quarters for no reason would be digging my own grave. There had only ever been one answer I could give.
“My quarters.”
Countless thoughts flashed through my mind, but little time passed. I answered without much delay, then took a deep breath and continued.
“I remained in my quarters immediately after the banquet ended. Then I was attacked.”
“Attacked?”
Most of those present hadn’t heard about it yet. As the crowd murmured, the Beast Miao King spoke, his face stern.
“Jin Taekyung is telling the truth. I received a report that assassins whose tribes could not be identified attacked them.”
Yayul Mok had been shaken by the turn of events, but he made his voice steady.
“That’s right. Some of the Inner Palace guards and I reached the scene about half an hour ago. We also confirmed that the warriors patrolling the area had been killed.”
After the Beast Miao King, Yayul Mok also came to my aid, and the murmuring around us grew louder.
But I had been watching Baeksang all along, and I realized once again that something was wrong.
“I, too, heard there had been another tragedy in the Inner Palace.”
His voice was cold, his eyes impassive. He turned to Yayul Mok.
“But those assassins entered the Inner Palace so easily, killed the warriors on patrol, and carried out their attack. They must have been formidable. Wouldn’t you say?”
Before I could stop him, Yayul Mok answered.
“Yes. There were around thirty of them, and every one was as skilled as an elite warrior—”
He never finished. He couldn’t.
Because Baeksang’s voice pierced everyone’s ears in the next moment.
“Strong enough to kill a Supreme Peak master who inherited the Fire King’s legacy?”

“And if this clumsy assassination attempt was meant to keep Jin Taekyung occupied, that makes no sense either. He would have stayed in his quarters if they’d left him alone. Why attack him and draw attention? The more you think about it, the stranger it becomes.”
The air shifted. Dozens of wide eyes turned on me, their stares prickling against my face.
Yet I felt calmer.
Not because I thought I could get out of this. I had already half accepted what was happening.
This trap was large and deep—far beyond anything I had imagined.
When did it start? How much of this was planned?
I stared at Baeksang, still searching for answers, and spoke.
“I don’t think this is the end.”
He nodded at once.
“Good instincts.”
“Something else to say?”
“No. Something to show you.”
Snap.
With his dry answer, Baeksang snapped his fingers. From the half-destroyed gate of the Western Yao Estate, a faint presence began to draw closer.
Step. Step.
Short, uneven strides. Slow footsteps.
Like someone who was ill. Or...
An old man.
I recognized that oddly familiar presence and closed my eyes. When an elderly voice reached me, I opened them again.
“U-Utu-ri of the Bai people. I came at the Great Chieftain’s summons.”
The old owner of the noodle shop stood before the gate.
