The culprit.
For a moment, I’d forgotten that I fit every condition myself.
Instead of holding up a lantern to search the distance, I should have looked at the ground beneath my feet.
“Uncle Baek, what do you—”
Yayul Mok had been staring at Baeksang in confusion.
Now he seemed to understand and fell silent.
Namho, who might have caught on even faster than I had, sighed softly.
“Hah.
I must be getting old.
To fall for a trick this shallow.”
Namho was only half right.
The trap was shallow, but the pit beneath it would be deep enough that, once I stepped in, I wouldn’t easily climb out.
Damn it.
I felt as though I were sinking into a swamp.
My chest tightened, and my mouth felt gritty, as if I’d been chewing sand.
I closed my eyes for a moment.
When I opened them, the estate had become a courtroom, and everyone’s place in it was clear.
“Did you hear what Great Chieftain Baeksang said?”
“The culprit?
Then could that Han Chinese man really be...?”
The warriors whispered among themselves.
They were the spectators.
“I knew this would happen!
Didn’t I say over and over that we should drive the Han Chinese out from the start?”
“Hmm.
It’s still too early to jump to conclusions.”
“Too early?
Even now you’re saying that?
Jin Taekyung is the only one capable of doing something like this!”
Unlike the whispering warriors, the chieftains were raising their voices to condemn me.
They were the jury.
And then there was Baeksang.
“You stand there so boldly.
As if you’ve done nothing wrong.”
He had spoken before them all.
He was the judge of this damn trial.
I looked at his impassive face.
“Of course I can stand here boldly.
I haven’t done anything wrong.”
There was no point worrying about courtesy anymore.
One of the chieftains bristled at my answer.
“You bastard!
How dare—”
“How dare I what?”
Ssshh!
The wave of qi I released shot toward him.
The chieftain who had stepped forward went white as a sheet.
“Ghk.”
I was already at the top of a hundred-foot pole.
One wrong step and I’d fall.
If I let the momentum of this turn against me, it would be over.
I kept the powerful wave of qi flowing and spoke quietly.
“This isn’t a place where any dog or cow can butt in.
Stay out of it.”
Someone swallowed hard.
Then a deep voice carried on the wind.
“What a racket.”
Heads turned.
A man everyone knew was walking through the gate of the Western Yao Estate.
The Beast Miao King.
His tiger-like eyes were wide, his frame as massive as a mountain ridge.
He radiated a pressure like Mount Tai itself, and everyone hurried to one knee.
“We pay our respects to the Palace Lord!”
Their voices rang out as one.
The Beast Miao King advanced slowly, more chieftains following behind him.
Then he spoke.
“Am I among the dogs and cattle you mentioned?”
There was no doubt who he meant.
I shook my head.
“No.”
“Then I have a question for you.”
His low voice reached my ears.
“Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
What connection do you have to the tragedy here today?”
He wasn’t asking because he suspected me.
He was trying to help.
I knew that better than anyone, and I answered without hesitation.
“None whatsoever.”
Whispers rose around us.
Baeksang, who had remained kneeling in silent respect, stood.
“Last year, a fire broke out in the western forest.
It happened because of the carelessness of drunken Bai warriors, and as a result, more than two hundred livestock and more than thirty houses burned down.”
His voice remained dry.
“A crime demands punishment.
I had to execute seven warriors of my own people with this hand.
Yet when I asked for their last words, every one of them told me the same thing.”
His unreadable eyes stayed on me, but his words were for the Beast Miao King.
“I am innocent.
I did not drink, and I did not start the fire.”
“Two Great Chieftains have disappeared from the Inner Palace, and some hundred warriors have been slaughtered.
A few flimsy words will not excuse anyone from this.”
The Beast Miao King closed his eyes.
I stared at Baeksang.
“Listening to you, I get the strange feeling I’ve already been declared the culprit without knowing it.”
“If you’re truly innocent, prove it.”
“Prove it?”
“Yes.
That’s the simplest way.
Produce evidence that you aren’t the culprit, and the matter is settled.”
I didn’t get a chance to answer.
No sooner had Baeksang finished speaking than he turned to the murmuring crowd and called out:
“I, Baeksang, Great Chieftain of the Bai people, will establish my own innocence before questioning the culprit.
Heaven and earth shall bear witness, as will the fifteen chieftains and hundred warriors who were with me!”
Damn it.
Was this what he’d been after from the start?
I had fully expected Baeksang to have established a sufficient alibi, but the timing and flow with which he revealed it were too perfect.
As though they had been waiting for this very moment, the chieftains following Baeksang raised their voices more loudly than anyone.
“Palace Lord, Great Chieftain Baeksang speaks the truth.
He was with us at the Southern Bai Estate from the moment the banquet ended.”
“The Jingpo Chieftain is correct!
I, along with the Lahu people, swear it before Heaven!”
“The Wa people vouch for Great Chieftain Baeksang as well!
When the tragedy occurred, we were meeting to prepare for tomorrow’s Tribal Grand Council!”
As their voices rose from all sides, Namho groaned behind me.
The Beast Miao King’s expression grew grave.
Nearly half the chieftains had openly declared themselves part of a faction.
But right now, not even the Beast Miao King could call them on it.
Two Great Chieftains had vanished from the Nanman Beast Palace, and close to a hundred lives had been brutally taken in the Inner Palace itself.
Against a disaster like that, a factional struggle—even one that had become an open secret—was a mere ripple.
And then the moment came.
“Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Now tell me: where were you at the time?”
A question I couldn’t avoid.
An answer I couldn’t refuse to give.
Baeksang’s words and the eyes fixed on me felt like an invisible noose tightening around my whole body.
At the same time, someone touched my waist.
Tap.
I didn’t turn around.
Namho had been standing behind me all along; I knew it was his hand.
Why?
He had a reason.
I sharpened my senses and followed the movement of his finger.
It lasted only a moment, barely brushing my clothes, but I understood what he was trying to tell me.
He was writing two characters.
Silence.
Namho was telling me not to speak.
Or perhaps to think again before I said what I was about to say.
The situation was taking an ominous turn.
What if I tell them I met Heugung?
Would they believe me?
More likely, Baeksang and his chieftains would turn it against me.
Heugung had said he slipped out of his residence without anyone noticing, and he had even changed his appearance with the Bone-Shrinking Technique.
I can’t prove it.
If Heugung were here, perhaps I could.
But unless the wrist he’d left behind could testify, my alibi was worthless.
On the other hand, saying I’d left my quarters for no reason would be digging my own grave.
There had only ever been one answer I could give.
“My quarters.”
Countless thoughts flashed through my mind, but little time passed.
I answered without much delay, then took a deep breath and continued.
“I remained in my quarters immediately after the banquet ended.
Then I was attacked.”
“Attacked?”
Most of those present hadn’t heard about it yet.
As the crowd murmured, the Beast Miao King spoke, his face stern.
“Jin Taekyung is telling the truth.
I received a report that assassins whose tribes could not be identified attacked them.”
Yayul Mok had been shaken by the turn of events, but he made his voice steady.
“That’s right.
Some of the Inner Palace guards and I reached the scene about half an hour ago.
We also confirmed that the warriors patrolling the area had been killed.”
After the Beast Miao King, Yayul Mok also came to my aid, and the murmuring around us grew louder.
But I had been watching Baeksang all along, and I realized once again that something was wrong.
“I, too, heard there had been another tragedy in the Inner Palace.”
His voice was cold, his eyes impassive.
He turned to Yayul Mok.
“But those assassins entered the Inner Palace so easily, killed the warriors on patrol, and carried out their attack.
They must have been formidable.
Wouldn’t you say?”
Before I could stop him, Yayul Mok answered.
“Yes.
There were around thirty of them, and every one was as skilled as an elite warrior—”
He never finished.
He couldn’t.
Because Baeksang’s voice pierced everyone’s ears in the next moment.
“Strong enough to kill a Supreme Peak master who inherited the Fire King’s legacy?”
“And if this clumsy assassination attempt was meant to keep Jin Taekyung occupied, that makes no sense either.
He would have stayed in his quarters if they’d left him alone.
Why attack him and draw attention?
The more you think about it, the stranger it becomes.”
The air shifted.
Dozens of wide eyes turned on me, their stares prickling against my face.
Yet I felt calmer.
Not because I thought I could get out of this.
I had already half accepted what was happening.
This trap was large and deep—far beyond anything I had imagined.
When did it start?
How much of this was planned?
I stared at Baeksang, still searching for answers, and spoke.
“I don’t think this is the end.”
He nodded at once.
“Good instincts.”
“Something else to say?”
“No.
Something to show you.”
Snap.
With his dry answer, Baeksang snapped his fingers.
From the half-destroyed gate of the Western Yao Estate, a faint presence began to draw closer.
Step.
Step.
Short, uneven strides.
Slow footsteps.
Like someone who was ill.
Or...
An old man.
I recognized that oddly familiar presence and closed my eyes.
When an elderly voice reached me, I opened them again.
“U-Utu-ri of the Bai people.
I came at the Great Chieftain’s summons.”
The old owner of the noodle shop stood before the gate.

chapters.title: Chapter 657
paragraphs: Something big is coming.
My gut was right. The old owner of the thin-noodle shop where I’d sat with Heugung not long ago had appeared.
Fuck.
Something big really had come.
I stared at the old shopkeeper, cursing inwardly.
I wasn’t the only one. As countless eyes turned toward him, a trembling voice came from between his age-spotted lips.
“U-Utu-ri of the Bai people. I came at the Great Chieftain’s summons.”
The Beast Miao King spoke, his face grim.
“I’ve never seen him before. Who is he?”
At a glance from Baeksang, the old shopkeeper answered at once.
“I sell thin noodles near the West Gate of the Outer Palace. I’ve made my living doing that for more than half my life.”
His words and actions taught me several new things.
First. The old shopkeeper’s name was Utu-ri, and he was one of the Bai people.
Second. Unlike at the noodle shop, Utu-ri could speak clearly and hear perfectly well. In short, he was full of life. Jirisan had its baby hero Utu-ri; Nanman had its noodle-selling Utu-ri.
Third. This Bai elder, spry enough to put his age to shame, had probably told Baeksang everything he’d seen and heard.
And fourth. I was probably fucked.
You have to understand. The owner here is over ninety, so his hearing is bad.
Heugung, you son of a bitch.
What he’d said at the noodle shop could hardly have been more wrong.
Bad hearing, my ass.
The only thing looking dim was my future.
The shopkeeper, supposedly over ninety, had heard the Beast Miao King from ten paces away.
“Utu-ri, I called you here to confirm one thing. Do you recognize anyone present?”
“Yes.”
The old shopkeeper nodded without hesitation, and I realized I had another item to add.
Fifth. Besides excellent hearing, Utu-ri had remarkable eyesight and memory.
That much was easy to tell. From the moment he’d entered the Western Yao Estate, he’d kept stealing glances at my face.
“That young man standing over there. The tallest one, with the broad build.”
The hand that had trembled like an aspen tree when he set down the bowls of noodles was, for some reason, perfectly still this time.
Damn it.
His finger pointed directly at me. I shut my mouth, the atmosphere around us began to stir, and the script Baeksang had meticulously prepared raced toward its conclusion.
“Are you certain it was him? You must not tell even the slightest lie.”
The old shopkeeper swallowed hard before answering.

“Yes, without a doubt. I may be old and worn-out, but I’m not so blind that I can’t recognize a customer standing right in front of me. His build was exceptionally large, and he was wearing a tiger mask, so he stood out in my memory.”
“Half the people in the Outer Palace must be wearing masks right now. Did you report him as suspicious for that reason alone?”
“N-No, sir. He lingered nearby before sitting down and ordering noodles. That was when I started to find him suspicious.”
“Suspicious? What exactly troubled you?”
“Well, the thing is...”
The old shopkeeper glanced at me, then continued cautiously.
“It was the mask, sir.”
“The mask?”
“Yes. He kept it on even while he ate. As though something terrible would happen if anyone saw his face.”
“I see. Continue.”
“But later, when he drank the broth, the mask must have felt too restrictive, because he raised it slightly. That was the first and only time I saw his face.”
So that was when.

If I showed my whole face, they might realize I was Han Chinese. But keeping the mask on would look suspicious too. I’d deliberately raised it only as far as the bottom of my nose while I ate, then lifted it for a moment at the very end...
And the old man who looked ready to die any day saw it and remembered.
At first, my excessive caution had drawn suspicion. Later, overlooking the existence of the old shopkeeper had brought me to this situation.
Baeksang, in his usual even tone, was bringing the matter to a close.
“Was he alone?”
“No. He shared a table with a middle-aged man.”
“Another middle-aged man. And afterward?”
“They left at almost the same time, then headed toward the main road by the West Gate.”
“Do you remember the other man’s face?”
“Yes, of course. I’ve lived in the Outer Palace all my life, but I’d never seen him around before, so I remember him clearly. The same goes for that young man.”
“Then they were certainly outsiders who entered during the Tribal Grand Council. If we make likenesses of them and investigate, it should be easy to identify them. When did they leave?”
“Around Insi. They stayed about as long as it takes to drink a cup of tea. The Outer Palace has been setting off firecrackers at regular intervals, so I remember the time clearly.”
The old shopkeeper answered without faltering. His eyes and voice were full of conviction.
Baeksang had gotten every answer he wanted. He gave a small nod.
“Thank you for your cooperation. You may go. I’ll have someone reward you.”
“Th-Thank you. Thank you, Great Chieftain!”
The old shopkeeper bowed repeatedly as he left.

He’d probably be rewarded handsomely for this. The little stall that filled up with three or four customers would become a large inn, and the wrinkled hands that boiled noodles would count silver nyang instead.
But the opportunity he’d found in his old age had become the worst crisis of my life.
“How strange. A man who ought to have been in the Inner Palace slipped out in secret, met with someone whose identity is unknown, and immediately afterward, this tragedy occurred.”
“Your earlier statement has already been exposed as a lie. Still, in light of what happened at Ailao Mountain, I’ll give you one last chance. Do you have anything to say in your defense?”
Countless thoughts flashed through my mind in the brief moment Baeksang’s low voice reached me.
The Western Yao Estate had fallen into suffocating silence. Everyone was looking at me.
Then Namho’s finger brushed my back again.
Sssrk.
Escape.
One character. It was enough to tell me what he meant.
Get out of here first. Worry about what comes next later.
If Namho had learned martial arts, that was the Sound Transmission he would have sent me. I’d probably have done the same in his place.
Would it have gone better if I’d told the truth?
I answered my own question. No.
Maybe it would have gone a little better than this. But Baeksang had prepared thoroughly. One way or another, he would have backed me into the same corner.
I could claim the old noodle seller was lying, but... come on. If Baeksang were stupid enough to fall for that, he wouldn’t have made it this far.
Besides, a master like Baeksang would realize just by looking at the wounds on the assassins who attacked us that most of them weren’t my handiwork.
Without Heugung there to corroborate my statement, telling the truth would only make me a shameless culprit.
Though I suppose that would beat being a culprit caught in a lie.
Either way, I was trapped. There was no getting around it.
And even now, things were hurtling toward the edge.
Sssrk.
A faint sound reached me through the brief silence. Leather shoes crushed blood-soaked grains of sand, while dozens of fluttering hems brushed the flowers in the garden.
In an instant, they had formed a ring around me.
Baeksang stood at its head.
“I’ll ask again. Your defense?”
My defense.
After careful consideration, I answered.
“I’m not giving you one. This whole thing’s filthy, you fucking bastard.”
Apparently, that wasn’t the answer they’d expected. Baeksang studied me with a look of surprise, then nodded.
“Are you admitting your guilt?”
“I admit I lied. That was stupid of me.”
“So you intend to deny the rest to the end.”
“Would you admit it in my place? There’s nothing to admit when I haven’t committed a crime. I’m just pissed that I walked into a trap I couldn’t avoid.”
“If you’ve been wronged, surrender peacefully. I’ll sort out right from wrong.”
“Yeah, fucking right. Right and wrong, my ass, you prick.”
At my scornful answer, Baeksang’s eyes darkened.
“Then I have no choice.”
At the same time—
Shing. Tsstststst!
A dazzling radiance surged from the pure-white blade he drew in a flash. Baeksang lowered his treasured sword, infused with Sword Force, and slowly stepped forward.
“Warriors of the Nanman Beast Palace, listen. We will use our full strength to seize the criminal Jin Taekyung. Not a single mistake will be tolerated—”
At that moment, a roar-like shout erupted from somewhere, drowning out the words that were about to leave Baeksang’s mouth.
“Baeksang!”
Only one person in all Nanman could address the Great Chieftain of the Bai people that way.
“All of you, stop!”
Whoosh!
A powerful wave of qi pressed down on us from every direction.
The Beast Miao King had halted the tightening ring with a single command. His eyes blazed as he glared at Baeksang.
“What do you think you’re doing?”
Everyone trembled beneath his fierce aura. Baeksang did not.
“Exactly what you see, Palace Lord. I intend to seize the criminal Jin Taekyung here.”
“Have you forgotten? He is a pavilion master of the Murim Alliance and a member of the Fire Gate Clan, our longtime ally.”
“Are you, the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, shielding a culprit for those reasons alone?”
“Nonsense! He is not the culprit. Have you already forgotten what happened at Ailao Mountain? He has no cause or reason to do such a thing!”
“But we have a witness who saw him, and clear evidence pointing to him.”
“That’s—”
“Everyone here remembers what happened at Ailao Mountain, myself included. That is why I’m taking the trouble to capture him. Of course, if he resists, we’ll take him dead or alive.”
“Baeksang!”
“I’m not finished.”
Baeksang’s cold voice continued.

“If Jin Taekyung forces his way out of here, I’ll cast a net over heaven and earth across all Nanman and hunt him down with everything we have. Before that, the other Han Chinese under his command will make fine examples.”
The Beast Miao King’s eyes widened. Baeksang was saying he would risk war with the Central Plains. Yayul Mok shouted, his face contorted.
“Uncle!”
“This is a conversation between tribal chieftains, not between lord and subject. The Young Palace Lord has no authority here. Stay out of it.”
“But how could you! How could you dare make such a unilateral decision on your own!”
“On my own...”
Baeksang muttered the words softly, then suddenly raised his head and looked at the sky.
The thick darkness around us had begun to lift. Light was slowly spreading from the east.
“Do you see? It’s already the hour of the Rabbit. Dawn is breaking.”
“What does that have to do with anything?”
“What if we begin the second day of the Tribal Grand Council right here? With a new matter on the agenda, of course...”
Tsst.
The sword in Baeksang’s hand shone more fiercely.
“Whether the Han Chinese Jin Taekyung lives or dies.”
At that moment, a bell sounded in my ears—a bell only one person in the world could hear.
Ding.

“Baeksang!”
Only one person in all Nanman could address the Great Chieftain of the Bai people that way.
“All of you, stop!”
Whoosh!
A powerful wave of qi pressed down on us from every direction.
The Beast Miao King had halted the tightening ring with a single command.
His eyes blazed as he glared at Baeksang.
“What do you think you’re doing?”
Everyone trembled beneath his fierce aura.
Baeksang did not.
“Exactly what you see, Palace Lord.
I intend to seize the criminal Jin Taekyung here.”
“Have you forgotten?
He is a pavilion master of the Murim Alliance and a member of the Fire Gate Clan, our longtime ally.”
“Are you, the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, shielding a culprit for those reasons alone?”
“Nonsense!
He is not the culprit.
Have you already forgotten what happened at Ailao Mountain?
He has no cause or reason to do such a thing!”
“But we have a witness who saw him, and clear evidence pointing to him.”
“That’s—”
“Everyone here remembers what happened at Ailao Mountain, myself included.
That is why I’m taking the trouble to capture him.
Of course, if he resists, we’ll take him dead or alive.”
“Baeksang!”
“I’m not finished.”
Baeksang’s cold voice continued.
“If Jin Taekyung forces his way out of here, I’ll cast a net over heaven and earth across all Nanman and hunt him down with everything we have.
Before that, the other Han Chinese under his command will make fine examples.”
The Beast Miao King’s eyes widened.
Baeksang was saying he would risk war with the Central Plains.
Yayul Mok shouted, his face contorted.
“Uncle!”
“This is a conversation between tribal chieftains, not between lord and subject.
The Young Palace Lord has no authority here.
Stay out of it.”
“But how could you!
How could you dare make such a unilateral decision on your own!”
“On my own...”
Baeksang muttered the words softly, then suddenly raised his head and looked at the sky.
The thick darkness around us had begun to lift.
Light was slowly spreading from the east.
“Do you see?
It’s already the hour of the Rabbit.
Dawn is breaking.”
“What does that have to do with anything?”
“What if we begin the second day of the Tribal Grand Council right here?
With a new matter on the agenda, of course...”
Tsst.
The sword in Baeksang’s hand shone more fiercely.
“Whether the Han Chinese Jin Taekyung lives or dies.”
At that moment, a bell sounded in my ears—a bell only one person in the world could hear.
Ding.
System An unexpected Quest, Either-Or, has been generated!

chapters.title: Chapter 658
paragraphs: Ding.
System An unexpected Quest, Either-Or, has been generated!
A System notification rang out. At the same time, a translucent holographic window sprang up in midair.

System An unexpected Quest, Either-Or, has been generated! Quest Either-Or Only two choices remain to you now. Will you resist with all your strength and escape this place? Or will you surrender quietly and allow yourself to be captured by them? The choice is entirely yours, and every choice will be followed by a corresponding result. Grade: None Restriction: Jin Taekyung Mission: Surrender or Resist (Incomplete) Reward: ??? Failure: ??? - This Quest contains two choices, and you must select exactly one of them. - Various factors around you will change depending on your choice. A certain person may die in the process. How will you proceed? Surrender / Resist
I had only one thought after reading the System window.
What a shitty situation.
Either-Or.
The sudden Quest was exactly what its title said.
Surrender or resist.
There were only two choices, and I had to make one. The situation—and the voices rising all around me—demanded it.
“I agree with Great Chieftain Baeksang.”
“Exactly! If the Palace Lord thinks this is an arbitrary decision, then let us convene the Tribal Grand Council right here and now!”
“If he is innocent, he should surrender quietly and submit to an investigation. What is the problem?”
A hollow laugh escaped me as I listened to the pro-Baeksang chieftains.
What’s the problem?
The biggest problem was that this was Murim, not the modern world.
Judicial corruption happened even in the twenty-first century. I didn’t need to see what would happen to me once Baeksang had me locked up.
They’ll brand me a criminal from the start and make sure I stay one.
There would be no fairness in the process. My ill-considered lie had already been exposed, and Baeksang had produced a witness and clear circumstantial evidence.
It was a carefully dug trap. Once I’d stepped into it, there was nowhere to go but down.
Still, some people spoke up for me.
“You’re all insane. Have you lost your minds? You intend to kill Jin Taekyung? Are you planning to start a war with all of Murim in the Central Plains?”
“We don’t even know for certain that he’s the culprit. Why would a pavilion master of the Murim Alliance and the Fire King’s disciple do such a thing?”
“He rescued no fewer than two hundred warriors from Ailao Mountain. And you claim he is the culprit? Even if you hate the Han Chinese, how can you act like ungrateful beasts?”
This time, it was the chieftains who followed the Beast Miao King shouting.
But of the dozen or so, only a few stepped forward. Many others watched in confusion or kept their mouths firmly shut.
Of course. I’m an outsider in the end.

The Nanman people had never felt particularly well disposed toward the Han Chinese. My actions at Ailao Mountain were the only reason a Han Chinese man like me had been granted the extraordinary privilege of attending the Tribal Grand Council. That was as far as they were willing to go.
I didn’t blame them. They could see which way things were turning.
Even if the Tribal Grand Council convened here and now, as Baeksang had suggested, it couldn’t turn this around.
Not even for the Beast Miao King.
I think I’m pretty fucked.
The Beast Miao King’s brow furrowed as my Sound Transmission reached him.
...You crazy bastard.
Why?
You can still joke at a time like this?
I’m telling you the truth. I can’t sit here bawling like a child. It wouldn’t make anything better.
At my Sound Transmission, which calmly faced reality, the Beast Miao King bit down hard on his lip.
I’m sorry. If the Tribal Grand Council is held as Baeksang says... there will be nothing I can do.
Still, it’s a relief that Great Hero Yayul seems to believe me.
Of course I believe you. That’s why I’m all the more sorry.
Then instead of apologizing, could you punch each of those bastards in the mouth? If that’s too awkward, I’ll do it.
Or use Flame Divine Palm.
Hah. At this point, you may as well be Old Master Jeok’s flesh and blood rather than his Disciple.
Jeok Cheongang.
At the three syllables of his name, a familiar face suddenly flashed before my eyes, and my mouth turned bitter. If Jeok Cheongang were in this situation, how would he have handled it?
No. If it were Old Master Jeok, things never would have reached this point.
I wasn’t nearly as strong as Jeok Cheongang. Despite thinking I’d grown used to Murim, I was still woefully inexperienced. And my enemies were more thorough and cunning than I’d imagined.
If this were Go... my actions would probably count as a bad move.
I didn’t know how to play Go. But when I was little, my father sometimes sat at the computer and played online.

His username was Jin Sedol, though his win rate was terrible. Whenever he lost to a user from China, he’d mutter, “That Chink bastard plays Go like shit... Taiwan number one,” and Mom would smack him on the back for swearing in front of me.
That was all ancient history.
A few years later, my father died suddenly in a Monster Wave. His Go account, steadily used through defeat after defeat, fell dormant.
But why was it that, all of a sudden, I remembered that day when I had watched my father losing at Go?
“Dad, are you losing again?”
“What do you mean, again? Dad’s only losing this game. No, it’s not even over yet.”
“But you lost yesterday and the day before. And I saw you losing earlier!”
“...My sweet boy. You’ve grown so big you can drive a nail straight through your father’s heart.”
But why do you always lose, Dad?
“Hmm. I made a bad move.”
“A handshake?”
“Not that kind of move. I mean a bad play. Like yesterday at the sports festival, when you kicked Minjun’s leg instead of the soccer ball by mistake and lost the game. A bad choice. Understand?”
“Uh-huh! So if you make a bad move, you lose at Go?”
“Not necessarily.”
Why?
“One bad move doesn’t end the game. You lose when you keep making them. Hmm. I shouldn’t have done that.”
“But I got sent off right away yesterday.”
“Son, wasn’t that because you fractured Minjun’s leg?”
“Ohh.”
“What do you mean, ‘ohh’? I nearly broke my back apologizing to Minjun’s parents. Anyway, what matters is not making bad moves over and over.”
“What happens if you do?”
“In Go, you lose your precious stones and eventually lose the game. That’s the price of bad choices.”
“I know! That’s why you always lose, Dad!”
“...Honey! Take Taekyung away! Honey!”
I didn’t know why that memory had come back to me now.
No. Maybe I did.
It had helped me make up my mind.
Can you promise me one thing?
Why have you gone quiet all of a sudden... A promise?
Yes. A promise.
I looked straight at the Beast Miao King and sent another Sound Transmission.
No matter what happens from this point on, promise me you’ll make sure the others can return safely to the Central Plains.
That’s all I need.
You... Surely you aren’t...
I’ll take that as a promise.
The Beast Miao King stared at me, eyes wide, as though he’d guessed what I intended. Then he nodded, his face troubled.
I promise. I’ll use every bit of power I have to protect your subordinates. I’ll clear your name, too.
Good. That’s enough.
I muttered inwardly and began walking toward Baeksang.
Or I would have, if two hands hadn’t reached from behind and seized my clothes.
Grab!
“Jin Taekyung. What are you planning to do?”
Yayul Mok’s face was rigid. Namho, who had already figured it out, spoke next.
“You foolish bastard. Are you planning to walk into a tiger’s mouth on your own?”
“I’m not sure whether it’s a tiger’s jaws or a fucking mutt’s.”
I shrugged.
“But things have come to this. What else can I do?”
Namho’s gaze grew darker than I’d ever seen it.
“Is it because of me and the others? You’re afraid we’ll be hurt if you escape?”
“Hmm. I don’t know.”
“If that’s what you’re thinking, forget it. None of us would want—”
“I know. I know how you all feel.”
I cut him off gently.
“But it would be the same if our positions were reversed. If the other members were in my place, or if Elder Namho were me right now, you wouldn’t run away alone either.”
“See you later.”
His eyes wavered, but he said nothing. I pulled my clothes free, gave them both a look in farewell, and walked on.
Step. Step.
Silence had settled all around us. My footsteps seemed to thunder as I crossed the space alone, while Baeksang watched me, as still as an undisturbed lake.
“Have you finally come to your senses?”
“Someone told me a long time ago that if you make too many bad moves in Go, you lose your precious stones and the game.”
If this were an actual game of Go, I’d play however I liked. To hell with bad moves.
So what if I lost? A famous professional player had once said that, in the end, it was only Go. And to me, it really would be only Go.
After losing, I could simply smash Baeksang’s head open with the Go board while saying, just like my father had, “That Chink bastard plays Go like shit.”
But this wasn’t a game. Here, a bad move would cost me my people instead of stones.
Ju Hwaran. Hyuk Mujin. Song Ilseom. Sama Pyo. Taishan. Namho...
Even if I got out of here, breaking through the Nanman Beast Palace’s net over heaven and earth with all of them would be nearly impossible.
They’d trusted me and followed me this far. I had to keep them alive.
Whatever it took.
“If you keep making bad moves, you lose your precious stones and eventually the game... Whoever told you that was wise.”
“He was a good man. At least he wasn’t a piece of shit like you.”
Shing! Shing! Shing!
Weapons came free on every side, as though everyone had agreed on a signal. Baeksang glanced at the tightening ring and waved his sleeve.
“For once, I commend you for avoiding a bad move. Even the Fire King’s disciple had no other choice.”
“I’m not doing this for praise from a piece of shit like you.”
“No matter. You’re going straight to the underground prison.”
“An underground prison. Can’t say I’m glad to hear that.”
“We’ll have iron balls weighing several thousand geun ready for you as well. You may look forward to them.”
“Sure. My balls are trembling with anticipation already.”
It was more or less what I’d expected. I answered calmly, then addressed Baeksang as he slowly sheathed his sword.
“But why aren’t you looking forward to it?”
“What?”
“Didn’t you say earlier that if I ran, you’d kill all my people?”
“Why bring that up now—”
I had no reason to hear the rest of his words. Nor did I need to.
Say that kind of bullshit to me, and you should expect a punch.
Along with a final word he could not hear, I thrust out a single fist like a ray of light.
Crack!
Without waiting to see the result, I shouted as fast as I could.
“Ah, I surrender! I surrenderrr!”
What are you going to do about it, fucker?

chapters.title: Chapter 659
paragraphs: Crack.
A large, fur-covered paw crushed a brittle leaf.
Fangs showed between parted jaws. The sleek body crouched deep in the grass was ready to hunt.
What kind of meat will I eat today?
All it had to do was spot its prey, sprint in, and sink its fangs into the back of its neck.
As long as it watched out for venomous beasts that appeared without warning, finding prey in Nanman was easy enough.
At least, it was for a black leopard near the top of the food chain.
Grrrr...
The leopard scanned its surroundings with bright yellow eyes, then let out a low growl.
It had sensed a great many presences in the distance and caught their scent on the wind.
Sniff, sniff.
Its senses were sharp, as a predator’s should be. It did not take long to identify the prey it had encountered sooner than expected.
Humans.
More precisely, a group of humans. Roughly a hundred of them were approaching.
Grrr.
The leopard gave an involuntary growl of irritation.
Humans were unwelcome. Small as they were, they sometimes hunted predators much larger than themselves. And the more of them there were, the stronger they became.
Just like now.
Swish.
The leopard rose from its crouch.
Hunting humans alone was for fools. It would be smarter to move elsewhere and find different prey.
It was about to do just that when—
“Whew. Whew...”
The leopard stopped and stared beyond the grass.
A human came running up, making strange noises, and squatted among the weeds.
“Ahh. I almost died.”
At the same time, sounds and smells that would have made even predators recoil filled the air. A glint flashed through the black leopard’s vertically slit pupils.
There was no doubt about it. This human had left the group to relieve himself.
He had no idea this place would be his grave.
Grrr.
One target. A stupid-looking human at that.
The leopard made its decision in an instant. The muscles in all four legs tightened, and its black body shot forward like an arrow.
Tap—whoosh!
Several dozen feet vanished in an instant. Only then did the human notice something and turn his head toward the leopard.
A beat too late. Fangs flashed inside the leopard’s wide-open jaws.
—Raaaar!
Thud! Crunch!
The sound of flesh being torn rang out beneath the beast’s thunderous roar. Large and small bodies tangled together and rolled across the ground.
A moment later, the survivor of that short, fierce struggle made himself heard.
“Phew!”
The man who emerged from the black fur had blood all over his face.
The leopard’s blood.
At the last moment, he had driven his sword into the head of the predator that ruled this stretch of forest. Now he panted for breath.
“Huff. Hah. Fuck. I nearly died taking a dump.”
An ambush while he was doing his business. Thinking back, it had been far too close.
A year or two ago, he would have ended up as the leopard’s dinner.
But like a seed putting out shoots, he had grown considerably since then.
“Getting beaten all the time really has improved my reflexes... But how do I get out from under this thing?”
The man—Hyuk Mujin—was still trapped beneath the impossibly heavy carcass of the black leopard, struggling and grunting, when—
“Strange. Was this the business you said you had to take care of?”
A familiar voice reached his ears, and his face lit up.
“Oh! Great Hero Song!”
Song Ilseom sighed.
“I told you not to call me Great Hero.”
“Why not? You’re helping someone in trouble. Doesn’t that make you a Great Hero?”
“You take after your superior. The words flow right out of you.”
“I’ll take that as a compliment. But don’t say it in front of Captain. Even you might find yourself getting beaten as freely as the words flow.”
Song Ilseom nodded at Hyuk Mujin’s heartfelt warning.
“...I’ll bear that in mind.”
“Good thinking. Now, could you get this thing off me? I can barely breathe. I keep seeing my father’s face.”
“Really? When did he die?”
“What are you talking about? He’s alive and well.”
Is he insane?
Song Ilseom gave the question a moment’s serious thought, then abandoned it and grabbed the leopard’s carcass.
Few people in the Fire Dragon Pavilion he had somehow joined were sane. The Pavilion Master was the worst of them.
Scrape. Thud.
Freed at last from the danger of being crushed to death, Hyuk Mujin brushed the dirt from his clothes.
“Whew. That was close. Where is everyone?”
“Setting up camp. The Young Bureau Head stayed there too. We’ve been riding nearly ten shichen without a break, so she seems to have decided we need to rest. A missive arrived while you were away.”
“A missive?”
“Yes. It seems the Nanman Beast Palace sent a messenger eagle. They must have further instructions.”
“Either way, that’s good news. The beasts have been moving so violently that I nearly shattered my rear end.”
“They need rest too. Still, the Nanman people must train them well. They have impressive stamina—every bit as much as grassland horses.”
About a day earlier, they had left the Outer Palace with the reconnaissance squad and pressed on without respite.
They had no idea when the Blood Monk, an old monster none of them had ever heard of before, might cross Guangxi and head south. A forced march was the obvious choice.
“When are we supposed to arrive?”
“According to the two tribal chieftains, in two days if we’re quick. Three at the latest. The Young Bureau Head seems to think the same.”
“Why do I get the feeling that means we have to make it in two?”
“Because we do. We need to move as quickly as possible to stop the Blood Monk.”
“As quickly as we’ve been moving?”
“Possibly faster.”
“...Faster might be a bit much.”
Hyuk Mujin grimaced, then nodded.
“Damn it. Not much choice, I guess.”
“You accepted that sooner than I expected.”
“Try following Captain around for a couple of years, Great Hero Song. You’ll learn to give up on anything. Your life included.”
“Unfortunately, that won’t happen.”
“Why not?”
“If not for the Young Bureau Head, I would never have come this far. She is the one and only reason I’m in this wretched Nanman.”
Hyuk Mujin shrugged at the curt reply.
“Hmm. Then I guess we’ll be seeing a lot of you.”
“What?”
“You just said it yourself. You came this far because of Young Lady Ju. And Young Lady Ju is going to stay with Captain, isn’t she?”
“Great Hero Song, you’re not as bright as I thought.”
Song Ilseom went still for a moment. Then he asked evenly, “Do you want to die?”
“No. Sorry.”
Hyuk Mujin answered at once. Keeping a wary eye on Song Ilseom, he pulled his sword from the leopard’s head.
Spurt.
Blood gushed from the gaping wound. Hyuk Mujin gave the blade a cursory wipe and sheathed it, then looked up at the sky.
“It’s night already.”
They had apparently set out at night, but while moving without a moment to think, the second night had already arrived.
And several more nights would pass before they returned to the Nanman Beast Palace.
“I’d rather not run into the Blood Monk, though. It’s hard not to worry with Captain gone. You feel the same way, don’t you, Great Hero Song?”
No answer came.
After a brief silence, what he heard behind him was not Song Ilseom’s voice, but the cold scrape of a blade leaving its sheath.
Shing.
Hyuk Mujin recognized the sound coming from behind him and swallowed dryly.
“Uh, about calling you dumb. I’m sorry. Are you really angry?”
Song Ilseom’s voice came back cold.
“...Shut up and turn around.”
“Great Hero Song. Please. I’m begging you.”
“I’m begging you. Shut up and turn around. Draw your sword again.”
He’s really lost it.
Tears in his eyes, Hyuk Mujin turned on trembling legs.
And then he understood why Song Ilseom’s voice had gone cold. Why he had told him to draw his sword.
“I thought they were on our side... Was I wrong?”
Rustle.
The dark grass shifted.
The reconnaissance squad—the hundred or so people who had traveled with them until now—stood beyond it. At their head, the two tribal chieftains emerged and regarded them with troubled expressions.
“You weren’t the only one who thought so. I regret that it’s come to this.”
“We received a missive bearing the Palace’s seal. It’s an order we cannot refuse.”
A missive.
At those two words, Song Ilseom had a vague sense that something serious had happened in the Inner Palace they had left behind.
But right now, only one person mattered.
“Where is the Young Bureau Head?”
Killing intent seeped into the question.
Chief Jang, a supporter of the Palace Lord who had favored Jin Taekyung since the Tribal Grand Council, sighed.
“Her sword was fiercer than I expected. She caught on quickly, too.”
“I’ll ask one last time. Where is she?”
Whoosh!
Killing intent poured from Song Ilseom, so savage that even the beasts with the reconnaissance squad backed away.
Sensing his fury, the other tribal chieftain hurried to answer.
“Sh-she’s safe. We only subdued her with a Pressure-Point Strike.”
Song Ilseom clenched his teeth without realizing it. Relief and regret surged through him together.
I should have stayed by her side, no matter what.
Given the size of the reconnaissance squad that had turned against them, staying probably would not have changed the outcome.
But he could not stop picturing Ju Hwaran fighting alone.
“...Damn it.”
As he spat out the curse, Song Ilseom slowly lowered the cherished weapon in his hand.
Hyuk Mujin, a little slower to grasp the situation, did the same.
Scrape. Thunk.
His carefully forged blade sank into the ground.
Chief Jang watched with a troubled look, then gestured. Warriors from the reconnaissance squad hurried forward, took their weapons, and bound them.
“...Great Hero Song. I think we’re fucked.”
Song Ilseom did not answer Hyuk Mujin this time either.
He couldn’t.
Tap, tap, tap.
Someone’s fingers tapped all over his body. As he felt his body stiffen under the Pressure-Point Strike, Song Ilseom muttered inwardly,
What the hell have you done, Jin Taekyung?

sentences.text: Crack.
A large, fur-covered paw crushed a brittle leaf.
Fangs showed between parted jaws.
The sleek body crouched deep in the grass was ready to hunt.
What kind of meat will I eat today?
All it had to do was spot its prey, sprint in, and sink its fangs into the back of its neck.
As long as it watched out for venomous beasts that appeared without warning, finding prey in Nanman was easy enough.
At least, it was for a black leopard near the top of the food chain.
Grrrr...
The leopard scanned its surroundings with bright yellow eyes, then let out a low growl.
It had sensed a great many presences in the distance and caught their scent on the wind.
Sniff, sniff.
Its senses were sharp, as a predator’s should be.
It did not take long to identify the prey it had encountered sooner than expected.
Humans.
More precisely, a group of humans.
Roughly a hundred of them were approaching.
Grrr.
The leopard gave an involuntary growl of irritation.
Humans were unwelcome.
Small as they were, they sometimes hunted predators much larger than themselves.
And the more of them there were, the stronger they became.
Just like now.
Swish.
The leopard rose from its crouch.
Hunting humans alone was for fools.
It would be smarter to move elsewhere and find different prey.
It was about to do just that when—
“Whew.
Whew...”
The leopard stopped and stared beyond the grass.
A human came running up, making strange noises, and squatted among the weeds.
“Ahh.
I almost died.”
At the same time, sounds and smells that would have made even predators recoil filled the air.
A glint flashed through the black leopard’s vertically slit pupils.
There was no doubt about it.
This human had left the group to relieve himself.
He had no idea this place would be his grave.
Grrr.
One target.
A stupid-looking human at that.
The leopard made its decision in an instant.
The muscles in all four legs tightened, and its black body shot forward like an arrow.
Tap—whoosh!
Several dozen feet vanished in an instant.
Only then did the human notice something and turn his head toward the leopard.
A beat too late.
Fangs flashed inside the leopard’s wide-open jaws.
—Raaaar!
Thud!
Crunch!
The sound of flesh being torn rang out beneath the beast’s thunderous roar.
Large and small bodies tangled together and rolled across the ground.
A moment later, the survivor of that short, fierce struggle made himself heard.
“Phew!”
The man who emerged from the black fur had blood all over his face.
The leopard’s blood.
At the last moment, he had driven his sword into the head of the predator that ruled this stretch of forest.
Now he panted for breath.
“Huff.
Hah.
Fuck.
I nearly died taking a dump.”
An ambush while he was doing his business.
Thinking back, it had been far too close.
A year or two ago, he would have ended up as the leopard’s dinner.
But like a seed putting out shoots, he had grown considerably since then.
“Getting beaten all the time really has improved my reflexes...
But how do I get out from under this thing?”
The man—Hyuk Mujin—was still trapped beneath the impossibly heavy carcass of the black leopard, struggling and grunting, when—
“Strange.
Was this the business you said you had to take care of?”
A familiar voice reached his ears, and his face lit up.
“Oh!
Great Hero Song!”
Song Ilseom sighed.
“I told you not to call me Great Hero.”
“Why not?
You’re helping someone in trouble.
Doesn’t that make you a Great Hero?”
“You take after your superior.
The words flow right out of you.”
“I’ll take that as a compliment.
But don’t say it in front of Captain.
Even you might find yourself getting beaten as freely as the words flow.”
Song Ilseom nodded at Hyuk Mujin’s heartfelt warning.
“...I’ll bear that in mind.”
“Good thinking.

I keep seeing my father’s face.”
“Really?
When did he die?”
“What are you talking about?
He’s alive and well.”
Is he insane?
Song Ilseom gave the question a moment’s serious thought, then abandoned it and grabbed the leopard’s carcass.
Few people in the Fire Dragon Pavilion he had somehow joined were sane.
The Pavilion Master was the worst of them.

Thud.

chapters.title: Chapter 660
paragraphs: “We’ve subdued them all. We struck their Sleep Acupoints too, so they won’t regain consciousness for at least a day.”
“...Good work.”
Chief Jang nodded at his warrior’s report, his expression troubled. Song Ilseom and Hyuk Mujin lay motionless, and their figures were reflected in his eyes.
“We don’t know what might happen. Keep a close watch on them. We’ll rest for two shichen and then move out.”
“Does that mean...?”
“Yes. They’re coming with us.”
“Chief... Forgive me for speaking out of turn, but wouldn’t it be better to send a few warriors to escort the prisoners to the Inner Palace separately?”
The warrior regretted asking as soon as the words were out. Chief Jang only stared at him.
“I’ll carry out your orders.”
He hurried away. Watching him go, Chief Jang sighed as the contents of the letter delivered by messenger eagle came back to him.
Heugung and Yohi, two Great Chieftains, have gone missing. The Western Yao Estate has been wiped out. And they’re blaming Jin Taekyung?
He had read it several times, unable to believe his eyes. But the words in the missive had not changed, and he had only one choice.
I’m sorry, all of you.
The apology would never reach them. Soon, though, they would understand that this was the best he could do under the circumstances.
This was a carefully planned plot. Jin Taekyung was caught up in it unexpectedly.
Chief Jang did not believe the missive’s accusation.

Everything he had seen of Jin Taekyung fit what the Han Chinese of the Central Plains called a Great Hero. If Jin had not risked his life fighting in the Poisonblood Grounds, more than two hundred warriors would never have returned to their families. Among those who had come home were warriors of Chief Jang’s own Zang people, including his blood relatives.
And even setting aside what I owe him, there isn’t a sound reason for him to have done it.

Nanman and the Central Plains had fallen out after the Great Faction War, but that was largely one-sided hostility born of the tremendous sacrifices Nanman had suffered. Why would Jin Taekyung, sent here as a representative of the Murim Alliance, cause such a tragedy?
Unless he wants to make an enemy of Nanman as well as Dark Heaven...
But Chief Jang could do nothing about the accusation now. Baeksang and his faction had already seized control of the situation.
However, the Palace Lord, the Beast Miao King, had secretly conveyed his intentions through a messenger eagle.
Detain the Han Chinese in the reconnaissance squad, but do not escort them to the Inner Palace.
Chief Jang understood exactly what the Beast Miao King meant.
If we take them to the Inner Palace, they’ll surely end up as hostages.

Fortunately, Chief Go, who was leading the reconnaissance squad alongside him, also followed the Beast Miao King. Since the two men shared the same opinion, they had their warriors subdue the three of them—not to make hostages of them, but to keep them in their own hands and protect them.

The timing helped. They were already on the move to watch for an old monster known as the Blood Monk. With a threat like that looming, Baeksang’s faction could hardly use their decision to keep the prisoners with the squad against them.
Just bear with it a little longer. At least until this is settled.
Chief Jang stepped toward the two unconscious men being carried away. He felt bad for them and meant to loosen their bindings a little.
“Stop a moment. Aren’t those ropes tied too tightly?”
“Chief! Don’t!”
“What do you mean, don’t? It’ll be fine—”
Squelch.
Ignoring the warriors, Chief Jang reached behind Hyuk Mujin’s back and frowned.
What is this?
Something damp and sticky. Then the stench reached him.
“Uh. There was... feces on his back,” a warrior said.
“That’s why we told you not to come any closer...”
His voice trailed off. Chief Jang looked from his hand to Hyuk Mujin and back again, then spoke in a low voice.
“The prisoner might shit again—no, escape. Tie the ropes tighter.”
“Yes, Chief.”
In the modern world, I’d been a model law-abiding citizen.

Until middle school, whenever the traffic light turned green, I would raise my hand high and cross the street. After becoming a Hunter, I paid all my insurance premiums and taxes on time, without ever delaying a payment or evading a cent.
I barely even complained about the national pension, though I’d get next to nothing from it when I grew old.
In short, prison and I had nothing to do with each other.
So why had I become so familiar with underground prisons in Murim when I hadn’t committed a crime?
I’d spent time in one at the Jin Family of Taiyuan, back when I was still a budding martial artist. At the Sichuan Tang Clan, I’d stayed in one for days to remain at Jeok Cheongang’s side.
This was my third visit, and it was nothing like the other two.
At the Jin Family of Taiyuan, it was practically a training hall. At the Sichuan Tang Clan, I was there for Jeok Cheongang’s treatment.
Not only was I imprisoned against my will, but anyone would have thought as I did if iron balls weighing more than a thousand geun each were hanging all over their body like accessories.
Clank.
“...Fuck, these are heavy.”

I muttered the curse under my breath. The enormous chains binding my limbs and the iron balls attached to them weighed so much that even I could barely move—and my Strength was far beyond human limits.
If I could use my internal energy, I might be able to figure something out...
Maybe I shouldn’t have punched Baeksang at the end.
I regretted it for a moment. But if he’d been that easy to deal with, I’d be in my quarters instead of an underground prison.

Besides, even after I’d punched him hard enough to break his nose, he hadn’t so much as batted an eye. He’d personally bound me while I stood there without resisting, then ordered his tribal chieftains:
“Lock the Han Chinese Jin Taekyung in the underground prison and bind him with ten thousand geun of weight.”
And this was the result.
They’d put me in the deepest part of the Nanman Beast Palace’s underground prison and given me a special pill that would keep me from using my internal energy for several days.
At least I should be grateful they didn’t use a Pressure-Point Strike on me.
The reason was simple.
My acupoints kept coming undone.
My perfect body, which had been recognized as a Heavenly Martial Physique by countless powerful masters, had simply performed its function to the fullest.
That didn’t mean I’d had any luck getting my internal energy to flow again.
“Ungh.”
I tensed my whole body, took a deep breath, and focused on my lower dantian, just as I’d done hundreds, if not thousands, of times before.
The next moment, the System alert I’d been hearing over and over for the past half day sounded in my ears again.
Beep.
System The energy of the Force-Sealing Pill is blocking your dantian! - You cannot use internal energy!
“Ah.”
I’d lost track of how many attempts I’d made. I’d given up counting after fifty.
“...Damn it.”
I let myself sag with a sigh and a curse. Then footsteps approached from somewhere in the distance.
Step. Step.
They echoed through the damp darkness. The pill kept me from using my internal energy, but my senses were as sharp as ever. I raised my head and peered beyond the bars.
Splash.

The footsteps stopped in front of my cell, sending filthy water from a puddle splashing against my knees. There wasn’t a single light down here, but my eyesight—good enough to rival a Mongolian’s—was more than enough to make out the visitor.
“What, are you a new jailer?”
“No manners, huh? You splash dirty water on me the moment you get here, then don’t even answer.”
Baeksang looked down at me in silence before replying quietly.
“You complain a great deal for a criminal.”
“Well, this is pretty mild, really.”
I tried to shrug, flinched under the weight of the iron balls, and went on.
“Someone else had his nose broken and took it pretty well. Didn’t he?”
I could see Baeksang’s brow furrow in the darkness. The bandage wrapped around his straight, prominent nose was visible as well.
“That must’ve hurt. You held up better than I expected. Be honest—you shed a tear after sending me down here, didn’t you?”
His reaction lasted only a moment. His voice was calm when he answered.
“It tickled. Perhaps because I sensed the fear in your punch.”
“What?”
“There was no internal energy behind it, and you didn’t put your full strength into it either. It was only a child venting his frustration.”
“I understand. You must have been afraid. If you had given it everything you had, neither you nor your subordinates would have remained unharmed.”
Shit. I lost that exchange badly.
He’d hit the mark. I shut my mouth before I could come up with a reply.
Baeksang watched me, his gaze as steady as ever.
“Why didn’t you leave? If you’d fled alone, you might at least have saved your life.”
I answered with an incredulous expression.
“You said you’d cast a net over heaven and earth, you bastard.”
“And I would have. But you still had a fair chance. At the very least, the Palace Lord wouldn’t have pursued you. He might even have hindered the pursuit.”

Baeksang wasn’t making a wild guess. From what I’d seen of the Beast Miao King, and what Jeok Cheongang had told me, he was exactly the sort of man who might throw me a lifeline when things were at their worst.

But I wasn’t foolish enough to nod along. It might already have been too late, but if I readily admitted that fact in front of Baeksang, his wariness toward the Beast Miao King would only grow stronger.
“I don’t know about that. We’re not even particularly close.”
“You’re thinking, at least. But you still have a long way to go.”
“Believe what you want. Be glad Old Master isn’t here. In two or three months, your head will be rolling around this place.”
“And you’re still a child who hasn’t outgrown his rashness.”
I let out a short laugh.
“Your mouth reeks of shit. Stop sucking Dark Heaven’s asshole. At least I’m here to protect my people.”
“No one else is around, so let’s be honest. You know too, don’t you? You know what you’re doing right now.”
This time, Baeksang fell silent.
Of course he did. By working with Dark Heaven, he was handing all of Nanman over to the Lord of Heaven.
“You betrayed a sworn brother you’ve known for decades. You deceived more than thirty tribal chieftains and countless people of Nanman. There’s no excuse that could justify any of it.”
At that moment, Baeksang, who had been watching me with a deep, unreadable gaze, suddenly spoke.
“Two days.”
“What?”
“Two days. At noon, two days from now, you’ll be executed in front of everyone.”

Something damp and sticky.
Then the stench reached him.
“Uh.
There was... feces on his back,” a warrior said.
“That’s why we told you not to come any closer...”
His voice trailed off.
Chief Jang looked from his hand to Hyuk Mujin and back again, then spoke in a low voice.
“The prisoner might shit again—no, escape.
Tie the ropes tighter.”
“Yes, Chief.”
In the modern world, I’d been a model law-abiding citizen.
Until middle school, whenever the traffic light turned green, I would raise my hand high and cross the street.
After becoming a Hunter, I paid all my insurance premiums and taxes on time, without ever delaying a payment or evading a cent.
I barely even complained about the national pension, though I’d get next to nothing from it when I grew old.
In short, prison and I had nothing to do with each other.
So why had I become so familiar with underground prisons in Murim when I hadn’t committed a crime?
I’d spent time in one at the Jin Family of Taiyuan, back when I was still a budding martial artist.
At the Sichuan Tang Clan, I’d stayed in one for days to remain at Jeok Cheongang’s side.
This was my third visit, and it was nothing like the other two.
At the Jin Family of Taiyuan, it was practically a training hall.
At the Sichuan Tang Clan, I was there for Jeok Cheongang’s treatment.
Not only was I imprisoned against my will, but anyone would have thought as I did if iron balls weighing more than a thousand geun each were hanging all over their body like accessories.
Clank.
“...Fuck, these are heavy.”
I muttered the curse under my breath.
The enormous chains binding my limbs and the iron balls attached to them weighed so much that even I could barely move—and my Strength was far beyond human limits.
If I could use my internal energy, I might be able to figure something out...
Maybe I shouldn’t have punched Baeksang at the end.
I regretted it for a moment.
But if he’d been that easy to deal with, I’d be in my quarters instead of an underground prison.
Besides, even after I’d punched him hard enough to break his nose, he hadn’t so much as batted an eye.
He’d personally bound me while I stood there without resisting, then ordered his tribal chieftains:
“Lock the Han Chinese Jin Taekyung in the underground prison and bind him with ten thousand geun of weight.”
And this was the result.
They’d put me in the deepest part of the Nanman Beast Palace’s underground prison and given me a special pill that would keep me from using my internal energy for several days.
At least I should be grateful they didn’t use a Pressure-Point Strike on me.
The reason was simple.
My acupoints kept coming undone.
My perfect body, which had been recognized as a Heavenly Martial Physique by countless powerful masters, had simply performed its function to the fullest.
That didn’t mean I’d had any luck getting my internal energy to flow again.
“Ungh.”
I tensed my whole body, took a deep breath, and focused on my lower dantian, just as I’d done hundreds, if not thousands, of times before.
The next moment, the System alert I’d been hearing over and over for the past half day sounded in my ears again.
Beep.
System The energy of the Force-Sealing Pill is blocking your dantian! - You cannot use internal energy!
“Ah.”
I’d lost track of how many attempts I’d made.
I’d given up counting after fifty.
“...Damn it.”
I let myself sag with a sigh and a curse.
Then footsteps approached from somewhere in the distance.
Step.
Step.
They echoed through the damp darkness.
The pill kept me from using my internal energy, but my senses were as sharp as ever.
I raised my head and peered beyond the bars.
Splash.
The footsteps stopped in front of my cell, sending filthy water from a puddle splashing against my knees.
There wasn’t a single light down here, but my eyesight—good enough to rival a Mongolian’s—was more than enough to make out the visitor.
“What, are you a new jailer?”
“No manners, huh?
You splash dirty water on me the moment you get here, then don’t even answer.”
Baeksang looked down at me in silence before replying quietly.
“You complain a great deal for a criminal.”
“Well, this is pretty mild, really.”
I tried to shrug, flinched under the weight of the iron balls, and went on.
“Someone else had his nose broken and took it pretty well.
Didn’t he?”
I could see Baeksang’s brow furrow in the darkness.
The bandage wrapped around his straight, prominent nose was visible as well.
“That must’ve hurt.
You held up better than I expected.
Be honest—you shed a tear after sending me down here, didn’t you?”
His reaction lasted only a moment.
His voice was calm when he answered.
“It tickled.
Perhaps because I sensed the fear in your punch.”
“What?”
“There was no internal energy behind it, and you didn’t put your full strength into it either.
It was only a child venting his frustration.”
“I understand.
You must have been afraid.
If you had given it everything you had, neither you nor your subordinates would have remained unharmed.”
Shit.
I lost that exchange badly.
He’d hit the mark.
I shut my mouth before I could come up with a reply.
Baeksang watched me, his gaze as steady as ever.
“Why didn’t you leave?
If you’d fled alone, you might at least have saved your life.”
I answered with an incredulous expression.
“You said you’d cast a net over heaven and earth, you bastard.”
“And I would have.
But you still had a fair chance.
At the very least, the Palace Lord wouldn’t have pursued you.
He might even have hindered the pursuit.”
Baeksang wasn’t making a wild guess.
From what I’d seen of the Beast Miao King, and what Jeok Cheongang had told me, he was exactly the sort of man who might throw me a lifeline when things were at their worst.
But I wasn’t foolish enough to nod along.
It might already have been too late, but if I readily admitted that fact in front of Baeksang, his wariness toward the Beast Miao King would only grow stronger.
“I don’t know about that.
We’re not even particularly close.”
“You’re thinking, at least.
But you still have a long way to go.”
“Believe what you want.
Be glad Old Master isn’t here.
In two or three months, your head will be rolling around this place.”
“And you’re still a child who hasn’t outgrown his rashness.”
I let out a short laugh.
“Your mouth reeks of shit.
Stop sucking Dark Heaven’s asshole.
At least I’m here to protect my people.”
“No one else is around, so let’s be honest.
You know too, don’t you?
You know what you’re doing right now.”
This time, Baeksang fell silent.
Of course he did.
By working with Dark Heaven, he was handing all of Nanman over to the Lord of Heaven.
“You betrayed a sworn brother you’ve known for decades.
You deceived more than thirty tribal chieftains and countless people of Nanman.
There’s no excuse that could justify any of it.”
At that moment, Baeksang, who had been watching me with a deep, unreadable gaze, suddenly spoke.
“Two days.”
“What?”
“Two days.
At noon, two days from now, you’ll be executed in front of everyone.”

chapters.title: Chapter 661
paragraphs: Two days from now, at noon.
And then, execution.
The two short words that slipped between Baeksang’s lips shot through my mind like bullets.
Execution in two days? Mine?
I swallowed the question rising in my throat. I couldn’t let Baeksang see me shaken. Not here.
Instead of giving in to despair, I tried the escape route that had already shut me out several times.
Logout.
Beep!
System Logout failed! Logout is unavailable in certain situations!
Fuck. Still doesn’t work.
I made myself speak calmly.
“Two days. Sooner than I expected.”
“My late father always said that once you’ve made up your mind, you should draw your sword without hesitation.”
“You’re not drawing that sword alone, are you?”
“I was the first to grasp its hilt, but I won’t be alone when it swings for your neck. Not even the Palace Lord can stop it.”
He won’t be swinging that sword alone...
I considered what he meant, then muttered almost to myself, “You must have been busy, reaching out to people all over the place in such a short time.”
“Twenty tribal chieftains, including me, have already joined together,” Baeksang said dryly. “And the matter on the agenda for the final day of the Tribal Grand Council will be...”
“Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan. No—my execution, now that I’m a criminal whose sins outrage heaven and humanity.”
“You understand quickly.”
“I’d have to be a fucking idiot not to, with things already this far along. Anyway, is that why you threw me into the underground prison first?”
“Of course. It was the easiest way. Though I didn’t expect you to surrender so readily.”
Baeksang did not deny it. Like a hunter looking down at captured prey, he gazed at me, bound by iron balls weighing nearly ten thousand geun, and continued in a low voice.
“To catch a tiger, you have to venture into the mountains and take the risk. But a tiger locked inside a cage is a different matter, wouldn’t you say?”
“I suppose so. Especially when there are twenty hunters instead of one.”
Baeksang had always had plenty of tribal chieftains behind him. But twenty?
That was more than half the thirty who remained after Heugung and Yohi disappeared. Some of the chieftains who had stood with the Beast Miao King had switched sides.
“What exactly did you promise them?”
“Revival for their tribes. Greater influence and enormous wealth.”
“Well. I figured it was something like that, but it’s damn simple.”
“But more than anything, it is effective.”
Maybe he was so candid because he knew we were alone. Whatever the reason, Baeksang was more honest today than I’d ever heard him. Worse, I couldn’t deny what he said.
The Nanman Beast Palace was an alliance of tribes. Each chieftain had sized up the situation and bet on the side most likely to win.
For the future of the tribe he ruled. For the wealth and glory he stood to gain.
And...
“The one who stands to gain the most is right in front of me. You’re going to take all of Nanman, aren’t you?”
Baeksang said nothing. I let out a hollow laugh.
“Interesting. It’s rotten right down to the roots.”
Baeksang had been watching me as though he could read my mind. Now he spoke without warning.
“Have you ever lived through a war?”
“What?”
“I asked if you have ever lived through a war.”
Why bring this up now?
I had no idea what he was after, but as the tiger in the cage, I didn’t have much choice except to listen.
“I lived through all of it. More than fifty years ago, I arrived in the Central Plains with the Palace Lord and ten thousand warriors. The first thing I saw was hell on earth.”
He went on, slowly and evenly.

“Fields were trampled flat. Blue rivers filled with blood and corpses. Every day—every moment, it seemed—people died across the land. Children who had lost their parents to the war were so hungry they tore bark from trees and ate it without even noticing their teeth being pulled out.”
War was always horrific. Someone might win in the end, but the road to victory was strewn with screams and death. Neither side could avoid it.

“It was a hellscape unlike anything I—or even the Palace Lord—had ever seen before. But we had a reason to fight, so none of us retreated. If the Demonic Cult took control of the Central Plains, Nanman would be next. We were there to protect the homeland where my family and friends lived.”
Baeksang’s voice echoed through the dark underground prison.

“More lives were lost than I could count. Some died fighting the enemy. Others sat staring at the sky after a battle and took their own lives. Sometimes we had to strike a lethal acupoint for a comrade writhing in pain.”

“Battle after battle, some died and the rest grew weary. But as the war turned in our favor, the hope we carried grew stronger. Soon we could go home. See the women we loved, our aging parents, or the children who must have grown so much while we were away.”
I hadn’t lived through it, but I could feel it. I hadn’t seen it, but I could picture it.

Ten thousand warriors making their way through jungles, across the Yangtze, over plains and mountains, until they finally reached the distant Central Plains. Then fighting the Demonic Cult’s Hundred Thousand Demonic Disciples as they surged in from every direction, day after day.

“When I stopped to count, fewer than one-tenth of the ten thousand warriors were still alive. Even the tide of battle, which had been slowly turning in our favor, eventually fell into a stalemate. The Palace Lord and I began to wonder why we had to remain there.”
Time was a law no one could oppose. Before that absolute law, which could move mountains and dry up rivers, even a master who had reached the Supreme Peak realm could do nothing.
It must have worn them down. Slowly, until they couldn’t bear any more.
As I thought it, Baeksang continued.
“Then, more than a decade into the war, the Martial God defeated the Heavenly Demon.”

The result of that life-and-death duel that shook heaven and earth was the Martial God’s victory. Once the Demonic Cult—which had devoured half the world—lost its central figure, the Heavenly Demon, it collapsed like a sandcastle.

“The remnants of the Demonic Cult retreated west. The Murim Alliance intended to pursue them to the end and wipe them out. With the Martial God—whom no one could stop now—at the fore, the Three Saints, the Ten Kings, and countless orthodox martial artists of the Murim Alliance advanced from every direction. We went with them.”

The balance had already been shifting toward the orthodox factions. With the Heavenly Demon dead, there was hardly a contest left. All they had to do was pursue the Hundred Thousand Demonic Disciples, now a defeated army, and root them out of the Central Plains.
“The war was as good as over. No. It should have been.”
Baeksang fell silent and stared into empty space.
Water seeped through a hairline crack in the ceiling and struck the cold floor.
Drip. Drip-drip.
I waited, but he said nothing. At last, I spoke.
“Baekhwi. Wasn’t that his name?”
Baeksang went rigid, his eyes trembling. I’d never seen him so shaken. I gave a small nod.
“So it was. I thought I might have remembered the name wrong.”
Crunch.
Something cracked between his clenched teeth. He looked at me, his eyes cold.
“Who told you that name?”
It had been Yayul Mok, but Baeksang didn’t need to know that.
I answered calmly.
“Does that really matter? What matters is that there’s still someone who remembers the name Baekhwi.”
“Someone like you has no right to speak that name.”
Whoosh!
Blade-sharp killing intent surged from Baeksang and shot through the gaps in the iron bars.
But why?
Strangely, I wasn’t afraid.
Maybe I felt a little compassion for a father who had lost his young child long ago. Whatever else Baeksang was, that was how I felt toward him now.
Baekhwi.
Baek, white. Hwi, shining.
A person’s name. Baeksang’s only child, whom he had cherished so dearly. Someone who would have become the Beast Miao King’s son-in-law if he had lived.
If he had lived.
I muttered the words inwardly, then ignored the killing intent pouring from Baeksang and asked,
“Did he lose his life while pursuing the Demonic Cult? Or...”
Boom! Rumble!
The rest of my question vanished beneath a roar. A tremendous shock wave shook the prison.
Baeksang had pulverized a section of wall with a single punch. He stared at me with eyes like frost.
“Do you want to die here and now?”
Considering my current situation, it was a fairly threatening statement. If Hyuk Mujin had been in my place, he probably would have pissed himself and begun practicing silent meditation.
But there were exceptions. Cheongpung might be a little excited because dying would be a first for him.
And then there was me, whose liver had probably enlarged from being knocked around everywhere.
“That wouldn’t be so bad. Though you can’t kill me right now anyway.”
“What?”

“There must be a reason you put off my execution for two days. Of course, that wasn’t a decision you made alone, either. Was it an order from the Southern Heaven Demon Empress? I heard you exchange missives on the first day of every month.”
“So stop posturing and tell me the story. Being locked alone in an underground prison gets lonely and boring. The Sichuan Tang Clan at least had other prisoners, so it wasn’t so bad.”
“You bastard!”
His shout rang through the prison. Trembling with rage, Baeksang reached out and seized the iron bars.
Creeeak!
Steel as thick as an adult’s forearm bent like taffy. Baeksang stepped through the gap, his eyes cold enough to sting.
“Hwi. Is that child’s death so amusing to you? Are you that curious?”
His aura was so vicious that it seemed he might draw his sword and cut me down at any moment.
But I did not care.
He feared the Southern Heaven Demon Empress too much to kill me here, and there was something I needed to know.
“I don’t find it amusing. But I am curious about one thing.”
“You truly—”
“Tell me.”
I cut him off in a flat voice, then continued slowly.
“Not how your only child died. I want to know what kind of lunatics turned you into one.”
“Tell me that.”
A heavy silence followed. Every second felt like fifteen minutes before Baeksang finally opened his mouth.
“Gansu. Great Snow Mountain.”
Haa...
His breath trembled. White vapor spilled into the freezing air of the underground prison, like the heavy snow that must have fallen that day.
“Back then, we were leading the Southern Army alongside the Zhongnan Sect.”
I swallowed the words that tried to burst out of me.
Oh, fuck. The Zhongnan Sect.
