chapters.title: Chapter 662
paragraphs: Was it about ten years ago? Back when I was devouring martial-arts novels, I sometimes found myself wondering.
No, more than sometimes.
What would I do if I were the protagonist of this novel?
It’s a little embarrassing to think about now, but I couldn’t help it. Anyone who’s read enough web novels comes with that feature built in.
I’d wonder whenever some idiot protagonist had a System window but never raised his Intelligence. Or whenever a female character appeared and he made an ass of himself.
If it were me...
That was how the fantasies always began.
But once I became a martial artist in the Murim, I learned that fantasy was fantasy and reality was reality.
All those masterpieces of martial fiction I’d read were nothing more than brilliantly arranged words on a page. The protagonists I’d thought were so cool didn’t exist in this world.
Old Master.
What.
There’s something I’ve been wondering about the Heavenly Demon. His surname wouldn’t happen to be Muk, would it?
...What the hell are you talking about all of a sudden? Not long ago, you were spouting off about things like the Wudang Demon Sword and the Huashan Gale Sword—titles I’ve never heard of in my life.
At first, I was sorry I’d never get to meet the protagonists from those novels, but I wasn’t disappointed. The martial artists of this world were pretty damn cool in their own right.
If anything had thoroughly shattered my fantasies, though, it was...
“We were leading the Southern Army alongside the Zhongnan Sect at the time.”
Right. Those three words that had just come out of Baeksang’s mouth.
The Zhongnan Sect.
A towering pillar of the orthodox Murim. One of the Nine Sects and One Gang. A prestigious sect that had endured for hundreds of years and shared Shaanxi Province with its eternal rival, Huashan.
No—I should probably say they used to share it.

The Sword Saint, Mae Jonghak, who had remained hidden from the world for so many years, was now the Alliance Leader. The Disciple he had taken in during his later years had gained tremendous fame, and as a result, the influence of their sect, Huashan, had grown to an extent that could not be compared to the past.
And the Zhongnan Sect?
Two of its three Supreme Peak masters are laid up and wheezing.
Jeok Cheongang had crushed the Roaring Fury Swordsman, and I’d crushed the Taeeul Merciless Sword.
At least Hyuk Sopyung, the young prodigy around my age known as the Zhongnan One Dragon, was a fairly decent guy. But so far, my impression of the Zhongnan Sect had been anything but good.
No. At least among the orthodox factions, it was the worst.
With higher-ups like that, they can forget about The Reign.
At this point, calling it the Fucknam Sect—or the Zhong-fucking-na Sect—would hardly be an exaggeration.

Well, the current Sect Leader, the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, might be different. But from everything I’d seen and heard in the Murim, my opinion of the Zhongnan Sect didn’t seem far from everyone else’s.
And now the Zhongnan Sect comes up in this story...
I could feel it. I could feel something coming.
Just as I unconsciously furrowed my brow, Baeksang continued speaking.

“The Sect Leader of the Zhongnan Sect at the time, Venerable Wusang, was righteous and wise. He stayed calm no matter what happened and treated everyone fairly, regardless of their background. That was why the Palace Lord and I agreed that he should command the Southern Army.”
“Venerable Wusang...”
“Yes. He was the master of the Zhongnan Sect’s current Sect Leader, the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord.”
I’d heard Jeok Cheongang mention the title a few times.
Granted, Jeok Cheongang usually called the Zhongnan Sect “a bunch of ill-mannered sons of bitches.” But even he’d described Venerable Wusang as “soft, but a fine man.”

“The trouble began soon after we entered Gansu. Defeated soldiers from the surrounding areas, who had been retreating in disarray, gathered at Great Snow Mountain. There were no fewer than two thousand of them.”
“...How the hell did two thousand defeated soldiers turn up in the surrounding area?”
“Do you think they were called the Hundred Thousand Demonic Disciples for nothing? They had lost the Heavenly Demon, but their numbers were still nothing to dismiss.”
“So what happened? Was there a battle at Great Snow Mountain?”
Baeksang slowly nodded.

“It was a battle we had every reason to win. At the time, the Western Army we belonged to had Venerable Wusang, a Supreme Peak master, as well as the Palace Lord, who had only just begun to be called the Beast Miao King. We were not inferior in either the number or the quality of our troops. If anything, we had a considerable advantage.”
“Sounds like the Western Army was pretty large.”
“Over four thousand in all. The enemy had no Supreme Peak master of note, so we had no reason to avoid the fight.”
“Hmm.”
Two Supreme Peak masters the enemy didn’t have. More than twice as many troops. And they were facing a defeated force already worn down by exhaustion and despair.
Anyone could see how that fight ought to end.
But if it had been that easy, Baeksang wouldn’t have lost his only son.
“There was a trap?”
Baeksang answered my sudden question in a voice as dry as sand.
“Yes. We split into three groups and advanced into Great Snow Mountain. What awaited us wasn’t a band of defeated soldiers, but an elite strike force of the Demonic Cult.”
“It was chaos from beginning to end. Arrows poured down like rain from above the gorge, while rocks weighing hundreds or thousands of geun crushed people and blocked the narrow paths.”
“By the time we knew it was a trap, it was too late. We fought desperately. Then I looked up and realized someone who should always have been at my side was gone.”
He didn’t say the name, but I knew he wasn’t talking about the Beast Miao King.
Baekhwi.
Baeksang’s only child. The heir who would inherit everything he had.
To set an example as a great chieftain, he had taken his young child with him to the battlefield. But he had probably cherished his son more than his own life.
And then, on a battlefield painted with corpses and blood, the fine young man he had raised had vanished without a trace during the final battle.
“For the first time, I was afraid. Hwi... That child was everything to me. No, more than that.”
Baeksang’s voice was hollow.

“But I had to regain my composure, if only for the warriors under my command. First, I requested support from the Zhongnan Sect and the other orthodox martial artists who had entered the area not far away. Then I helped the Palace Lord fight the enemy.”
The ambush had caught them by surprise. The fighting had been fierce, but the Beast Miao King, Baeksang, and the Nanman warriors had refused to retreat.
They fought harder than ever and finally won, though it cost them countless lives.
“Only after the battle in the gorge ended did I learn where he had gone. He and dozens of warriors had pursued some of the enemy down a side path. I was relieved.”
“Why?” I asked.
“The path connected to territory that definitely belonged to our allies. I believed that the people who had received my request for support would have saved Hwi—that child.”
I closed my mouth.
It wasn’t anger or grief that broke a person. It was trust.
And when that trust was betrayed, despair followed. I could see it in Baeksang now.
“What do you think happened?”
I didn’t answer. He probably hadn’t expected me to. After a moment, he went on.

“He... didn’t even leave a body behind. The corpses of the warriors who went with him lay scattered everywhere, hacked apart by an enemy we couldn’t identify. Only later did I learn it was the Great Snow Fiend, the fiend who ruled Great Snow Mountain.”

“Reinforcements? There were no such things. They said the messenger who had set out to request support had been killed by the enemy while on his way to the other allied forces. I was overwhelmed by grief and despair, unable to do anything. And it was only later that I learned the truth.”
At that moment, Baeksang’s entire body trembled.
And I saw an emotion rise in eyes that had always been cold and still.
“The messenger wasn’t killed by the enemy. He was killed by our allies.”
Anger. Hatred.
“They weren’t unable to help us. They chose not to.”
It was the quiet, desperate scream of a man whose trust had been betrayed.
“If they had come, he could have lived. But they did not come. They killed the messenger, ignored my desperate request, and chose to pursue the retreating enemy instead. Do you know why?”
What pools up will eventually overflow. Baeksang had spent decades letting it out, yet the hatred and betrayal kept filling him until they spilled over again.
As they did now.
“Because we were nothing but savages from the Outer Lands!”
“Because we weren’t Han Chinese like them, could never become Han Chinese, and they couldn’t sacrifice themselves for savages like us!”
Boom! Crash!
A powerful, violent wave of energy whipped through the air.
The floor and walls, made from solid rock, crumbled. Streams of tangible internal energy poured from his fist and grazed my face.
Ssst!
A sharp pain stung my forehead. I felt hot blood run down it.
But I didn’t move. I only watched, waiting until Baeksang’s eyes, flashing with killing intent, turned toward me.
“The Central Plains—the Han Chinese—betrayed us. We reached out to them when they were most desperate, and after we’d fought for them at the risk of our lives for ten years, they betrayed us!”
Decades of hatred were aimed squarely at me.
Only then did I open my mouth.
“Why didn’t you tell Venerable Wusang? He would’ve brought everything to light.”
“Venerable Wusang?”
Baeksang laughed. It was the first time I’d heard him laugh, and the sound was so empty it hardly counted.
“Yes. He would have. If he’d been alive.”
“You mean...”

“His Internal Injury had flared up before the battle. He fought anyway, and the Great Snow Fiend killed him. Enraged by his death, the Zhongnan Sect killed the messenger we sent, ignored our request for help, and pursued the enemy. The dozens of other sects, large and small, assigned to the Western Army did the same.”
“What?”

“You find it hard to believe? So did I. Only one person—the Palace Lord—tried to uncover the truth of it all. But when the Great Faction War ended, every pretense and every ugly stain was buried with it.”

“Then, while everyone but us basked in victory and peace, the messenger’s body disappeared from where it had been kept. The last piece of evidence, bearing traces of the Zhongnan Sect’s martial arts, was gone.”
These fucking lunatics.
I swallowed a groan.
I could barely breathe. If Baeksang was telling the truth, no one—not even me—could condemn his anger.
He’d fought with his life on the line, and betrayal was all he got in return.
The most fucked-up part of all this was the instinctive certainty that this long-ago incident, which had left behind not even a shred of evidence, had probably really happened.
Damn it.
When I first came to the Murim, I’d been counted among the Han Chinese. I knew how people from the Central Plains looked at the people of Nanman.
I knew how shallow human feelings could be, and how easily greed took hold.
Baeksang had kept fighting for victory even after his son disappeared. The allies he trusted hadn’t done the same.

Enraged by Venerable Wusang’s death, the Zhongnan Sect had ignored the Nanman Beast Palace’s plea and chased the enemy. The other sects of the Western Army had been blinded by fear of losing their own men and greed for credit.
And the result of everything they’d done was standing right in front of me.
“You said earlier that this land—Nanman—was rotten.”
Drip. Trickle.
In the aftermath of what had just happened, foul-smelling water poured from the cracked ceiling.
Beyond the falling water, Baeksang’s eyes gleamed coldly.
“That day, you people showed me what I had to do.”

chapters.title: Chapter 663
paragraphs: “That day, you people showed me which path I should take.”
With those words spat out in a bitter voice, his story—neither short nor long—came to an end. I silently stared into Baeksang’s coldly gleaming eyes.
What did I want to say to him?
I wasn’t sure.

The man standing before me in dazzling white robes had lived through a darkness I couldn’t begin to imagine. He had fought for a righteous cause, only to be betrayed. He had lost the child he cherished more than his own life.
There could only be one reason he had kept living.
Revenge.
Baeksang wasn’t wrong. After he lost his only child, the betrayal of the Central Plains people had lit a torch in the darkness where he wandered. By its light, he’d found the only path he could see.
The path of revenge.
He had followed that thorny road of pain and fury all the way here. Looking at him, I suddenly remembered someone else.
“...The Head Elder.”
Confusion flickered in Baeksang’s eyes at my involuntary mutter. I clicked my tongue bitterly.
“It’s nothing. You just reminded me of someone I used to know.”
“How so?”
“He was a fucking idiot, too. Just like you. A puppet controlled by Dark Heaven.”
“What?”
“But I could understand him. He had his reasons.”
“...He was betrayed.”
“Yeah. By his own flesh and blood.”
Baeksang looked down at me in silence. Then he asked, “What happened to him?”
“I killed him. With my own hands.”
“He was an elder of my family, but I had no choice. Things had already gone too far.”
“Do you wish to condemn me?”
I let out a short laugh.
Condemn him? What would that change now?
“Condemning someone with words alone doesn’t do a damn thing. It wouldn’t stop you. That was the main reason I had to kill the Head Elder.”
That was how an avenger met his end.
They stepped onto a path they had never wanted to take, then lost their way forever. They were like moths rushing toward a single torch—the torch of revenge.
“After I killed him, I wondered something. If the Jin Family of Taiyuan and I had lost that battle... would getting his revenge have finally made him happy?”
“That...”
“Probably not. He lived only for revenge, but at some point, his anger must have dulled, and watching innocent people be sacrificed must have left him feeling guilty.”
I didn’t wait for Baeksang to answer.
“Just like you do now.”
I calmly looked into Baeksang’s twisted face.

“I definitely don’t understand you. I’ve never gone through what you did, and I’ve never burned with revenge for decades. But at the same time, I admit it. At least as far as I’m concerned, your anger toward the Central Plains people and the Han Chinese is justified.”
“Justified?” Baeksang repeated, his face rigid.
He clearly hadn’t expected that answer, but I meant every word. I meant what I said next, too.
“Yeah. I would’ve done the same thing if I were you. No—if I had been in your place, perhaps the entire Central Plains would already have been my enemy.”
I remembered the day I’d gone to the Ares Guild.
I had been alone then, but there hadn’t been the slightest hesitation in my steps.
It wasn’t because I had possessed enough strength to make that choice. It was because I had been genuinely furious over Kim Hwajong’s death.
And I had brought down the Ares Guild.
If I’d been Baeksang instead of Jin Taekyung, I would have fought to bring down the Central Plains.
But...
“Is that anger of yours justified toward the people of Nanman, too?”
“Some of them might understand you. But what did the people killed because you joined forces with Dark Heaven do wrong? What about their families? Their lovers and friends?”
Baeksang jerked. I kept my voice steady.

“When I first set foot in Nanman, I heard some news. A Miao village had been massacred by a group of Han Chinese. Those Han Chinese had slaughtered a hundred people, men, women, and children alike, but in the end, both sides had been destroyed by poison.”
Being locked alone in an underground prison gave me plenty of time to think. I’d gone over everything that had happened since I arrived, and I was certain of one thing.
“No matter how I look at it, it’s strange. Even if there was a fight, how did not one person survive?”
It had been planned from the beginning. Wipe out a Miao village, and hostility toward the Han Chinese would boil over across all of Nanman.

“And that’s not all. There were the Thousand-Year Spiders suddenly leaving the Poisonblood Grounds, and what happened at the Western Yao Estate. Add the Miao village, and the dead number well over three hundred.”
All that had happened in just seven days and nights since I came to the Nanman Beast Palace. Compared with the decades Baeksang had spent consumed by revenge, it was barely any time at all.
What frightened me more was what lay ahead. If Baeksang was to have his revenge in full, war with the Central Plains wasn’t merely possible. It was inevitable.
“Just how...”
I looked at him, torn between pity and anger.
How much more blood are you going to spill, Baeksang?
Splash. Splash.
With each step, foul water long pooled on the prison floor splashed in every direction. The man walking through it paid no attention to his snow-white robes getting dirty.
No—his mind was so full that he hadn’t noticed.
Splash...
His already-soaked leather shoes came to an abrupt stop.
While crossing the underground prison alone, the middle-aged man, Baeksang, suddenly looked back over his shoulder.
Dark. Cold. Silent.
Like the path he had walked. Like the path the man imprisoned behind him would have to walk.

But Jin Taekyung would never walk as far as he had. Only two days remained until his public execution. Baeksang’s path had stretched across decades; Jin Taekyung’s was short, with its end in plain sight.
It’s as good as over. He won’t escape.
Baeksang already knew roughly how skilled Jin Taekyung was. A Supreme Peak master who stood out even in the Central Plains, where countless prestigious sects had taken root.
Baeksang hadn’t used his full strength when they briefly exchanged moves a few days ago. Still, he had known instinctively.
Half a move above me. No... perhaps a full move.

Jin Taekyung was a monster beyond anything Baeksang had imagined. But with his internal energy sealed and iron balls of enormous weight restraining him, he couldn’t survive even if his master, the Fire King, came for him.
Besides, something bound him more tightly than the iron balls.
The Han Chinese under his command.
Jin Taekyung cared about his people. That was why he had surrendered and allowed himself to be imprisoned instead of escaping.
What a fool.
In Baeksang’s eyes, compassion was the monstrous young man’s greatest weakness. Nothing made a martial artist less like a martial artist.
And yet nothing made a person more human.
On the day blood stained the snow of Great Snow Mountain, that was what Baeksang had so desperately wanted from his allies.
Come to think of it, Hwi was about his age then.
Baeksang stared blankly into the empty air. In the darkness where nothing existed, a face briefly passed through his mind.
An infant becoming a boy. A boy becoming a young man.
His only child, more upright than anyone, who had shone as brightly as his name, Hwi.
The smiling face of the child he would never see again.
Crunch.
Without realizing it, Baeksang clenched his fist tightly. His neatly trimmed nails dug into his flesh, and blood began to flow.
Drip. Drip-drip.
He looked down. Red drops spread through the stagnant water around his feet. Each small ripple traced the outline of a face.
How much more blood are you going to spill, Baeksang?
Jin Taekyung’s last words kept ringing in his ears. But Baeksang’s answer was the same now as it had been then.
I crossed that river long ago. I can never go back.
He had crossed that river a long time ago.
Half-mad with despair and rage, Baeksang had met a beautiful woman whose identity he did not know. She had offered him something more alluring than her looks.
No. Something he could not refuse.
Choose. Do so, and it will surely come to pass.
He hadn’t hesitated. With a purpose to live for, he had gladly taken her outstretched hand. He had never once regretted that decision.
No. He must not regret it.
But why...?
With the fruit of all those decades almost within his grasp, why was he wavering now?
Baeksang swallowed the sound rising in his throat and gritted his teeth. He looked at his filthy leather shoes and the hems of robes that could no longer be called white.
In two days. Everything ends. Everything.
At his feet, drops of blood spread through the pooled water. Dirty long before his blood touched it, the water slowly turned red.
Like the path he had walked. Like the path still ahead of him.
Splash.
Baeksang stamped through the puddle and started walking again, Jin Taekyung’s voice still echoing in his ears through the silence.
Baeksang left, and I was alone again.
The chains pulled taut around me, and the iron balls weighing ten thousand geun held me fast. My whole body was growing stiff.
Damn.
Now that he was gone, I kind of wished he’d stayed. Maybe I should have begged him to spare me.

Still, I didn’t regret it. I’d said everything I needed to say, and groveling for my life wouldn’t have gotten me anywhere. Baeksang had lived for revenge alone. He wasn’t going to tear up like an auntie watching a human-interest documentary just because I begged him.
That didn’t mean I planned to let them drag me out in two days and quietly put me to death.
Are you crazy? I have to survive somehow.
I’d meant it when I said his anger was justified. That didn’t mean I deserved to die at his hands. As far as I was concerned, the Head Elder and Baeksang were both idiots with tragic stories.
And I intended to stop this new idiot I had met after traveling all the way to a foreign land, no matter what it took.
But how do I get out?
All that talking and thinking had left my throat dry. I was swallowing what little spit I had when something cold touched the top of my head.
Tap.
“Huh?”
It was water. It might have been stale and tasteless, but the important thing was that it was water. The ceiling had probably opened up farther when Baeksang smashed the surrounding walls.
Well, that helps.
I muttered inwardly and tilted my head back toward the ceiling.
The next moment, through the crack in the ceiling, I found myself looking into a pair of eyes I hadn’t expected to see.
Huge, clear eyes like a calf’s.
“...Why are you up there?”
Their owner answered.
“Taishan. Hungry. Got locked in underground prison because they said Taishan eats too much.”
“Ah.”
Fair enough.

sentences.text: “That day, you people showed me which path I should take.”
With those words spat out in a bitter voice, his story—neither short nor long—came to an end.
I silently stared into Baeksang’s coldly gleaming eyes.
What did I want to say to him?
I wasn’t sure.
The man standing before me in dazzling white robes had lived through a darkness I couldn’t begin to imagine.
He had fought for a righteous cause, only to be betrayed.
He had lost the child he cherished more than his own life.
There could only be one reason he had kept living.
Revenge.
Baeksang wasn’t wrong.
After he lost his only child, the betrayal of the Central Plains people had lit a torch in the darkness where he wandered.
By its light, he’d found the only path he could see.
The path of revenge.
He had followed that thorny road of pain and fury all the way here.
Looking at him, I suddenly remembered someone else.
“...The Head Elder.”
Confusion flickered in Baeksang’s eyes at my involuntary mutter.
I clicked my tongue bitterly.
“It’s nothing.
You just reminded me of someone I used to know.”
“How so?”
“He was a fucking idiot, too.
Just like you.
A puppet controlled by Dark Heaven.”
“What?”
“But I could understand him.
He had his reasons.”
“...He was betrayed.”
“Yeah.
By his own flesh and blood.”
Baeksang looked down at me in silence.
Then he asked, “What happened to him?”
“I killed him.
With my own hands.”
“He was an elder of my family, but I had no choice.
Things had already gone too far.”
“Do you wish to condemn me?”
I let out a short laugh.
Condemn him?
What would that change now?
“Condemning someone with words alone doesn’t do a damn thing.
It wouldn’t stop you.
That was the main reason I had to kill the Head Elder.”
That was how an avenger met his end.
They stepped onto a path they had never wanted to take, then lost their way forever.
They were like moths rushing toward a single torch—the torch of revenge.
“After I killed him, I wondered something.
If the Jin Family of Taiyuan and I had lost that battle... would getting his revenge have finally made him happy?”
“That...”
“Probably not.
He lived only for revenge, but at some point, his anger must have dulled, and watching innocent people be sacrificed must have left him feeling guilty.”
I didn’t wait for Baeksang to answer.
“Just like you do now.”
I calmly looked into Baeksang’s twisted face.
“I definitely don’t understand you.
I’ve never gone through what you did, and I’ve never burned with revenge for decades.
But at the same time, I admit it.
At least as far as I’m concerned, your anger toward the Central Plains people and the Han Chinese is justified.”
“Justified?” Baeksang repeated, his face rigid.
He clearly hadn’t expected that answer, but I meant every word.
I meant what I said next, too.
“Yeah.
I would’ve done the same thing if I were you.
No—if I had been in your place, perhaps the entire Central Plains would already have been my enemy.”
I remembered the day I’d gone to the Ares Guild.
I had been alone then, but there hadn’t been the slightest hesitation in my steps.
It wasn’t because I had possessed enough strength to make that choice.
It was because I had been genuinely furious over Kim Hwajong’s death.
And I had brought down the Ares Guild.
If I’d been Baeksang instead of Jin Taekyung, I would have fought to bring down the Central Plains.
But...
“Is that anger of yours justified toward the people of Nanman, too?”
“Some of them might understand you.
But what did the people killed because you joined forces with Dark Heaven do wrong?
What about their families?
Their lovers and friends?”
Baeksang jerked.
I kept my voice steady.
“When I first set foot in Nanman, I heard some news.
A Miao village had been massacred by a group of Han Chinese.
Those Han Chinese had slaughtered a hundred people, men, women, and children alike, but in the end, both sides had been destroyed by poison.”
Being locked alone in an underground prison gave me plenty of time to think.
I’d gone over everything that had happened since I arrived, and I was certain of one thing.
“No matter how I look at it, it’s strange.
Even if there was a fight, how did not one person survive?”
It had been planned from the beginning.
Wipe out a Miao village, and hostility toward the Han Chinese would boil over across all of Nanman.
“And that’s not all.
There were the Thousand-Year Spiders suddenly leaving the Poisonblood Grounds, and what happened at the Western Yao Estate.
Add the Miao village, and the dead number well over three hundred.”
All that had happened in just seven days and nights since I came to the Nanman Beast Palace.
Compared with the decades Baeksang had spent consumed by revenge, it was barely any time at all.
What frightened me more was what lay ahead.
If Baeksang was to have his revenge in full, war with the Central Plains wasn’t merely possible.
It was inevitable.
“Just how...”
I looked at him, torn between pity and anger.
How much more blood are you going to spill, Baeksang?
Splash.
Splash.
With each step, foul water long pooled on the prison floor splashed in every direction.
The man walking through it paid no attention to his snow-white robes getting dirty.
No—his mind was so full that he hadn’t noticed.
Splash...
His already-soaked leather shoes came to an abrupt stop.
While crossing the underground prison alone, the middle-aged man, Baeksang, suddenly looked back over his shoulder.
Dark.
Cold.
Silent.
Like the path he had walked.
Like the path the man imprisoned behind him would have to walk.
But Jin Taekyung would never walk as far as he had.
Only two days remained until his public execution.
Baeksang’s path had stretched across decades; Jin Taekyung’s was short, with its end in plain sight.
It’s as good as over.
He won’t escape.
Baeksang already knew roughly how skilled Jin Taekyung was.
A Supreme Peak master who stood out even in the Central Plains, where countless prestigious sects had taken root.
Baeksang hadn’t used his full strength when they briefly exchanged moves a few days ago.
Still, he had known instinctively.
Half a move above me.
No... perhaps a full move.
Jin Taekyung was a monster beyond anything Baeksang had imagined.
But with his internal energy sealed and iron balls of enormous weight restraining him, he couldn’t survive even if his master, the Fire King, came for him.
Besides, something bound him more tightly than the iron balls.
The Han Chinese under his command.
Jin Taekyung cared about his people.
That was why he had surrendered and allowed himself to be imprisoned instead of escaping.
What a fool.
In Baeksang’s eyes, compassion was the monstrous young man’s greatest weakness.
Nothing made a martial artist less like a martial artist.
And yet nothing made a person more human.
On the day blood stained the snow of Great Snow Mountain, that was what Baeksang had so desperately wanted from his allies.
Come to think of it, Hwi was about his age then.
Baeksang stared blankly into the empty air.

A boy becoming a young man.
His only child, more upright than anyone, who had shone as brightly as his name, Hwi.
The smiling face of the child he would never see again.
Crunch.

His neatly trimmed nails dug into his flesh, and blood began to flow.

Everything ends.
Everything.

paragraphs: Unlike modern prisons, where human rights have been mixed in just enough to make them palatable, underground prisons in the Murim served their purpose exceptionally well.
The concept of human rights didn’t exist here in the first place.
The underground prison of the Sichuan Tang Clan, for example, had been closer to a torture chamber than a place meant to hold prisoners.
Even the old guard who had died during Dark Heaven’s attack had been a torture expert with decades of experience. He would often reminisce about his prime with a pleased smile.
“Those days right after the Great Faction War were wonderful. We had three or four head of notorious fiends brought in every day.”
“...Head? Not people?”
“Yes. When we lined up fifteen or so of the beasts and got to work, the response was incredible. They were so happy they nearly passed out.”
He even counted people the way you counted animals.

I had never bothered to ask for details, but it was hard to imagine prisoners screaming with delight because he’d given them pretty irezumi tattoos with the small knife he kept tucked so carefully into his belt.
Like hell they were tattoos.
It was obvious.
Bones and flesh splitting apart, blood spraying everywhere—something like that.
I’d gone a little off track. Anyway, most underground prisons in the Murim were more or less the same.
Cold, damp, and nine times out of ten, buried deep underground.
Just like the underground prison of the Nanman Beast Palace where I was locked up. And...
“Pavilion Master. Taishan hungry. Got locked in underground prison because Taishan eats too much.”
“Ah.”
The difference between me and that accursed bastard was only one floor.
The third and fourth underground floors, for example.
So this is how it turned out.
In a way, it was a coincidence born of an aging, poorly built prison taking a considerable blow.
I stared blankly at the ceiling, then gave a quiet laugh at Taishan, who was blinking his enormous eyes through the small hole above me.
“Pavilion Master, why laugh?”
“Because I’m happy to see you.”
“Happy? Pavilion Master happy to see Taishan?”
“Yeah, you bastard. I’m so happy I could die.”
“Oh. Then Taishan happy to see Pavilion Master too.”
It was a conversation that made no sense out of context, but every time I saw his eyes peering through the gap, I couldn’t help laughing.
Seeing a familiar face was one thing. If things went well, I might be able to get out of here sooner than expected.
Besides, Taishan was the only person who could answer the question worrying me most.
“What about everyone else? They’re all doing okay, right?”
At my question, his enormous calf-like eyes filled with tears.
“Are you... crying?”
“Sniff. Pavilion Master.”
No way.
Dread hit me. I hurried to ask, “Stop sniveling and tell me what happened.”
“Taishan... sniff. Couldn’t help it. It’s so unfair.”
Damn it. My vision went dark. I could already picture the members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion lying there as cold corpses.
Or were they tortured? But how could they do that?
It had only been half a day since I’d surrendered on the condition that the Fire Dragon Pavilion members would be kept safe.
The Beast Miao King himself had promised me. No matter how powerful Baeksang’s faction had become, they couldn’t do this.
If they were harmed, then what the hell did I surrender for...?
Just as the thought ran hollowly through my head, Taishan spoke through his tears.
“I still can’t believe it. By now, everyone must be eating without Taishan.”
“Taishan hates Lord. Hates Namho too. It’s so unfair.”
“Pavilion Master. Speaking of which, do you have anything to eat?”
What the hell was going on?
I fell silent for a moment, then answered from the bottom of my heart.
“No, you fucking bastard.”
“Aw. Taishan hungry.”
“...Come down. Come down right now.”
That son of a bitch. He really wanted to die.
My blood pressure shot up, and rage took over my entire body. I thrashed harder than I had at any point since being locked in the underground prison.
Clatter! Clank!
If not for these goddamn heavy iron balls, I would have started by punching that bastard in the mouth.
Taishan watched me panting with interest before speaking.
“Namho and Lord are doing well. They’re being held in different places, so Taishan doesn’t know much, but White Tiger’s master told Taishan.”
“White Tiger’s master? Yayul Mok?”
“Oh. Taishan remembers. Right. Yayul Mok.”
It seemed the Beast Miao King had stepped in after all. I stopped thrashing and let out a sigh of relief.
“You should’ve said that first, you lunatic. You nearly gave me a heart attack.”
“Taishan hasn’t eaten for two whole shichen. Taishan’s mind is hazy.”

“...People don’t usually call it hunger after two shichen. More importantly, how did you end up locked in here? Great Hero Yayul would’ve stopped it before it got this far. There’s no way you were locked up just for eating too much.”
“Taishan was treated unfairly. A Nanman man was going to leave after giving Taishan a mouse-dropping-sized portion of food. Taishan grabbed his wrist to ask for more, and the bone broke.”
“Taishan was surprised and grabbed his other wrist. That one broke too. It was obviously a trap.”
Clatter! Clank! Clank!
“Pavilion Master, calm down. Taishan was angry too, but Taishan held it in and surrendered, just like Pavilion Master.”
“...Come down. This time, really come down.”
I was already trying to keep a low profile, and this bastard had broken both arms of the man who came to feed him?
At this rate, I was going to die of rage before noon two days from now.
I walked into the tiger’s den to save a bastard like that?
I barely managed to calm my anger before asking, “Then what about the others? Not Namho or Sama Pyo. Everyone else?”
“Hmm. Ah.”
Taishan rolled his enormous eyes around as he thought, then answered.
“I heard they were captured.”
“Captured?”
“Yeah. But they said they weren’t coming here. Taishan doesn’t know why, but White Tiger’s master said it was safer that way.”
Ju Hwaran, Song Ilseom, and Hyuk Mujin.
For a moment, my heart sank at the news that all three had been captured. But I agreed with Yayul Mok that it was much safer that way.
Baeksang’s influence can’t reach that far right now.

The two tribal chieftains leading the squad were loyal to the Beast Miao King. Some of the Nanman people I’d rescued from the Poisonblood Grounds were their kinsmen, too. Unlike the other chieftains who had gone over to Baeksang, they wouldn’t switch sides easily.
The three of them are more likely to be in danger than they are now if the reconnaissance squad runs into the Blood Monk.
The Blood Monk was an unidentified old monster who had stained Guizhou with blood single-handedly, wielding Supreme Peak martial prowess.
Almost nothing was known about him. But if he really was a subordinate of the Southern Heaven Demon Empress, as I suspected, things could take the worst possible turn.
He would certainly head south on the Southern Heaven Demon Empress’s orders. And if he encountered the reconnaissance squad, the three people among them would fall into his hands as well.
“...Damn it.”
But for now, I had no time to worry about that.
They were on the move even now, while I was trapped deep underground, unable to move an inch.
All I can do is hope I’m wrong about the Blood Monk.
So there were only two things I could do.
The first was prayer.
The second was...
Escape.
Ding.

I nodded and thought, I don’t know who developed the System, but that’s one shitty Quest title.
“So, Pavilion Master. Do you have anything to eat?”
...Correction. That bastard was the shittiest of all.
Among the countless martial artists on the continent, river pirates were an especially rough and free-spirited bunch.
They didn’t want laws restricting them or the authorities arresting them. They didn’t want to live decent lives, either.
Sudal, the Deputy Stronghold Lord of the Water Dragon Stronghold, had become a river pirate for exactly those reasons.
Unlike his father, who had lived and died a good fisherman, Sudal had boldly resolved to live and die as an adventurer.
He’d done fairly well as a river pirate. Only recently had he begun to wonder what he was doing with his life.
What the hell am I doing?
Nothing. Every day, he sat at the bow and stared at the calm river. When the sun got too hot, he went swimming. That was all.

His immediate superior, who ruled the Yangtze in Sichuan, had been summoned to League headquarters by the revered Alliance Leader. Meanwhile, Sudal and his men had come down the tributaries to backwater Yunnan and were wasting their days.
By now, merchant ships loaded with all kinds of valuable goods must be traveling through Sichuan.
The Yangtze was a gold mine right now. With war approaching, all sorts of supplies were moving along it.
Sudal knew that and desperately wanted to return immediately. But every time he did, one man’s presence kept flashing before his eyes.
“I’ll come running whenever you call!”
That was the boast he’d made seven days and nights ago. Naturally, he hadn’t meant a word of it.
But the much younger man had smiled warmly and answered,
“Oh, good. Then stay nearby.”
“Excuse me?”
“Heh heh. Did someone stick a marlin in your ear? I said stay nearby. I’ll need another favor when we head back.”
“Great Hero Jin, forgive me, but we have a living to make...”
“A living. That’s nice. But you have to be alive to make one, don’t you?”
“Come on, I’m asking a favor! Just a favor!”
“Gasp.”
“For fuck’s sake. I might just snap every mast and burn the whole lot down. Want to swim to Sichuan?”
He called it a favor, but it was a threat.
What could Sudal do? In the Murim, whoever had the stronger martial arts was king.
Worse, that monstrous young man’s Master was a crazy old monster who really was called a king.
Jin Taekyung, you bastard...

Swallowing his tears, Sudal had nodded. For more than seven days and nights, he and his men had stayed on a tributary at the edge of Yunnan where they couldn’t even spot a small boat, doing nothing but catching fish.
Until an idea occurred to him yesterday.
Wait. Why am I doing this? It’ll be a while before that Jin Taekyung bastard comes back.
Sudal had only ever operated on the Yangtze, but even he knew what a godforsaken dump Nanman was.
He didn’t know exactly what Jin Taekyung’s mission was. Still, if it had brought him all the way here, it couldn’t be simple.
But did he really need to worry about someone who wasn’t even here and whine like a dog that needed to shit?
He gave his adventurous life some serious thought, then ordered his men,
“Hey, boys. Let’s go get some fresh air.”
“Excuse me?”
“Where?”
“Guizhou’s right next door. Let’s make a sweep through it, raid the place, and come back.”
His ambitious plan didn’t go over well.
“Deputy Stronghold Lord, have you lost your mind?”
“Fuck. If you want to die, die alone. Why should the rest of us get cremated when you’re not even the Stronghold Lord?”
But Sudal had a plan for that, too.
“Dunk that bastard. The Yangtze... the Yangtze...”
“The Yangtze dip?”
“Yeah. That thing Jin Taekyung does all the time.”
After sending two of them into the water one after another, the complaints disappeared. Under Sudal’s spirited command, three swift ships traveled along the western tributary toward Guizhou.
At last, after all this time, they found a target.
Just like now.
“There’s a ship roughly two hundred zhang ahead!”
“Seize it! Don’t let it get away!”
How long had it been since their last raid? Sudal stood tall at the stern like a Great General, smiling with satisfaction as the ship drew rapidly closer.
Then, before fifteen minutes had passed, he realized something was wrong.
Whoosh!
The ship was almost upon them now. There was no crew and no captain.
Only one person waited for them.
“A swift ship of the Yangtze River Channel League. What fortunate timing.”
The bald, middle-aged man holding a blood-soaked Zen staff smiled broadly at the frozen Sudal.
“Does this ship go to Nanman too?”

Taishan grabbed his wrist to ask for more, and the bone broke.”
“Taishan was surprised and grabbed his other wrist.
That one broke too.
It was obviously a trap.”
Clatter!
Clank!
Clank!
“Pavilion Master, calm down.
Taishan was angry too, but Taishan held it in and surrendered, just like Pavilion Master.”
“...Come down.
This time, really come down.”
I was already trying to keep a low profile, and this bastard had broken both arms of the man who came to feed him?
At this rate, I was going to die of rage before noon two days from now.
I walked into the tiger’s den to save a bastard like that?
I barely managed to calm my anger before asking, “Then what about the others?
Not Namho or Sama Pyo.
Everyone else?”
“Hmm.
Ah.”
Taishan rolled his enormous eyes around as he thought, then answered.
“I heard they were captured.”
“Captured?”
“Yeah.
But they said they weren’t coming here.
Taishan doesn’t know why, but White Tiger’s master said it was safer that way.”
Ju Hwaran, Song Ilseom, and Hyuk Mujin.
For a moment, my heart sank at the news that all three had been captured.
But I agreed with Yayul Mok that it was much safer that way.
Baeksang’s influence can’t reach that far right now.
The two tribal chieftains leading the squad were loyal to the Beast Miao King.
Some of the Nanman people I’d rescued from the Poisonblood Grounds were their kinsmen, too.
Unlike the other chieftains who had gone over to Baeksang, they wouldn’t switch sides easily.
The three of them are more likely to be in danger than they are now if the reconnaissance squad runs into the Blood Monk.
The Blood Monk was an unidentified old monster who had stained Guizhou with blood single-handedly, wielding Supreme Peak martial prowess.
Almost nothing was known about him.
But if he really was a subordinate of the Southern Heaven Demon Empress, as I suspected, things could take the worst possible turn.
He would certainly head south on the Southern Heaven Demon Empress’s orders.
And if he encountered the reconnaissance squad, the three people among them would fall into his hands as well.
“...Damn it.”
But for now, I had no time to worry about that.
They were on the move even now, while I was trapped deep underground, unable to move an inch.
All I can do is hope I’m wrong about the Blood Monk.
So there were only two things I could do.
The first was prayer.
The second was...
Escape.
Ding.
System A new Quest has been generated!
Would you like to check the linked Quest, Escape from Namshank?
Y / N
I nodded and thought, I don’t know who developed the System, but that’s one shitty Quest title.
“So, Pavilion Master.
Do you have anything to eat?”
...Correction.
That bastard was the shittiest of all.
Among the countless martial artists on the continent, river pirates were an especially rough and free-spirited bunch.
They didn’t want laws restricting them or the authorities arresting them.
They didn’t want to live decent lives, either.
Sudal, the Deputy Stronghold Lord of the Water Dragon Stronghold, had become a river pirate for exactly those reasons.
Unlike his father, who had lived and died a good fisherman, Sudal had boldly resolved to live and die as an adventurer.
He’d done fairly well as a river pirate.
Only recently had he begun to wonder what he was doing with his life.
What the hell am I doing?
Nothing.
Every day, he sat at the bow and stared at the calm river.
When the sun got too hot, he went swimming.
That was all.
His immediate superior, who ruled the Yangtze in Sichuan, had been summoned to League headquarters by the revered Alliance Leader.
Meanwhile, Sudal and his men had come down the tributaries to backwater Yunnan and were wasting their days.
By now, merchant ships loaded with all kinds of valuable goods must be traveling through Sichuan.
The Yangtze was a gold mine right now.
With war approaching, all sorts of supplies were moving along it.
Sudal knew that and desperately wanted to return immediately.
But every time he did, one man’s presence kept flashing before his eyes.
“I’ll come running whenever you call!”
That was the boast he’d made seven days and nights ago.
Naturally, he hadn’t meant a word of it.
But the much younger man had smiled warmly and answered,
“Oh, good.
Then stay nearby.”
“Excuse me?”
“Heh heh.
Did someone stick a marlin in your ear?
I said stay nearby.
I’ll need another favor when we head back.”
“Great Hero Jin, forgive me, but we have a living to make...”
“A living.
That’s nice.
But you have to be alive to make one, don’t you?”
“Come on, I’m asking a favor!
Just a favor!”
“Gasp.”
“For fuck’s sake.
I might just snap every mast and burn the whole lot down.
Want to swim to Sichuan?”
He called it a favor, but it was a threat.
What could Sudal do?
In the Murim, whoever had the stronger martial arts was king.
Worse, that monstrous young man’s Master was a crazy old monster who really was called a king.
Jin Taekyung, you bastard...
Swallowing his tears, Sudal had nodded.
For more than seven days and nights, he and his men had stayed on a tributary at the edge of Yunnan where they couldn’t even spot a small boat, doing nothing but catching fish.
Until an idea occurred to him yesterday.
Wait.
Why am I doing this?
It’ll be a while before that Jin Taekyung bastard comes back.
Sudal had only ever operated on the Yangtze, but even he knew what a godforsaken dump Nanman was.
He didn’t know exactly what Jin Taekyung’s mission was.
Still, if it had brought him all the way here, it couldn’t be simple.
But did he really need to worry about someone who wasn’t even here and whine like a dog that needed to shit?
He gave his adventurous life some serious thought, then ordered his men,
“Hey, boys.
Let’s go get some fresh air.”
“Excuse me?”
“Where?”
“Guizhou’s right next door.
Let’s make a sweep through it, raid the place, and come back.”
His ambitious plan didn’t go over well.
“Deputy Stronghold Lord, have you lost your mind?”
“Fuck.
If you want to die, die alone.
Why should the rest of us get cremated when you’re not even the Stronghold Lord?”
But Sudal had a plan for that, too.
“Dunk that bastard.
The Yangtze... the Yangtze...”
“The Yangtze dip?”
“Yeah.
That thing Jin Taekyung does all the time.”
After sending two of them into the water one after another, the complaints disappeared.
Under Sudal’s spirited command, three swift ships traveled along the western tributary toward Guizhou.
At last, after all this time, they found a target.
Just like now.
“There’s a ship roughly two hundred zhang ahead!”
“Seize it!
Don’t let it get away!”
How long had it been since their last raid?
Sudal stood tall at the stern like a Great General, smiling with satisfaction as the ship drew rapidly closer.
Then, before fifteen minutes had passed, he realized something was wrong.
Whoosh!
The ship was almost upon them now.
There was no crew and no captain.
Only one person waited for them.
“A swift ship of the Yangtze River Channel League.
What fortunate timing.”
The bald, middle-aged man holding a blood-soaked Zen staff smiled broadly at the frozen Sudal.
“Does this ship go to Nanman too?”

chapters.title: Chapter 665
paragraphs: Tap. Drip-drip.
Water dripped through the silence. I shifted away from the liquid falling through a crack in the underground prison’s ceiling and looked into the air before me.

System Quest Escape from Namshank You have ended up imprisoned in the underground prison of the Nanman Beast Palace after all. Dark, damp, and silent, this place resembles the future that awaits you. But it is still too soon to give up on life. Time remaining until execution: Two days You must escape the underground prison within the allotted time. Whether you survive alone or together is entirely up to you. If you fail, only death awaits. But remember: with a strong Will and even a single thread of goodwill, a path to life will open. Grade: Supreme Peak Restriction: Jin Taekyung Mission: Escape the underground prison before the execution (Incomplete) Reward: Linked Quest ??? Failure: Death
I had already checked the Quest window countless times.
I stared at the translucent holographic window as if I could bore a hole through it, but no miracle occurred that changed the words written on the final line.
Failure: Death.
It wasn’t the first time.
From the moment I first set foot in the Murim until now, I had received this kind of goddamn Quest several times. Of course, in the beginning, I had been utterly dumbfounded.
Back then, I really thought I was going to die a dog’s death.
I’d fought countless battles as a Hunter, but death had always frightened me. Or rather, what frightened me was everything I’d have to leave behind.
At least if I died in a Gate, my family would get a death benefit. If I died in Murim, they’d get nothing.

Still, there was no comparing who I’d been then to who I was now. Every crisis had given my guts a forced Botox injection. They’d grown bigger by the day, and my body and mind had toughened along with them.
But...
I’ve never been in a situation like this.
There was a simple reason I’d survived every brush with death. I’d either had someone beside me to fight with, or, when I had to face an enemy alone, I’d been ready to put my life on the line.
I’d fought and struggled to the bitter end. And I’d survived.
Clatter.
But never with enormous iron balls hanging all over my body and my internal energy sealed.
“...Damn it.”
I muttered under my breath and closed my eyes. The words from the Quest description seemed to appear against the darkness.
With a strong Will and even a single thread of goodwill, a path to life will open.
The System sometimes sent me messages I couldn’t tell apart from hints or complete nonsense. Was this just encouragement? Or was it the clue I needed to escape?
As I sat there thinking with my eyes closed, liquid fell from above, struck the floor, and splashed onto the back of my hand.
Tap. Splatter.
It was too sticky to be groundwater, and its temperature was warm enough to make me feel grimy.
I opened my eyes at once, but without even looking at the ceiling, I spoke.
“...You crazy bastard. I told you to quit drooling.”
I heard a slurp as Taishan swallowed.
“Sorry. Taishan was too hungry.”
“If you’re hungry, why are you putting your mouth against a hole in the floor? Just sit still.”
“But if Taishan keeps licking, it’s surprisingly salty.”
“Licking? What?”
“Rock. This place is a rock restaurant.”
“Oh, for crying out loud.”
“Crying out loud? Is that some kind of sauce?”
This crazy bastard...
I swallowed the curse rising in my throat. Getting angry at him would only waste what little energy I had. It wouldn’t change anything.

Besides, Taishan wasn’t in much better shape than I was. I had no idea what sort of creature he was made of—his vital points were so thick that the Pressure-Point Strike hadn’t worked—but his internal energy had been sealed, and his whole body was bound. Even Taishan’s natural strength couldn’t get him out of that.
“Pavilion Master. Taishan hungry. Taishan wants to get out soon.”
Listening to his quiet whining, I suddenly felt something that could only be called guilt.
This is all my fault.
“...Hey, Taishan.”
“Pavilion Master. Why did you call Taishan?”
“I’m sorry.”
“Huh?”
“I’m sorry. I mean it.”
I looked up as I spoke. Through a hole the size of a child’s fist, I could see one enormous, clear eye, like a calf’s.
It held a look of complete bewilderment.
I’d always thought Taishan had a heart far more innocent than his age or size suggested. He was like a clean sheet of paper.
I sighed.
“I should’ve made a better call. I didn’t. I made a mistake.”
A painful misjudgment. In baduk terms, a terrible move.
I had locked myself inside the underground prison to clean up the consequences of that mistake, but... damn it. I still had doubts about whether it had really been the right choice.
Taishan studied me as if I’d said something strange.
“Taishan is okay.”
“You’re okay?”
“Mm-hmm. Taishan is really okay.”

I lowered my head. He probably didn’t even understand what was happening. Right now, the most important thing to him was that he was hungry. The second most important was that he had no way to do anything about it.
Maybe that’s better for him.
Then he spoke again, and I realized he was far sharper than I’d given him credit for.
“Pavilion Master doesn’t need to feel sorry for Taishan.”
I looked up in surprise. Taishan met my eyes and spoke clearly.
“Taishan knows. Taishan is stupid.”
“What?”

“Ever since Taishan was little, people called him stupid and made fun of him. They came and hit him whenever they were bored. If Taishan hadn’t met Lord... maybe someone would still hit Taishan every day, and Taishan would cry. It was hard.”
This wasn’t the Taishan I was used to. His whole manner had changed, and his words flowed without a pause as I stared up at him.

“But Lord was different. Even when Taishan said something wrong, Lord understood. When Taishan ate a lot, Lord patted him on the back and told him to eat slowly. So Taishan decided to give his life to Lord.”

“Then, a little while ago, Lord told Taishan we should trust Pavilion Master. He said Pavilion Master seemed different from the other people in the orthodox faction. Thinking about it now, Lord was right. A few days ago, when stupid Taishan couldn’t save Lord, Pavilion Master did.”

“Taishan likes the Fire Dragon Pavilion now. Taishan likes little, cute Namho, and Hyuk Mujin, even if he’s annoying sometimes. Taishan likes fierce Song Ilseom and Ju Hwaran, who’s pretty as a flower. And after Lord, Taishan likes Pavilion Master best.”
I was speechless. Beyond the hole, his eye curved gently.
“Taishan trusts Lord, and Lord trusts the Pavilion Master. So Pavilion Master, trust yourself. The Pavilion Master will definitely find a way. Just like always.”
Taishan gave a little giggle. For a while, all I could do was stare.
It felt as if someone had hit me in the back of the head with a club. I’d never expected Taishan, of all people, to say those things.
And I’d never expected his words to give me more strength than anything else could right now.
Yeah. Come to think of it, there’s always been a way.
In the Murim, I seemed to have lived a life rather close to death.
Jopil. The Head Elder. The Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Blood Lord. The Western Heaven Demon Lord...
Danger had waited wherever I went. Each time, I’d taken the word death from where I kept it buried in my heart, turned it over, and made myself a promise.
I would never die. I could never die here.
A strong Will.
Was that what the Quest meant? Or...
Something else connected to a strong Will.
A certain thing the Slaughter Saint had said to me in Hubei just a few months ago flashed through my mind like lightning.
“Huh. You monstrous bastard. You finally opened your Middle Dantian, so now you can handle qi properly.”
I’d asked him, “I already know how to handle it. Don’t you know how much internal energy I have?”
The Slaughter Saint had merely let out a short laugh without answering. Then he had shaken his head and disappeared, saying I wouldn’t understand even if he told me now.

But now I thought I was beginning to understand why he’d said it. How ridiculous I must have looked to him: a young fool boasting that he could handle qi because he had several jiazi of internal energy.
The Three Dantians.
The three greatest and most important passages in the human body.
But the Lower Dantian was only a vessel, filled and emptied of internal energy again and again. I hadn’t grasped even a quarter of what the Middle Dantian could do or how it worked.
Now, though, things were different.
No. I understood a little.
It wasn’t internal energy that moved the Middle Dantian.
It was Will.
Strong, unwavering Will.
The Middle Dantian had belonged to the realm of enlightenment from the start, not internal energy.

It lay somewhere in an unknown domain, half a step beyond even those chosen masters whose limits were no longer decided by how much internal energy they possessed. A sacred realm one had to pass through to rise from human birth toward the realm of gods.

Since martial arts had first appeared in this world, countless masters must have met success or failure along this path. Some had crumbled like dry leaves. Others had become giants who left their footprints on the long history of martial arts.
And today, I took half a step closer to those giants.
Whoosh.
As if entranced, I reached out. Hidden among the air around me, the qi of the world rippled toward my fingertips.
Just as Baeksang was about to enter his quarters, he sensed that an uninvited guest had arrived before him.
This is...
The qi was faint but unmistakably familiar. It would have been stranger if Baeksang hadn’t recognized it.
Perhaps the guest waiting inside had wanted him to.
“You may all go.”
The guards who were about to open the door stopped. The graying Captain of the Guards, who had served at Baeksang’s side for more than thirty years, spoke up.
“My lord, even so...”
“That’s enough. Guard the grounds.”
After staring at Baeksang for a moment at his cold words, the captain scattered throughout the manor with his subordinates.
Baeksang glanced at them, then gripped the door handle firmly and pushed.
The door slid open.
Night had fallen outside, but his quarters were brightly lit. The residence was spacious, as befitted a Great Chieftain, yet furnished with almost nothing.
One person waited inside.
“You’re late. Where have you been?”
Baeksang answered calmly.
“You already know, don’t you, Palace Lord?”
A bitter smile touched the lips of his uninvited guest, the Beast Miao King.

chapters.title: Chapter 666
paragraphs: Baeksang’s voice remained calm despite the Beast Miao King’s sudden, uninvited arrival.
“You already know, don’t you, Palace Lord?”
The Beast Miao King smiled bitterly.

Baeksang was right. A considerable number of tribal chieftains had turned against him, but he was still the master of the Nanman Beast Palace. Within the Inner Palace, at least, he knew Baeksang’s every move.
“You spent quite a while in the underground prison. What did you and that boy have to talk about for so long?”
Baeksang faltered as he remembered his conversation with Jin Taekyung. Only for a moment.
“I told him he would be executed at noon two days from now, in front of everyone.”
“And?”
“I told him no one could stop it.”
The remark was aimed squarely at him. The Beast Miao King’s eyes darkened.
“Do you truly believe that?”
“Of course.”
“And if I refuse to let it happen?”
“The Palace Lord stands at the forefront, nothing more. The authority to decide Nanman’s great affairs belongs solely to the Tribal Grand Council.”
Baeksang spoke quietly, then went on.
“Have you forgotten the oath our ancestors made hundreds of years ago, when they gathered beneath a single banner on this land?”
“The outcome will not change. Tomorrow, the final Tribal Grand Council will take up the execution of the Han Chinese Jin Taekyung.”
The Beast Miao King regarded Baeksang with a grave expression. He knew the balance of power had already tipped. But if he had given up on Jin Taekyung, he would never have come here.
“Is that all?”
“Twenty tribal chieftains, myself included, have already agreed. If you defy the will of the Tribal Grand Council and choose another course...”
“That is not what I’m asking.”
The Beast Miao King cut off Baeksang’s words and continued with a sigh.
“Did you tell Jin Taekyung about Hwi?”

A crack appeared in Baeksang’s impassive expression. It had been true in the past, and it remained true now: after decades of wearing an iron mask, only the child he could no longer keep by his side could shake him.
The Beast Miao King knew that better than anyone.
“I haven’t planted anyone in the underground prison. I only suspected it. Seeing how shaken you were, so unlike yourself, confirmed it.”
“How could I not know? We’ve spent our whole lives together.”
Baeksang fell silent. We. The word struck him with unexpected force. Once, it had come naturally to them both. Now it felt strange.
And yet...
Grind.
“That was when you and I stood on the same path, Palace Lord.”
The Beast Miao King shook his head.
“We still do. We have never once parted ways.”
“It’s too late.”
“It isn’t. We’re still sworn brothers, bound together in our hearts. Even now, we can put right what went wrong.”
“To me, those bonds belong to a distant past.”
“And you’ve been trapped in that past all this time, little brother.”
“I remember that day too. How could I forget the day a child more upright and radiant than anyone vanished from this land?”
Baeksang clenched his teeth. The memory was painful even to summon.
Yet he knew something else, too. When the truth of that day had come to light, someone had been just as furious and grief-stricken as he was.
None of it had done any good.
“Neither of us could do anything. The evidence of their crimes was gone, and everything was buried beneath the peace that followed.”
Countless footprints left on a sandy shore vanished when the next wave rolled in.
But Baeksang remembered. He had etched the faces of those who turned away from his child in danger into his flesh and bones, and turned them over in his heart ever since.
He had believed they were all walking side by side across the vast sandy shore called the Central Plains. In truth, his people had been sent ahead simply because they were foreigners.
“I can’t forget any of it, and I can’t undo it. So why do you...!”
Baeksang stopped as his voice began to rise. Sorrow had settled over the Beast Miao King’s face.
“Do you think I’ve forgotten? I’m a sorry excuse for a father who had no choice but to outlive his children.”
More than fifty years ago, the Beast Miao King’s children had been among the ten thousand warriors who went to the Central Plains. They never set foot on Nanman soil alive again.

“I still regret it. What if I hadn’t become Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace? What if I hadn’t gone to the battlefield? What if I’d at least refused when they asked to fight alongside their father?”

“You’re right, little brother. We were powerless. We burned with anger and howled with grief, but there was nothing we could do. We had to return to Nanman. Everyone was too exhausted to turn away the peace that had finally come after ten years and begin another war.”
The Beast Miao King let out a hollow laugh. At the time, Nanman had been only one power among the Outer Lands, and the gap between it and the Central Plains was vast.
Even against the Zhongnan Sect alone, Nanman had been at a disadvantage.

Venerable Wusang, the Sect Leader of the time, had earned the respect of many through his bearing as a Great Hero. When he died in the final battle at Great Snow Mountain, countless sects and martial artists came to Mount Zhongnan.
“I merely made a choice. Between the dead and the living, between revenge and the greater cause.”
What followed was known to everyone.
The Beast Miao King led the survivors home to Nanman and faced a flood of accusations from those who had lost family.

“My life was filled with regrets. But I never regretted that choice—not even once. Because we united as one, grew stronger and more prosperous than before, and gained the power to hold the criminals of the past to account.”
Baeksang’s face hardened at this story he had never heard before. Yet as he looked at the Beast Miao King, something he could not understand stirred in his eyes.
“But you’ll side with the Central Plains again.”
“Yes,” the Beast Miao King answered without hesitation. “I will.”
“Why in the world...”
“Because burning down an entire forest over one diseased tree would be foolish.”
“We need to uproot what made the tree sick. If we set fire to the forest instead, those flames will reach us next.”
The Beast Miao King went on with a sigh.
“Once it was the Demonic Cult. Now it’s Dark Heaven. We fought to protect the forest. This land is part of it too.”
Neither the people of the Central Plains nor the people of Nanman would acknowledge it, but the Beast Miao King knew. Though they lived far apart, they shared the forest called the world.
And...
“You know it too, Baeksang.”
The man who understood it best was his sworn younger brother, looking back at him now with wavering eyes.

“I know. I know that no matter what this foolish older brother says, none of it will reach your ears. You will say that it is an old affair you no longer even remember, and that the Baeksang of that time died a long time ago.”
The Beast Miao King’s children had been killed by the Demonic Cult, but Baeksang’s only child had been sacrificed because people he had believed were allies turned their backs on him.
His anger toward the Central Plains was bound to run deeper and wider.
But the Beast Miao King had watched Baeksang for a long time. He had already guessed.
“If you don’t stop now... you’ll regret it. You regretted the past, you regret the present, and you’ll regret what comes next.”
Baeksang wanted to tell him he would have no regrets.
For Hwi, the child who had been his whole world, he could do anything.
Let them call him a vengeance fiend while he lived. Let them call him a Fiend after he died. He would smile and walk this path all the same.
Then why...
Why? Why in the world?
Why would the thought he had repeated hundreds and thousands of times in his heart over the years refuse to pass through his lips at this very moment?
He had already gone too far to turn back. So why?
Why are you doing this, Baeksang?
As Baeksang put that question to his hollow heart and found no answer, the Beast Miao King’s quiet voice reached his ears.
“I could step down as Palace Lord.”
Baeksang’s pupils shook at the unexpected words. But the Beast Miao King continued in a calmer voice than ever.
“You heard me. If you want me to, I’ll give up the position right now.”
Baeksang struggled to make sense of it. If the position became vacant, one of the remaining Great Chieftains would be appointed the new Palace Lord through the Tribal Grand Council.
But with Heugung and Yohi both gone, the meaning of the Beast Miao King’s offer was clear.
“You would make me, of all people, the new Palace Lord?”
“Yes. That’s what I said.”
“Palace Lord. Have you gone mad?”
“Of course not.”
The thirty-two tribal chieftains held the real power in the Nanman Beast Palace, but the authority of the Palace Lord’s title could not be ignored. To offer it now, of all times, was absurd.
“What in the world is this...”
Baeksang stared at him, unable to understand. Then he fell silent.
Something about the Beast Miao King’s manner—so calm, so unlike him—had brought a realization.
No. Surely not.
The thought flashed through Baeksang’s mind. At the same moment, the Beast Miao King slowly spoke.
“Half a shichen. Half a shichen is enough. Open the way for them.”
Half a shichen. Them.
That was all Baeksang needed to turn suspicion into certainty. He asked, his voice seething, “Why? Why would you go this far?”
The Beast Miao King’s answer came without the slightest tremor or hesitation.
“Because they came to help us. Just as we once did.”
“And I’ll help you. As I always have.”
It’s too late for that.
Baeksang spat the words inwardly and moved to summon the Captain of the Guards waiting outside.
Or tried to.
For some reason, he could neither take a step nor part his lips.
Baeksang closed his eyes. A voice he should have let go long ago still echoed in his ears.
How much more blood do you intend to spill, Baeksang?
The figures moved through the darkness in silence, keeping out of sight.
Whoosh, whoosh, whoosh!
They shot in the same direction, so fast that the wind split around them and leaves trembled in their wake.
By the time anyone noticed, it was already too late.
Swish. Thud.
A body stiffened and fell. One of the figures caught the torch from his hand and moved his lips.
“Open the underground prison.”
Fwoosh.
The wavering torchlight revealed Yayul Mok’s face.
