paragraphs: Baeksang stood alone before a mirror.

The mirror Southern Heaven Demon Empress had given him was large enough to reflect his entire body, unlike an ordinary one. Its surface was smooth, without a single scratch. Even in the Central Plains, let alone Nanman, a mirror of such quality would be hard to find.
But Baeksang looked into it for one reason alone: in his reflection, he could see the face of the son who looked just like him.
This has never happened before.
For more than forty years, he had steadied himself whenever he wavered. He had done it countless times to reach this position. Yet now he was more shaken than ever.
That must mean the grand plan I’ve spent decades carrying out is nearing its end.
A door opened behind him, and a familiar face appeared. Baeksang met the Captain of the Guards’ eyes in the mirror.
“Have you brought him?”
The Captain hesitated at the sight of his lord standing lost in thought, then answered.
“He’s on his way.”
“Then why are you here?”
“An urgent report.”
“An urgent report...”
Baeksang let the words trail off and crooked a finger. The Captain approached and lowered his voice.
“Last night, a massive wildfire was spotted three hundred li to the north.”
“Ailao Mountain.”
“Yes.”
“Jin Taekyung must have started it.”
“We need to confirm that, but given everything that’s happened, he’s the most likely culprit.”
“It was Jin Taekyung. Once again, it seems glory-blinded moths have rushed toward the flames.”
“The small and midsized tribes near Ailao Mountain joined forces, or so we’re told. They attacked him with five hundred warriors and a hundred beasts, but...”
Baeksang waved him silent. He had heard enough. Five hundred stragglers hastily gathered together could do nothing to Jin Taekyung.
The saying the few cannot overcome the many meant different things depending on who the opponent was. Jin Taekyung clearly lay outside the equation.
“I can guess how that ended. What happened to Jin Taekyung afterward?”
“They say he routed the warriors, then headed toward Ailao Mountain alone.”
“He must have a purpose. The Poisonblood Grounds, perhaps?”
“The fire was too fierce for anyone to confirm where he went. It started at the mountain’s entrance and has already spread halfway up.”
“He means to see this through.”

Ailao Mountain was among the most forbidding mountains in Nanman. Its slopes were treacherous, its valleys deep. Winding ridges stretched for a hundred li beneath a seemingly endless cover of ancient trees.
Now that a wildfire had settled over Ailao Mountain, it would take at least three full days and nights before there was even a sign of the flames dying down.
The whole mountain might burn.

If it was a coincidence, it was a remarkable one. Fire had not swept through Ailao Mountain in over two hundred years. The last time it had, someone from the Fire Gate Clan had used the entire mountain for kindling to destroy the Five Poisons Sect.
That was how Nanman found peace again.
But would it happen that way this time?
Baeksang studied his reflection in silence, then spoke.
“Evacuate every tribesperson living nearby. Choose three thousand capable warriors and blockade Ailao Mountain.”
The Captain of the Guards had continued his report impassively, but a flicker of agitation crossed his face.
“Three thousand? When we’ve already ordered a general mobilization across Nanman?”
“We need to hold Jin Taekyung there, if only as a precaution.”
“But my lord, even with that many men, we can’t surround the entire mountain...”
“For all its size, Ailao Mountain has few passable entrances. Deploy them accordingly.”
After a moment’s thought, the Captain bowed his head.
“As you command.”
“What of the other chieftains?”
“As I reported, five chieftains have disappeared. So have the warriors under the two chieftains who set out earlier with the scouting party.”
“So it comes to this. They refuse to accept reality.”
Baeksang’s voice was calm.
The missing chieftains were the ones who had never switched sides. Their loyalty to the Beast Miao King had held firm. Some had even spat at Baeksang when he tried to win them over.
“My lord, they’ve undoubtedly betrayed us. It isn’t too late to send men after them—”
Baeksang shook his head.
“Someone told me not long ago that one diseased tree does not make an entire forest sick. We need only thin out the afflicted trees.”
“You mean...”
“Thirty-two tribes have shared this land for centuries. I’ve often wondered how much longer that arrangement ought to last.”
The Captain’s eyes widened as he grasped his meaning.
“Thirty-two is too many to bring together behind one purpose,” Baeksang continued, his voice low. “It’s time to thin out the diseased trees and put the forest in order.”
Expulsion. Or elimination.
The will of the man who had driven out this land’s longtime ruler and taken his throne was unmistakable.
The Captain stared at his lord, mouth open, before asking, “What should we do?”
“If they leave, let them. Should they return home and rally their warriors, we’ll have both a justification and the strength to act.”
The Captain knew the balance of power had tipped long ago. But one man still worried him.
“If the Palace Lord—no, if Yayul Cheok joins them, it won’t be so simple.”
Baeksang regarded him for a moment.
“Long ago, while I was staying in the Central Plains, I heard an interesting story.”
“My lord?”

“A monkey was born from stone. Its nature was so fierce, and its strength so great, that Shakyamuni, whom the monks of the Central Plains revere, offered it a wager: could it escape the palm of his hand?”
His calm voice held the Captain’s attention.

“The monkey snorted and accepted. It rode a cloud to the edge of the world and even scribbled on five pillars it found there. Only when it returned did it learn that those pillars had been Shakyamuni’s fingers.”
Baeksang slowly opened his hand toward the mirror.
The enormous Palace Lord’s Hall seemed to fit in his palm. Sky and river, earth and mountain—even if the mirror had shown all of Nanman, it would have fit there too.
“Yayul Cheok is no different. Now that I hold this position, he can never escape.”
“Then...”
“We have word that he went east. Take a thousand Bai warriors and pursue him yourself.”
“As you command.”
The Captain bowed, then moved his lips again.
“I beg your pardon, but we’re dealing with the Beast Miao King. As a precaution, perhaps you should deploy the Baekcheon Unit.”
Baeksang silently shook his head. The Baekcheon Unit was the blade he had secretly honed for decades.
He had to draw and wield it when it was most needed.
“That will be all. Our guest has arrived. You may go.”
He was speaking to the Captain, but his gaze—fixed on the mirror throughout their conversation—had found the old man standing in the open doorway.
“Then I’ll take my leave.”
After confirming that the Captain of the Guards had left the Palace Lord’s Hall, Baeksang slowly turned around.
“You’ve come, Head Elder.”
The greeting was matter-of-fact. The answer was not.
“Shut that filthy mouth of yours.”
THUD.
An old man approached, leaning on a cane. Age spots covered his face, and every patch of exposed skin was wrinkled. Anger burned in the corners of his eyes, where fluid had gathered.
“You wretched bastard.”
“I see you overheard us.”
“Do you think this old man doesn’t know what’s in your black heart? You meant for me to hear, didn’t you?”
“If you mean what I said about Yayul Cheok—the villain who defied the Tribal Grand Council to save a murderer, then betrayed the Nanman Beast Palace—yes.”
“You bastard!”
WHOOSH! CLACK.
The old man swung his cane with all his strength. Baeksang caught it in one hand.
There was little force behind the blow, and no internal energy to speak of. Baeksang took the cane from him with ease, then flicked his sleeve. Invisible qi forced the old man down into a seat.
“You’ve aged since I last saw you. Your temper hasn’t changed, though.”
The old man trembled.
“If I’d known you would do this, I’d have beaten you to death with my own hands long ago.”
“But far too much time has passed for that. Yayul Cheok has betrayed the Palace and fled. The fate of the Miao people now rests with a boy you once caught stealing fruit wine and scolded soundly.”

“It’s time to leave the distant past behind and think about what comes next. With the Chieftain and Lesser Chieftain gone, everything depends on the choice you make as Great Chieftain of the Miao people.”
The old man—the Miao Head Elder—glared at Baeksang for a long moment.
“So you’ve seized Nanman after all. Such ugly greed.”
“Call it what you like. There’s nothing I won’t do to obtain what I so desperately want.”
“You’re Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace now. What more could you want? Do you mean to get your hands on the Beast King Stone and become a god?”
Baeksang shook his head.
“I have no interest in some ancient sacred treasure passed down only by word of mouth. What I want now is the future—and your wise choice, Head Elder.”
“The boy I remember wasn’t like this.”
“I changed. Everything does.”
“The Palace Lord trusted you. Even though I told him to be so wary, he trusted his one and only sworn brother.”
“Not every act of trust needs to be repaid.”
“It isn’t too late. Even now—”
“I crossed that river long ago. Once you’re on a tiger’s back, you can’t climb down. Now it’s your turn to get on, Head Elder.”
CRACK.
Bones shifted in the old man’s tightly clenched fist.
“So that’s what you want from this old man. You want me to betray the Palace Lord?”
“Of course not.”
Baeksang picked up his teacup.
“I want all the Miao people to betray him. You included.”
“Read the situation carefully, if you want to save more than ten thousand of your people.”
“You bastard!”
“Remember: this is my first and last offer.”
Baeksang tilted the teacup.
The Head Elder squeezed his eyes shut.
After a short silence, his hoarse voice broke through.
“Impossible.”
CLACK.
Baeksang set down the teacup and stared at the Head Elder with deeply sunken eyes.
“Won’t you regret that answer?”
“Kill me instead. Ask any Miao person, and you’ll hear the same answer.”
“You haven’t disappointed me.”
Baeksang snapped his fingers. The closed door opened, revealing Bai warriors.
“Lock up the entire Miao leadership in the underground prison, including the Head Elder.”
The warriors bowed, took the Head Elder by either arm, and pulled him to his feet.
The old man, whose day of death was approaching, cried out in a ringing voice.
“Baeksang! You bastard! Aren’t you afraid of Heaven?”
By the time his scream had gradually faded into the distance, Baeksang was looking down at the empty teacup and muttering.
“What more is there to fear? Heaven’s will brought me this far.”
There had been a time when he resented Heaven.
After the Great Faction War ended and he returned to Nanman, Baeksang spent every day drunk. He drank as though each day were his last, then despaired when the next morning’s sunlight woke him.
Why did you let me live? Why?
Those days had been more painful than death.
But he could not spend forever writhing in grief. There was something he had to do.
Something he had to do.
Baeksang looked through the window at the blue sky.
Is this truly your will? No... Have you ever watched over me even once?
As always, he waited in vain for an answer.
Except for the unfamiliar voice that pierced his ears the next moment.
“Um... Shall I refill your tea?”
Baeksang turned toward it.
A pretty maid stood at the half-open door, looking at him.
“No need.”
“But your cup is empty.”
“I said there’s no—”
He stopped. After studying the maid for a moment, he said, “Come in.”
At his quiet command, the warriors who had moved to stop her stepped back. The door closed firmly behind her.
She hurried over in small steps and slowly tilted the teapot above his cup.
Trickle.
Steam rose, carrying the scent of tea. Yet Baeksang felt a throb of pain, as though he had inhaled Poison Mist.
Baeksang silently watched the teacup fill before suddenly speaking.
“Whose face is that, Demon Empress?”
The maid—Southern Heaven Demon Empress—smiled.
“A girl who worked in the Inner Palace. So young and fresh. She was too cute to resist.”
“Did you kill her?”
“Oh my. Does that matter so much?”
“That...”
“How interesting. Hundreds of people have already died, and you are worried about the life of one maid.”
Baeksang fell silent, then answered evenly.
“I only asked because it might disrupt the plan. Anything that happens in the Inner Palace is quickly discovered.”
“Ah, I see. Well, if that’s your concern...”
Southern Heaven Demon Empress gave him a coy smile and picked up the teacup.
“You needn’t worry about that. If there’s a problem, it’s at Ailao Mountain, not the Inner Palace.”
“Ailao Mountain? Do you mean...?”
“Yes. Jin Taekyung. That child has done something. We still haven’t heard from them, so I’m sure of it.”
Baeksang thought for a moment.
“It was a trap?”
“That’s right. A trap laid to catch the old tiger who had left the Palace. I never expected the young tiger to get caught in it instead.”
CLICK.
She set down her cup, amusement in her voice.
“Of course, I didn’t expect the young tiger to be strong enough to break it, either.”
“It must have been a thorough trap, for you to be so confident in it.”
“Two Supreme Peak masters. One was the Black Hand Fist Demon. The other...”
She paused and smiled at Baeksang.
“At any rate, he was strong. Far stronger than the Black Hand Fist Demon.”
“It is astonishing. I thought those two would be able to deal with the Beast Miao King. It seems the Lord of Heaven was not interested in that child for no reason.”
For Baeksang, each revelation was more startling than the last. Jin Taekyung had not only killed two Supreme Peak masters single-handedly—the Lord of Heaven himself was also interested in him.
Baeksang also realized his own judgment had been sound.
Jin Taekyung.
The young man’s face came to mind. Baeksang had never been able to get a firm measure of him.
He looked at the smiling Demon Empress.
“You’ll take action yourself now.”
A Supreme Peak master was a formidable asset. With two of them dead, Baeksang thought her intervention inevitable.
At least, that was what he thought until he heard her answer the next moment.
“No? Why would I?”
She let out a short laugh.
“I do not have time to worry about that. Even if one of the major pieces has died, the current situation will not be overturned. What matters is the grand plan.”
“You mean...?”
“The Beast Miao King and Jin Taekyung no longer matter. Secure the Inner Palace and Outer Palace. Gather every force you have.”
Southern Heaven Demon Empress rose and crossed the room almost as though she were dancing. Her voice rang with delight.
“Three days. No more than three days.”
“Be ready. That day, everything will begin—and end.”
THUD.
The door opened and closed.
Long afterward, Baeksang remained where he was, frozen.
That day was coming.
The day he had longed for more than anyone in the world—and feared more than anyone.

The old man—the Miao Head Elder—glared at Baeksang for a long moment.
“So you’ve seized Nanman after all.
Such ugly greed.”
“Call it what you like.
There’s nothing I won’t do to obtain what I so desperately want.”
“You’re Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace now.
What more could you want?
Do you mean to get your hands on the Beast King Stone and become a god?”
Baeksang shook his head.
“I have no interest in some ancient sacred treasure passed down only by word of mouth.
What I want now is the future—and your wise choice, Head Elder.”
“The boy I remember wasn’t like this.”
“I changed.
Everything does.”
“The Palace Lord trusted you.
Even though I told him to be so wary, he trusted his one and only sworn brother.”
“Not every act of trust needs to be repaid.”
“It isn’t too late.
Even now—”
“I crossed that river long ago.
Once you’re on a tiger’s back, you can’t climb down.
Now it’s your turn to get on, Head Elder.”
CRACK.
Bones shifted in the old man’s tightly clenched fist.
“So that’s what you want from this old man.
You want me to betray the Palace Lord?”
“Of course not.”
Baeksang picked up his teacup.
“I want all the Miao people to betray him.
You included.”
“Read the situation carefully, if you want to save more than ten thousand of your people.”
“You bastard!”
“Remember: this is my first and last offer.”
Baeksang tilted the teacup.
The Head Elder squeezed his eyes shut.
After a short silence, his hoarse voice broke through.
“Impossible.”
CLACK.
Baeksang set down the teacup and stared at the Head Elder with deeply sunken eyes.
“Won’t you regret that answer?”
“Kill me instead.
Ask any Miao person, and you’ll hear the same answer.”
“You haven’t disappointed me.”
Baeksang snapped his fingers.
The closed door opened, revealing Bai warriors.
“Lock up the entire Miao leadership in the underground prison, including the Head Elder.”
The warriors bowed, took the Head Elder by either arm, and pulled him to his feet.
The old man, whose day of death was approaching, cried out in a ringing voice.
“Baeksang!
You bastard!
Aren’t you afraid of Heaven?”
By the time his scream had gradually faded into the distance, Baeksang was looking down at the empty teacup and muttering.
“What more is there to fear?
Heaven’s will brought me this far.”
There had been a time when he resented Heaven.
After the Great Faction War ended and he returned to Nanman, Baeksang spent every day drunk.
He drank as though each day were his last, then despaired when the next morning’s sunlight woke him.
Why did you let me live?
Why?
Those days had been more painful than death.
But he could not spend forever writhing in grief.
There was something he had to do.
Something he had to do.
Baeksang looked through the window at the blue sky.
Is this truly your will?
No...
Have you ever watched over me even once?
As always, he waited in vain for an answer.
Except for the unfamiliar voice that pierced his ears the next moment.
Shall I refill your tea?”
Baeksang turned toward it.
A pretty maid stood at the half-open door, looking at him.
“No need.”
“But your cup is empty.”
“I said there’s no—”
He stopped.
After studying the maid for a moment, he said, “Come in.”
At his quiet command, the warriors who had moved to stop her stepped back.
The door closed firmly behind her.
She hurried over in small steps and slowly tilted the teapot above his cup.
Trickle.
Steam rose, carrying the scent of tea.
Yet Baeksang felt a throb of pain, as though he had inhaled Poison Mist.
Baeksang silently watched the teacup fill before suddenly speaking.
“Whose face is that, Demon Empress?”
The maid—Southern Heaven Demon Empress—smiled.
“A girl who worked in the Inner Palace.
So young and fresh.
She was too cute to resist.”
“Did you kill her?”
“Oh my.
Does that matter so much?”
“That...”
“How interesting.
Hundreds of people have already died, and you are worried about the life of one maid.”
Baeksang fell silent, then answered evenly.
“I only asked because it might disrupt the plan.
Anything that happens in the Inner Palace is quickly discovered.”
“Ah, I see.
Well, if that’s your concern...”
Southern Heaven Demon Empress gave him a coy smile and picked up the teacup.
“You needn’t worry about that.
If there’s a problem, it’s at Ailao Mountain, not the Inner Palace.”
“Ailao Mountain?
Do you mean...?”
“Yes.
Jin Taekyung.
That child has done something.
We still haven’t heard from them, so I’m sure of it.”
Baeksang thought for a moment.
“It was a trap?”
“That’s right.
A trap laid to catch the old tiger who had left the Palace.
I never expected the young tiger to get caught in it instead.”
CLICK.
She set down her cup, amusement in her voice.
“Of course, I didn’t expect the young tiger to be strong enough to break it, either.”
“It must have been a thorough trap, for you to be so confident in it.”
“Two Supreme Peak masters.
One was the Black Hand Fist Demon.
The other...”
She paused and smiled at Baeksang.
“At any rate, he was strong.
Far stronger than the Black Hand Fist Demon.”
“It is astonishing.
I thought those two would be able to deal with the Beast Miao King.
It seems the Lord of Heaven was not interested in that child for no reason.”
For Baeksang, each revelation was more startling than the last.
Jin Taekyung had not only killed two Supreme Peak masters single-handedly—the Lord of Heaven himself was also interested in him.
Baeksang also realized his own judgment had been sound.
Jin Taekyung.
The young man’s face came to mind.
Baeksang had never been able to get a firm measure of him.
He looked at the smiling Demon Empress.
“You’ll take action yourself now.”
A Supreme Peak master was a formidable asset.
With two of them dead, Baeksang thought her intervention inevitable.
At least, that was what he thought until he heard her answer the next moment.
“No?
Why would I?”
She let out a short laugh.
“I do not have time to worry about that.
Even if one of the major pieces has died, the current situation will not be overturned.
What matters is the grand plan.”
“You mean...?”
“The Beast Miao King and Jin Taekyung no longer matter.
Secure the Inner Palace and Outer Palace.
Gather every force you have.”
Southern Heaven Demon Empress rose and crossed the room almost as though she were dancing.
Her voice rang with delight.
“Three days.
No more than three days.”
“Be ready.
That day, everything will begin—and end.”
THUD.
The door opened and closed.
Long afterward, Baeksang remained where he was, frozen.
That day was coming.
The day he had longed for more than anyone in the world—and feared more than anyone.

chapters.title: Chapter 689
paragraphs: Drip. Drip.
Cold.
That was Yohi’s first thought when she opened her eyes.
She stared blankly at the drops falling onto her forehead. Then memories she had briefly forgotten began to return, one by one.
This is...
She remembered who she was. The life she had lived. What had happened at the Western Yao Estate, and what she had seen in the Poisonblood Grounds.
And...
I love you, Yohi.
The face and voice of that man made her shudder even now. Behind him lay a massive White Tiger and a young man.
All of it—
“Gasp...!”
Yohi shot upright, barely swallowing the scream about to burst from her lips.
With everything that had happened before she collapsed rushing back to her, she looked around in fear.
Where am I?

She did not recognize the place. Darkness blurred its outlines, and silence lay all around her. There was too little light to make anything out clearly, but she could tell she was enclosed on every side.
As though someone had prepared a prison for her.
Heugung.
No. The man who had stolen Heugung’s name.

At the thought of the man whose entire life had been a lie, Yohi instinctively reached for her waist. She always wore her flexible sword wrapped around it like a sash, ready for an emergency. But her hand found only silk soaked with blood and dirt.
Ah. That’s right.
She remembered losing her flexible sword after being drugged by an unidentified substance.
She had never taken the antidote, so naturally, her internal energy would still be sealed...
“Huh?”
The sound slipped out before she could stop it. Yohi clapped a hand over her mouth, though her wide eyes gave away her surprise.
How?
She forced herself to calm down and checked her body again. Then a third time.
There was no mistaking it.
The seal on my internal energy... It’s gone.
She could feel the internal energy she had built up through countless elixirs filling her lower dantian.
But why? And how?
Heugung should have captured all of us.
She could make no sense of it. Why was she alone in this enclosed space? Why had the seal been lifted?

At the end, no one had been able to stop Heugung. Jin Taekyung was badly injured and would not wake for at least several days. The White Tiger, a spiritual creature capable of holding its own against a Peak master, had been left on the brink of death by a surprise attack.
And Yohi herself had collapsed under the pill’s effects without so much as swinging her sword.
So how can the seal be gone?
She was not even tied up with rope or chains. Her martial arts might not be especially formidable, but she had reached the early Peak realm.
For Dark Heaven, this would have been a strangely careless way to hold her.
Could it be...?
Yohi swallowed, keeping the rest of the thought to herself. She rose carefully and took a closer look around.
Her eyes had adjusted to the dark. With internal energy sharpening her vision, she could now see farther into it.
This is...
The moment she understood the shape of the place, her breath caught.
It was enormous—far too large to have been made to imprison one person.

The size alone was not what unsettled her. It seemed to extend for hundreds of zhang in every direction, but that hardly mattered beside the cold, damp stone surrounding her. It covered the floor, the walls, even the ceiling.
An impregnable fortress with no way in or out.
What in the world is this place?
Yohi was staring at the stone and the thick vines spread across it when a wind blew from somewhere.
Swoooosh.
The vines swayed. Yohi stood with her mouth open, letting the cool air wash over her. Something fell from above, and she reached out.
Rustle. Tap.
She caught it between her fingers.
It was a leaf from one of the vines, fallen past her silky hair. Unlike the leaves she had seen in the Poisonblood Grounds, it was green and full of life.
Then a realization struck her.
Wait. Wind?
Wind could not blow through a sealed space. There had to be an opening—and one large enough to let in a gust that could shake those thick vines.
Yet search as she might, Yohi could find no gap.
That can’t be right.

She felt along the stone surrounding her, then struck it with internal energy. She even tried imitating the Wall Lizard Technique, which she had never learned, and climbed the vines in case there was an opening overhead.
Every attempt came to nothing.
She had stopped despairing over being captured by Dark Heaven. Now she was simply at a loss in a place she could not understand.
There has to be an exit, at least.
More than two shichen had passed since she woke, and she had spent that time searching. She had found nothing resembling an exit, let alone a gap.
Then who had put her here? And how?
Yohi sank to the ground and leaned against the stone wall. Warmth and softness met her back, making her feel a little better.
“Hm?”
Something was wrong.
She blinked, then slowly tipped her head back without moving away.
A pair of blue-white eyes looked down at her through the dimness.
“Ah.”
—Grrr.
A suffocating silence fell.
Yohi rose slowly, looking from the cliff-like wall behind her to the massive White Tiger protruding from it. Only its upper body showed, as though the rest had been cut away.
What is this?
She tried to take stock of the situation.
First, she was in an enormous place she knew nothing about.
Second, stone blocked even the sky, as though she were trapped inside a cliff. There was no visible exit.
Third, a White Tiger with half its body missing had appeared from the wall. No—it had suddenly sprung out of it.
Fourth, there were only two possible explanations.
A dream. Or the afterlife.
Yohi did not hesitate. She slammed her head against the rock wall.
Thud.
Her skull rang, but she did not wake up. The afterlife it was.
Besides, that White Tiger floating there with only its upper body showing looked familiar.
That’s the one.
Snow-white fur that could almost be called silver. Blue-white eyes.
It was the White Tiger that Young Palace Lord Yayul Mok treasured.
Muyaho should have been dead. Yet here it was without a scratch, calmly tilting its head at her. Yohi was certain now: she was in the afterlife.
No wonder there’s no exit.
How was she supposed to know? She had never been here before.
It felt as though a hopelessly tangled thread had finally come loose. With that moment of enlightenment, Yohi’s shoulders began to shake.
“Sniff... You fucking bastard, Heugung...”
The crisis facing Nanman? Her dignity as Great Chieftain of the Yao people?
What did any of that matter? She was dead.
The only one watching her was a half-severed tiger ghost. Then she thought of her mother, who had died twenty years ago, and tears poured down her face.
“Waaah! Waaaaah!”
At her cries, which sounded almost like a wild beast’s roar, Muyaho approached with a look that seemed to ask if she was one of its own kind. It licked away her tears.
—Grrr.
A rough tongue swept across her whole face.
Her senses did seem awfully vivid for a ghost. Then again, anyone who claimed the dead could not feel anything had probably never been to the afterlife either.
Yohi buried her face in Muyaho’s soft fur and wept.
At least, that was what she did until her hand grasped something soft and swishing.
Grab.
—Hiss!
At first, she was too busy crying to notice. Then she wondered what she had caught.
At Muyaho’s sharp cry, she raised her head and saw the long, snow-white tail in her hand.
What? It’s a tail. I thought it was something else.
Yohi buried her face in the fur again. A moment later, she lifted her head.
One fact had hit her like a blow to the back of the head.
Wait. Why does it have a tail?
Ordinarily, that would not have been strange. Tigers had tails. Even the rats infesting the Western Yao Estate’s storerooms had tails.
But moments ago, this White Tiger ghost had been floating there with only its upper body visible. Now it was whole.
Could it be?
Yohi sprang up and reached for the wall where Muyaho had first appeared.
Tap.
It was cold and hard, just as before. She could not guess its thickness, and she saw no gap.
Still, she was not ready to give up.
There’s something I don’t understand. There has to be.
With her composure returning, reason told her this was neither a dream nor the afterlife. It was something strange—something the human mind could not easily make sense of.
As though it had read her thoughts, Muyaho stopped circling her and moved.
—Grrrr.
The massive White Tiger bent its hind legs to one side. Yohi caught a hint of meaning in its clear blue-white eyes.
“You want me to ride you? On your back?”
—Grrr.
“Hah.”
She had heard it was intelligent. She had not realized just how intelligent.
Yohi studied Muyaho with fresh amazement, then carefully climbed onto its back. When she gripped its white fur, it stretched a huge forepaw toward the wall.
Clomp.
It was so enormous that a single step brought the rock wall right in front of them. Yohi squeezed her eyes shut.
Please.
The plea had barely formed when—
Swoooosh!
A strange sensation swept through her, as though she were being pulled somewhere. Yohi slowly opened her eyes.
“Ah.”
It was bright. Warm.
Light instead of darkness. Trees overflowing with life instead of cold rock walls. A place filled with every kind of flower instead of vines.
An entirely new world lay before her. For a moment, its peace and beauty made her forget everything else.
“W-What is this place...?”
Her question trailed off. This time, Muyaho gave no answer.
The white tiger shot down a path lined with plants and flowers without a moment’s hesitation.
Tap-tap. Swoooosh!

A refreshing wind scattered around them, wrapping around their entire bodies. At the same time, beyond the scenery rushing past them, countless animals of every shape and color watched them with curious eyes.
Mountain birds nested in impossibly tall trees. A roe deer and a wild boar basked together amid the thick grass. There was even a bear letting the mismatched pair lean against its body.
What in the world did I just see?
The thought vanished almost as soon as it came.
Why did none of the animals seem to care about the food chain? She did not know. It did not matter.
Here, simply by being in this place, everything felt natural.
This is... This is impossible.
The words dark arts flashed through her mind.
Then the path that had seemed to go on forever ended at a small pond.
Someone was there.
“Jin Taekyung!”
It was him.
His well-balanced, muscular body and red armor covering his upper body stood out clearly even from a distance. He was collapsed, half-submerged in the clear water.

Only a little over ten zhang remained between them. But contrary to Yohi’s desperate urgency, the White Tiger’s paws, which had moved forward without pause until now, were fixed in place as though nailed to the ground.
—Grrrr.
Its low growl sounded as though it were calling to someone.
Yohi sensed something and turned to follow its blue-white gaze.
She saw it.
No—she felt it before she saw it.
Swoooosh.
A cool wind carrying an unfamiliar energy stirred the leaves of a tree larger than any she had ever seen. Green leaves rained down.
And then—
Rustle.
Beneath the vast shade of the great tree, a Black Tiger as dark as the shadows rose to its feet.

chapters.title: Chapter 690
paragraphs: The Nanman people revered martial prowess.
Like the Han Chinese of the Central Plains, they farmed, raised livestock, and mined gold and silver from the rivers and mountains. But in the end, what mattered most to them was strength.
What good was wealth? A plentiful harvest and a pen full of livestock still had to be defended.
Warriors. And ferocious beasts capable of fighting alongside them.
They were swords to drive into an enemy’s chest and shields to protect this land.

After a long history of struggle, the Nanman people knew this well. Even after the Five Poisons Sect was destroyed and the Nanman Beast Palace was established, they devoted considerable effort to raising warriors and beasts alike.
Great tribes and small tribes were no different. Without strength, they would be pushed aside and brought to ruin.

Yohi, Great Chieftain of the Yao people and one of the leaders of Nanman’s four great tribes, thought much the same way. If anything, her ambition made her more zealous than the other tribal chieftains.

She invested the gold and silver she had received for turning a blind eye to Baeksang’s actions in her tribe’s fighting strength. She recruited talented young people and trained them as warriors. She studied the strengths and weaknesses of different beasts and even improved them through selective breeding.
But...
Rustle.
The moment that thing rose from the shade, Yohi felt her heart sink. She had faced countless ferocious beasts, yet this one struck her like a bolt of lightning through the crown of her head.
In sheer size and strength, no beast could match an elephant. As large as a small hill, it had a long, thick trunk strong enough to snap trees and sharp tusks that could pierce armor.
But that thing—that Black Tiger—was different.
Yohi felt the tremendous, overwhelming aura emanating from the black tiger, unlike anything she had seen before.
Th-This is...
It was not simply a matter of size or appearance. If an elephant was a small hill, the Black Tiger was Taishan.
It had neither an elephant’s long, thick trunk nor its sharp tusks. Yet simply standing there, it seemed powerful enough to cut through and crush anything.
Beast was not the word for it. A spiritual creature? No, that would not do either.
The Black Tiger reflected in her eyes now radiated an aura far deeper and more overwhelming than that of any spiritual creature.
What in the world is that...?
As Yohi swallowed a low groan, a cool wind flowed outward from the Black Tiger and swept over the clearing.
Swoooosh.
Grass and flowers bent in every direction, and the clear water in the small pond rippled. As the wind passed over her, a memory flashed through Yohi’s mind.
I’ve felt this wind before. Twice.

She had thought nothing of it at the time. Now she remembered: a wind like this had blown just before she lost consciousness from the pill Heugung gave her, and again when she first woke in that vast, unfamiliar space.
Then was it the Black Tiger that saved us from Heugung...?

Yohi’s eyelids trembled. But before she could speak, the Black Tiger turned away. It had been watching the unfamiliar intruder in silence, its blue-white eyes much like Muyaho’s. Now it disappeared behind the enormous tree.
Swoooosh.
The wind slowly died down.
Yohi approached the tree cautiously, but the Black Tiger was nowhere to be seen beneath its broad shade.
It had vanished like a ghost, without a trace or the faintest sign of its presence.
How?
She felt bewitched. If Muyaho had not called out just then, she might have stood there in a daze for a long time.
—Grrr.
Tap.
A damp nose touched her elbow. Yohi jerked her head up as though waking from sleep and remembered someone she had forgotten for a moment.
Jin Taekyung.
Her mind was still tangled with unanswered questions, but something more important needed her attention. She hurried to the pond and checked his condition.
A faint breath escaped his nose and mouth. Fortunately, he had only fallen into a deep sleep from accumulated fatigue. His condition was not bad.
In fact, he seemed much better than when she had last seen him.
Is it my imagination?

Yohi tilted her head and took hold of both his arms. No matter how clear the water was, his wounds would struggle to heal if it seeped into them. She meant to pull him out of the pond, where he lay half-submerged.
But just as she started to lift him—
Tap.
A snow-white forepaw came down over the back of her hand. Yohi thought she understood the gesture.
“You want me to leave him there?”
—Grrr.
“I’m sorry, but I can’t do th—”
—Grrrr!
Slash. Splash!
It happened in an instant. A sudden pain sent Yohi tumbling into the pond. She stared at the White Tiger in shock.
The back of her hand stung. Blood from the skin grazed by its sharp claws spread red across the water’s surface.
Why?
Her confusion lasted only a moment. Soon she understood why the remarkably intelligent White Tiger had done it.
Sss.
“The wound... Is it healing?”
It was. Yohi stared wide-eyed at the back of her hand beneath the clear water.
The cut flesh slowly knitted together, and the bleeding stopped. Slowly, but unmistakably. The sight was so astonishing that she forgot the pain of the wound closing.
She lifted her hand for a closer look. The flesh stopped healing, and a faint trickle of blood appeared again.
The pond. It stopped because I took my hand out.
She dipped her hand back into the water. At once, the wound began to close.
“...A pond that heals wounds.”

It sounded even more far-fetched than the legendary gongcheong seokyu, an elixir said to grant a jiazi’s worth of internal energy with a single drop. Yet Yohi was no longer surprised. She had seen it with her own eyes and felt it for herself.
This strange space could not be explained by the four words Mystic Gate Formation. Then there was the unknown Black Tiger—and the wound on her hand, already healed without a trace.
At last, she thought she understood how Muyaho had survived a sword wound to the nape of its neck.
“So that’s why you stopped me. He’ll recover faster if he stays in the pond.”
—Grrr.
Muyaho gave a faint growl and slowly licked the back of her hand.
“Then did that Black Tiger that vanished a moment ago save us? Was it the one that treated you and Jin Taekyung too?”
Muyaho nodded emphatically.
“Why? Do you know what the Black Tiger is? Who its master is? Do you know where we are?”
Muyaho hesitated, then shook its head.

Only seven days and nights ago, Muyaho had followed the Beast Miao King and Jin Taekyung to Ailao Mountain and already encountered the Black Tiger once. Yet even to an innate spiritual creature like Muyaho, the Black Tiger’s existence was an incomprehensible mystery.
“Haah. You don’t know either.”
—Whiiine.
“It’s all right.”
Yohi stroked the dejected Muyaho’s neck, though her own thoughts remained tangled. She knew too little to make sense of anything.
Where were they? How much time had passed? And when would Jin Taekyung regain consciousness?
At least one thing was certain: the unknown Black Tiger had shown them goodwill.
It has nothing to do with Dark Heaven, at least. If it did, we’d all be dead.
Her gaze settled on Jin Taekyung. He lay half-submerged, motionless as a corpse. Whether he knew anything of what was happening around him, he slept on with a perfectly peaceful expression.
If I had been the one who collapsed instead of him... If Jin Taekyung had been awake, every problem would have been solved.
Perhaps it was only a foolish thought born of desperation. Yet somewhere along the way, Yohi had come to trust him from the bottom of her heart.

He had the martial prowess to defeat two Supreme Peak masters alone, and he had compassion and a sense of what was right. She merely wore the hide of a Great Chieftain while being little better than a traitor. He had done more than anyone to save Nanman from danger.
If she could not trust him, whom could she trust?
If Baeksang and Dark Heaven have begun moving in earnest, Palace Lord Yayul won’t be able to oppose them with his strength alone. There’s not enough time.
Most of what Yohi feared was already coming to pass.

While she had no way to mark the passing time, the Beast Miao King had been branded a traitor. He had escaped the Nanman Beast Palace, now enemy territory, and vanished. All of Nanman was boiling like an iron cauldron over hot coals.
No—perhaps it was lava that would melt even the cauldron.

Warriors from every tribe that had answered the general mobilization order marched toward the Outer Palace. With their entire leadership imprisoned, the Miao people held their breath amid the chaos. And in a secret refuge known to no one, the Southern Heaven Demon Empress smiled brightly on the verge of completing her grand plan.
Yohi knew none of this. She could not have known. Trapped in this strange, unknown space, all she could do was pray.
If Heaven exists, please...
Please wake him as soon as possible. Even if I have to die, please wake at least one person from this deep sleep.
But with her eyes squeezed shut around that desperate wish, Yohi missed the tiny, unmistakable change right in front of her.
Tap.
A finger moved ever so slightly. Concentric ripples spread across the water, traveling farther and farther outward.
I dreamed.
I knew it was a dream for a simple reason. The moment I opened my eyes, I saw a face that was endlessly familiar. I heard a voice, too, one that time had slowly begun to erase from my memory.
“Oh, what got you up at this hour? Why aren’t you sleeping more?”
My throat tightened. My chest ached.
Holding back the tears that surged into my eyes, I greeted him.
It’s been a long time, Dad.
But my lips moved of their own accord, and the voice that came out was thick with sleep.
Dunno. I just woke up.
Only then did I realize I had no part to play in this dream. I could only watch an old memory unfold.
My father, who had no way of knowing that, grinned.
“You little punk, I’m touched. How did this sleepyhead know Dad was leaving for work and wake up all on his own? Huh?”
His rough fingers poked my cheek. The younger me grumbled at the teasing.
“Ah, stop it. I’m going back to sleep.”
“You punk. Why go back to sleep? The sun’s already high in the sky.”
“What time is it?”
“Six o’clock. Perfect time to start the day, isn’t it?”
“Yeah. I really don’t think so.”
The younger me buried his face in the pillow. My father laughed and got to his feet.
“Sleep, son. Dad’s off to work.”
“Huh? Already? It’s only six.”
“I have to head out of town early. Might be home late today.”
I repeated the words desperately in my head.
I can’t let him go. Dad, please don’t go. Please.
But the younger me was different. He was young and thoughtless. He had no idea that this moment would become his last memory with his father.
“Yeees. Have a good day.”
The words came out thick with sleep. My father grinned at me and ruffled my hair affectionately.
“Okay. See you later.”
That was all. My father would turn away. The door would close. A few hours later, my homeroom teacher would call me in.
That was how I remembered it.
But...
“By the way, son.”
At the sudden sound of his voice, I shot upright.
This time it was my own will—not the younger me’s, but mine, now in my late twenties.
My father tapped the watch on his wrist and spoke with a laugh in his voice.
“Shouldn’t you be getting up soon?”
At that moment—
Crack.
Everything around me shattered and fell away. The familiar ceiling. The room. My father’s face.
Something cold washed over my whole body.
Splash!
Through the spray of water scattering in every direction, I saw a woman’s wide-open eyes.
A trembling voice soon pierced my ears.
Who knows.
I muttered inwardly, like the young boy in the dream that still felt so vivid.
Dunno. I just woke up.

chapters.title: Chapter 691
paragraphs: Sometimes a dream is so wonderful, so hard to leave behind, that you don’t want to wake up. Even after you do, you keep your eyes closed a while longer, going over everything that happened in it.
But as always, things didn’t go the way I wanted.
“Jin Taekyung!”
—Grrr!
Two figures, one large and one small, rushed at me with cries that sounded almost like screams. It wasn’t hard to guess what was about to happen.
Or to prevent it.
Thwack. Splash!
I tripped Yohi and shoved away Muyaho’s drooling muzzle. Then I closed my eyes again.
“Three seconds. Just leave me alone for three seconds.”
I counted to three in my head. Very slowly. I recalled everything I’d seen in the dream, held it in my mind, and opened my eyes again.
Above me was an unfamiliar sky. I couldn’t even tell whether it was day or night.
An unfamiliar sky, huh?
That was a new one. How could the sky I saw whenever I looked up feel unfamiliar? But there it was, right in front of my eyes.
I pushed myself upright, my body throbbing.
“First, a question. You’re not about to tell me Dark Heaven took over Nanman while I was unconscious, are you?”
Soaked from her fall into the pond, Yohi stared at me in disbelief.
“That’s what you say after tripping me the moment you wake up?”
“You rushed at me the moment I opened my eyes. And look at the sky. I’d believe you if you told me this was hell.”
“What would you do if it was?”
“Who knows?”
I looked around.
A pond full of clear water. Lush trees and plants. Mountain birds chirped in the thickets surrounding us, where wild animals watched with curious eyes.
The scenery’s a little too nice for hell.
I shrugged.
“I’d already be dead. Might as well go back to sleep.”
“...Sleep? Are you out of your mind?”
“No. In fact, everything is still spinning in front of my eyes.”
It was true. Just sitting up made my whole body ache and left me dizzy.
Still...
“I do seem to be alive. Definitely.”
Yes. I’d survived again.
The pain washing over me and the System notifications ringing in my ears were proof enough.
Ding.
System You have unchecked notifications. Would you like to check the new notifications? Y / N
I was about to open the System window when I remembered something and turned my head.
Blue-white eyes shone as they watched me warily. Behind them, a tail spun like a propeller. I let out a quiet laugh.
“Yeah. I’m alive thanks to you.”
—Kraaang!
With a whoosh!
Muyaho hurled his enormous body at me as though he’d been waiting for those words.
My not-quite-healed body screamed beneath his weight, but that was all right. It was a good kind of pain. It reminded me I was alive.
Crunch.
It was starting to feel less good.

Fortunately, Muyaho’s assassination attempt—which had made me suspect he might actually be Dark Heaven—ended in failure. After confirming that my ribs were still in place, I asked what I was most curious about.
“Where’s Heugung? Why don’t I see him?”
Yohi’s face stiffened the instant I said his name.
“Don’t even mention that bastard.”
“Wait. Don’t tell me...”
“Yes. It’s what you’re thinking.”
“Heugung proposed to you?”
“What a lunatic. No matter how much he likes you, how could he propose then?”
Yohi stared at me as though I were the lunatic.
“He wasn’t the Heugung we knew. He fooled all of us.”
“I’ll say. Once he used the Bone-Shrinking Technique, he turned out to be a pretty good-looking guy.”
“...The Bone-Shrinking Technique? You knew?”
“Of course. He sent me a secret letter, and we met.”
“Then you knew Dark Heaven had planted him as a spy?”
“Of course I knew th—what?”
What had I just heard?
I thought for a moment before asking, “Is that true?”
“Do I look like I’m lying?”
Fuck. It’s true.
Only then did I remember the Quest to follow the tracking scent. Now I understood why the System had singled out Yohi by name.
“Okay. I take back what I said about Heugung being good-looking. My apologies.”
I shouldn’t have said it at all. To hell with his looks—the mood had gone cold long ago. Yohi answered with a sigh.
“It doesn’t matter. I survived thanks to you.”
“Oh, and I’m sorry about the proposal thing.”
“That’s fine. He did propose.”
“What?”
“He did. Though it was less a proposal than a threat from someone who had my life in his hands.”
“Did you... accept?”
“I’ve been meaning to ask. Are you actually fucking insane?”
“Uh, sorry. My head’s a mess. I keep saying stupid things.”
The back of my head still tingled. It was true that I had once suspected Heugung, but after running into the two old monsters in the Poisonblood Grounds, I had erased even that slight suspicion.
But Heugung, that bastard, was Dark Heaven’s lackey?
He’d been the knife in the sleeve. One last move the Southern Heaven Demon Empress had kept in reserve.
And the question that came to me again at this point was how Yohi and Muyaho had managed to avoid that move. From what Yohi had said earlier, they must have been in serious trouble.
“What happened to Heugung?”
“He’s dead.”
After a moment, she added, “Probably.”
“Probably?”
“We don’t know exactly what happened. That White Tiger was at death’s door, and I passed out because of the pill he gave me. When I woke up, I was here.”

The rest of her account was brief. They didn’t know where they were or how much time had passed outside. Muyaho had been moments from death, and I’d been severely injured. Both of us had survived thanks to this mysterious pond.
“I know. It must sound impossible. But really...”
“I get it.”
“What?”
“I get it. All of it.”
What was so hard to believe about a pond that healed wounds?
Only people of this world would be unable to understand such a phenomenon.
I had come from the modern world, where potions, Magic, monsters, and Gates existed. Even if a few Orcs crawled out from those bushes right now, I was confident I wouldn’t bat an eye.
On second thought, I might raise an eyebrow. Orcs appearing in Murim wouldn’t exactly be normal.
Unless an actual Gate opened here, like back home.
I reached out and skimmed the still surface of the pond.
Its effects were much like a potion’s. My father making an entrance like General Kim Jwa-jin couldn’t have been the only reason I’d shaken off the exhaustion in my mind and body so quickly.

Beep.
System —A mysterious power rejects the System! —The target cannot be identified!
There it was.
I’d expected as much. Everything about this place was a mystery, from one thing to the next.
And Yohi was about to give me one more.

Ailao Mountain’s Wraith...

Ding.

sentences.text: Sometimes a dream is so wonderful, so hard to leave behind, that you don’t want to wake up.
Even after you do, you keep your eyes closed a while longer, going over everything that happened in it.
But as always, things didn’t go the way I wanted.
“Jin Taekyung!”
—Grrr!
Two figures, one large and one small, rushed at me with cries that sounded almost like screams.
It wasn’t hard to guess what was about to happen.
Or to prevent it.
Thwack.
Splash!
I tripped Yohi and shoved away Muyaho’s drooling muzzle.
Then I closed my eyes again.
“Three seconds.
Just leave me alone for three seconds.”
I counted to three in my head.
Very slowly.
I recalled everything I’d seen in the dream, held it in my mind, and opened my eyes again.
Above me was an unfamiliar sky.
I couldn’t even tell whether it was day or night.
An unfamiliar sky, huh?
That was a new one.
How could the sky I saw whenever I looked up feel unfamiliar?
But there it was, right in front of my eyes.
I pushed myself upright, my body throbbing.
“First, a question.
You’re not about to tell me Dark Heaven took over Nanman while I was unconscious, are you?”
Soaked from her fall into the pond, Yohi stared at me in disbelief.
“That’s what you say after tripping me the moment you wake up?”
“You rushed at me the moment I opened my eyes.
And look at the sky.
I’d believe you if you told me this was hell.”
“What would you do if it was?”
“Who knows?”
I looked around.
A pond full of clear water.
Lush trees and plants.
Mountain birds chirped in the thickets surrounding us, where wild animals watched with curious eyes.
The scenery’s a little too nice for hell.
I shrugged.
“I’d already be dead.
Might as well go back to sleep.”
“...Sleep?
Are you out of your mind?”
“No.
In fact, everything is still spinning in front of my eyes.”
It was true.
Just sitting up made my whole body ache and left me dizzy.
Still...
“I do seem to be alive.
Definitely.”
Yes.
I’d survived again.
The pain washing over me and the System notifications ringing in my ears were proof enough.
Ding.
System You have unchecked notifications.
Would you like to check the new notifications?
Y / N
I was about to open the System window when I remembered something and turned my head.
Blue-white eyes shone as they watched me warily.
Behind them, a tail spun like a propeller.
I let out a quiet laugh.
“Yeah.
I’m alive thanks to you.”
—Kraaang!
With a whoosh!
Muyaho hurled his enormous body at me as though he’d been waiting for those words.
My not-quite-healed body screamed beneath his weight, but that was all right.
It was a good kind of pain.
It reminded me I was alive.
Crunch.
It was starting to feel less good.
Fortunately, Muyaho’s assassination attempt—which had made me suspect he might actually be Dark Heaven—ended in failure.
After confirming that my ribs were still in place, I asked what I was most curious about.
“Where’s Heugung?
Why don’t I see him?”
Yohi’s face stiffened the instant I said his name.
“Don’t even mention that bastard.”
“Wait.
Don’t tell me...”
“Yes.
It’s what you’re thinking.”
“Heugung proposed to you?”
“What a lunatic.
No matter how much he likes you, how could he propose then?”
Yohi stared at me as though I were the lunatic.
“He wasn’t the Heugung we knew.
He fooled all of us.”
“I’ll say.
Once he used the Bone-Shrinking Technique, he turned out to be a pretty good-looking guy.”
“...The Bone-Shrinking Technique?
You knew?”
“Of course.
He sent me a secret letter, and we met.”
“Then you knew Dark Heaven had planted him as a spy?”
“Of course I knew th—what?”
What had I just heard?
I thought for a moment before asking, “Is that true?”
“Do I look like I’m lying?”
Fuck.
It’s true.
Only then did I remember the Quest to follow the tracking scent.
Now I understood why the System had singled out Yohi by name.
“Okay.
I take back what I said about Heugung being good-looking.
My apologies.”
I shouldn’t have said it at all.
To hell with his looks—the mood had gone cold long ago.
Yohi answered with a sigh.
“It doesn’t matter.
I survived thanks to you.”
“Oh, and I’m sorry about the proposal thing.”
“That’s fine.
He did propose.”
“What?”
“He did.
Though it was less a proposal than a threat from someone who had my life in his hands.”
“Did you... accept?”
“I’ve been meaning to ask.
Are you actually fucking insane?”
“Uh, sorry.
My head’s a mess.
I keep saying stupid things.”
The back of my head still tingled.
It was true that I had once suspected Heugung, but after running into the two old monsters in the Poisonblood Grounds, I had erased even that slight suspicion.
But Heugung, that bastard, was Dark Heaven’s lackey?
He’d been the knife in the sleeve.
One last move the Southern Heaven Demon Empress had kept in reserve.
And the question that came to me again at this point was how Yohi and Muyaho had managed to avoid that move.
From what Yohi had said earlier, they must have been in serious trouble.
“What happened to Heugung?”
“He’s dead.”
After a moment, she added, “Probably.”
“Probably?”
“We don’t know exactly what happened.
That White Tiger was at death’s door, and I passed out because of the pill he gave me.

The rest of her account was brief.

chapters.title: Chapter 692
paragraphs: Sometimes instinct beats reason.
Like the moment I saw the Water God Dragon’s Origin Essence nestled so prettily in the Black Tiger’s mouth.
“You bastard. When did you steal that?”
The words slipped out before I could stop them.
The Black Tiger gave me a cold look, then sent a thought my way.
—“Steal” is a strong word.
It was a little strong.
Even if he really had stolen the Water God Dragon’s Origin Essence, he could swallow it whenever he wanted. Under the circumstances, I was the one who had to apologize.
“Fine. I’m sorry.”
I held out both hands politely.
“Now spit it out. You can see my palm, right? Spit it out here. Ptooey. Come on.”
—It was astonishing.
“Yeah, I’m pretty shocked too. I get it, so first, could you just...”
—I felt the power within it. Then I saw a vast stretch of time.
I stopped. “Time?”
—Yes. It was several hundred years of time and memory, visible only to beings of the same kind. Everything belonging to an imugi who had failed to become a dragon was contained within it.
—At the end of those ancient memories, there was a human. Young, rough, and endlessly reckless.
The Black Tiger’s blue-white eyes, so much like Muyaho’s, rested on me. Then another thought echoed through my mind in what sounded like a man’s calm voice.
—Be grateful to that imugi. If I had not seen his memories, you would all have met the same end as that unpleasant human.

The world was full of unpleasant humans. Turn the whole place upside down and shake them out, and there’d be enough to fill the Yangtze and then some. But I had a pretty good idea who the Black Tiger meant.
“Don’t tell me... Heugung?”
—I do not know his name. Unlike you, though, he had only one forepaw.
Technically, it was a hand. That wasn’t important right now.
I looked at the Black Tiger with fresh eyes.
“Should I start by thanking you for saving me?”
—It does not matter. It was my choice.
“Then I’ll thank you anyway. I mean it.”
The Black Tiger glanced at me, turned, and began to walk. I fell into step behind him.
“I have a few questions.”
—How tiresome.
“What? You’ll answer them all sincerely even though it’s a bother?”
—No.
“Oh. Thanks for agreeing so readily.”
—...Human communication is truly strange. Have too many years passed?
I ignored that and asked the most important question first.
“How much time has passed?”
His tail hung stiffly, plainly showing his displeasure. Still, the answer came.
—You have been here for one day, by human reckoning.
“One day?”
Ordinarily, that would be no time at all.
But under the circumstances, it was a different story.

The Great Snow Fiend and the Black Hand Fist Demon had warned of the bloodbath about to sweep Nanman. With even the Beast Miao King’s whereabouts unknown, no one was left to stop the Southern Heaven Demon Empress.
Damn it.
The situation had been unavoidable, but it wouldn’t have been strange if thousands—or tens of thousands—had died during the one day I was unconscious.
I clenched my teeth, swallowed a curse, and forced out the words.
“An exit. Tell me how to get out of here.”
—You intend to leave?
“Yeah. I’m grateful you saved me, but I can’t waste any more time.”
—You intend to save your own kind from danger. Recklessly, as you did before.
—Do not worry. I cannot read human memories. I saw you in the imugi’s memories and made a guess. I imagine you fought so fiercely for much the same reason.
“...You were watching?”
—Yes. From beginning to end. As always, I watched everything that happened here.
The Black Tiger turned his head toward me, his thoughts as calm as ever.
—But I saw no reason to involve myself in human affairs. Not until you brought out that.
My eyes widened. Not because I knew he meant the Water God Dragon’s Origin Essence.

I remembered reaching for the Origin Essence in one last desperate attempt to stay alive—only to hesitate when a chill wind blew in from somewhere. At the same time, I sensed something strange and let go of the Origin Essence. Muyaho arrived immediately afterward and saved my life.
“Then that wind...”
My voice trailed off. The Black Tiger’s answer sounded in my head.
—You were about to do something foolish. If you defy what is ordained, that is defying Heaven. Had I done nothing, you would have died, unable to overcome the power left behind by the imugi.
I watched him walk along the endless cliff.
“Not once, but twice.”
—What do you mean?
“You saved me twice.”
The Black Tiger gave a small snort.
—I merely felt sorry for someone who had handed everything they possessed to a foolish human. Without that reason, you deserved to die.
“That’s a little unfair. I don’t know why you hate humans, but I’ve never done anything bad enough to deserve that.”
—Even after you tried to take innocent lives and set fire to their peaceful home?
“What?”
Instead of answering, the Black Tiger nodded toward the foot of the cliff.

Countless beasts, their bodies blackened in places, drank from an unfamiliar stream. There were thousands of them by my rough estimate. With all the others that might be sheltering somewhere in this seemingly boundless place, I couldn’t begin to guess the total.
What the hell...?
I stood on the cliff, staring down at them.
—The inferno you unleashed is still devouring the entire mountain. If the flames had spread unchecked, everything would have burned away long ago.
—Yes, I led them here. Just as I did seven days and nights ago.
Seven days and nights ago.
That had been the very day the Beast Miao King and I received the emergency report and headed for Ailao Mountain.
I searched my memory, and realization struck.
The beasts.
I remembered clearly. Of the three hundred or so warriors stationed at Ailao Mountain, about two hundred had returned alive.
The beasts hadn’t.
I hadn’t seen them anywhere—not on Ailao Mountain, not in the Poisonblood Grounds.
“You were the one who did that too. You saved the wild beasts.”
—Monsters that should never have been there were set loose. I had not interfered in human affairs for hundreds of years, but that time I could not stand aside.
Ordinarily, I might have let that pass. But I was listening closely to the Black Tiger’s thoughts, and I caught the oddity at once.
“Set loose?”
—You did not know?
Faint contempt entered his blue-white eyes.
—Humans did all of it. Your kind has done such things since long ago, and I have remained here and watched.
Damn it.
I’d only been able to guess what had happened at Ailao Mountain. Now the Black Tiger had confirmed it.
Dark Heaven had been behind that, too.
If only we’d found out a little sooner.

With belated regret, I looked at the Black Tiger. I thought I was beginning to understand why he had acted that way that day. I remembered his back as he repeatedly appeared and disappeared, even though he could have escaped at any time.
“You weren’t attacking us that day.”
—Yes. That was not my mission.
“You were trying to show us where the Thousand-Year Spider was.”
—I could not simply watch while a foul monster disturbed this mountain. Humans planted the seed, so humans should reap it. That is the natural order.
He walked on. The path along the cliff grew narrower and steeper, and birds nesting on rugged peaks above the clouds watched us with curious eyes.
How long had we been walking? Clouds and mist surrounded us, and the ground below seemed impossibly far away.
I’m sure this place wasn’t this big.
When I first woke, I’d thought it was a forest around a small pond. Now I could see vast mountain ranges, valleys, and green pastures.
What the hell is this place?
I could no longer begin to guess. Staring at the impossible landscape, I finally asked, “Where are we?”
—A land filled with life. A place where all things live in harmony.
What kind of nonsense was that?
For some reason, I remembered the church deacon who used to give me spicy rice cakes when I was little while shouting, “Jesus, heaven! Unbelievers, hell!”
“Even so, this can’t be heaven.”
—The kingdom of heaven? A fitting description, in its way. But this place lies deep within the land, where no one can enter without my permission. It is very close to where you were.
“Then... are we in the Poisonblood Grounds?”
A few paces ahead, the Black Tiger gave a small nod.
—It is.
“But this place...”
The words stuck in my throat. The Poisonblood Grounds?
I wouldn’t have believed we were anywhere on Ailao Mountain. There were no raging flames here, none of the eerie feeling that hung over the mountain.
—Enough. This is a place that you humans can neither invade nor understand.
He was right. Murim had all manner of strange things, Mystic Gate Formations among them, but what lay before me went far beyond anything they could do.
“Ha. The Poisonblood Grounds. This is the Poisonblood Grounds.”
Laughing hollowly, I followed him up the peak.
As we neared the summit, his thought reached me again.
—Poisonblood Grounds is its current name. As I did, humans changed many things over the passage of time.
“What was it called before?”
—The Sacred Land.
“What?”
—That was in a past as distant as the imugi’s memories. Beasts, not humans, ruled this land then. The few humans lived in groups within their own territories and worshiped us.
“Huh.”
I had no words.
This forbidden place, where no one could set foot, had once been called the Sacred Land. And if there had been so few people in Nanman back then... how long ago was that?
Five hundred years? A thousand?
This is driving me crazy.
Even if I’d put every point into Intelligence from the start, I’d have felt like an idiot right now.
I shook my head and opened my mouth toward the Black Tiger, who had stopped walking before I noticed.
“Then you. What exactly are you?”
—Did you not call me an apparition yourself?
“I’m asking what they called you when this place was the Sacred Land.”
The Black Tiger was silent for a moment before moving his massive body. Something wistful passed through his blue-white eyes.
—A guardian spirit.
“What?”
—Long ago, that was what people called me. The mountain lord who guarded Ailao Mountain. A guardian spirit born alongside the sacred stone.
